title: Artificial intelligence, or AI
one_liner: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is concerned with building systems that simulate intelligent behavior.
content: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is concerned with building systems that simulate intelligent behavior. It encompasses a wide range of approaches, including those based on logic, search, and probabilistic reasoning. Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns to
motivation_md: Artificial intelligence aims to build systems that can simulate intelligent behavior, enabling machines to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence.
recap_md:
- Artificial intelligence (AI) builds systems simulating intelligent behavior.
- AI includes approaches based on logic, search, and probabilistic reasoning.
- Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns from data.

title: Machine learning
one_liner: Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns to make decisions by fitting mathematical models to observed data.
content: Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns to make decisions by fitting mathematical models to observed data. This area has seen explosive growth and is now (incorrectly) almost synonymous with the term AI.
motivation_md: Machine learning exists to enable systems to learn from data and improve decision-making without explicit programming.
recap_md:
- Machine learning fits mathematical models to data to make decisions.
- It is a subset of AI.
- Machine learning has grown rapidly and is often (incorrectly) equated with AI.

title: deep neural network (or deep network for short)
one_liner: A deep neural network (or deep network for short) is a type of machine learning model.
content: A deep neural network (or deep network for short) is a type of machine learning model, and the process of fitting these models to data is referred to as deep learning. At the time of writing, deep networks are the most powerful and practical machine learning
motivation_md: Deep neural networks provide powerful models capable of learning complex patterns from data, making them central to modern machine learning.
recap_md:
- Deep neural networks are a type of machine learning model.
- Training these models is called deep learning.
- Deep networks are currently the most powerful and practical machine learning models.

title: deep learning

content: Deep learning is the process of fitting deep neural network models to data. At the time of writing, deep networks are the most powerful and practical machine learning

title: Supervised learning
one_liner: Supervised learning models define a mapping from input data to an output prediction.
content: Supervised learning models define a mapping from input data to an output prediction. In the following sections, we discuss the inputs, the outputs, the model itself, and what is meant by “training” a model.
motivation_md: Supervised learning exists to create models that can predict outputs from inputs based on labeled training data.
recap_md:
- Supervised learning maps input data to output predictions.
- It involves defining inputs, outputs, and the model.
- Training a model means adjusting it to fit data.

title: regression problem
one_liner: A regression problem involves predicting a continuous number based on input characteristics.
content: The model in figure 1.2a predicts the price of a house based on input characteristics such as the square footage and the number of bedrooms. This is a regression problem because the model returns a continuous number (rather than a category assignment).
motivation_md: Regression problems address tasks where the goal is to predict continuous numerical values from input features.
recap_md:
- Regression problems predict continuous numerical outputs.
- Example: predicting house price from features like size and bedrooms.
- Outputs are numbers, not categories.

title: multivariate regression problem
one_liner: A multivariate regression problem predicts more than one continuous number from input data.
content: In contrast, the model in figure 1.2b takes the chemical structure of a molecule as an input and predicts both the freezing and boiling points. This is a multivariate regression problem since it predicts more than one number.
motivation_md: Multivariate regression problems extend regression to predict multiple continuous outputs simultaneously.
recap_md:
- Multivariate regression predicts multiple continuous outputs.
- Example: predicting freezing and boiling points from molecular structure.
- It outputs more than one number.

title: binary classification problem
one_liner: A binary classification problem assigns inputs to one of two categories.
content: The model in figure 1.2c receives a text string containing a restaurant review as input and predicts whether the review is positive or negative. This is a binary classification problem because the model attempts to assign the input to one of two categories. The output vector contains the probabilities that the input belongs to each category. Fig-
motivation_md: Binary classification problems solve tasks where inputs must be categorized into one of two classes, such as sentiment analysis.
recap_md:
- Binary classification assigns inputs to two categories.
- Example: predicting if a restaurant review is positive or negative.
- Outputs are probabilities for each category.

title: multiclass classification problems
one_liner: Multiclass classification problems assign the input to one of N > 2 categories, returning a vector of size N with probabilities for each category.
content: Figures 1.2d and 1.2e depict multiclass classification problems. Here, the model assigns the input to one of N > 2 categories. In the first case, the input is an audio file, and the model predicts which genre of music it contains. In the second case, the input is an image, and the model predicts which object it contains. In each case, the model returns a vector of size N that contains the probabilities of the N categories.
motivation_md: Multiclass classification problems arise when inputs must be categorized into more than two classes, requiring models to output probabilities across multiple categories.
recap_md:
- Multiclass classification assigns inputs to one of N > 2 categories.
- The model outputs a vector of size N with category probabilities.
- Examples include predicting music genre from audio or object type from images.

title: tabular data
one_liner: Tabular data consists of fixed-length vectors with no internal structure, where changing input order does not affect model predictions.
content: The input data in figure 1.2 varies widely. In the house pricing example, the input is a fixed-length vector containing values that characterize the property. This is an example of tabular data because it has no internal structure; if we change the order of the inputs and build a new model, then we expect the model prediction to remain the same.
motivation_md: Tabular data represents structured inputs without internal order, simplifying modeling since input permutations do not affect predictions.
recap_md:
- Tabular data is a fixed-length vector describing features.
- It has no internal structure or order.
- Model predictions remain the same if input order changes.

title: importance of input order in text data
aliases: importance of word order in text
one_liner: Order is important in text data; for example, "my wife ate the chicken" differs from "the chicken ate my wife."
content: Order is important; "my wife ate the chicken" is not the same as "the chicken ate my wife." The text must be encoded into numerical form before passing it to the model. Here, we use a fixed vocabulary of size 10,000 and simply concatenate the word indices.
motivation_md: Text data requires preserving word order because meaning depends on sequence, so models must encode text numerically respecting this order.
recap_md:
- Word order affects meaning in text data.
- "My wife ate the chicken" differs from "the chicken ate my wife."
- Text is encoded numerically using a fixed vocabulary and concatenated word indices.

title: high-dimensional audio input representation
one_liner: Digital audio input is very high-dimensional, e.g., a 10-second clip sampled at 44.1 kHz contains 441,000 integers.
content: A 10-second clip is very high-dimensional (i.e., contains many entries). Digital audio is usually sampled at 44.1 kHz and represented by 16-bit integers, so a ten-second clip consists of 441,000 integers. Clearly, supervised learning models will have to be able to handle such high-dimensional inputs.
motivation_md: Audio data is high-dimensional due to high sampling rates and bit depth, challenging models to process large input vectors effectively.
recap_md:
- Digital audio is sampled at 44.1 kHz with 16-bit integers.
- A 10-second clip contains 441,000 integers.
- Audio inputs are very high-dimensional for models to process.

title: spatial structure in image input data
one_liner: Image input data contains spatial structure; pixels close vertically are related even if not adjacent in the input vector.
content: The concatenated RGB values at every pixel produce an enormous input vector. Moreover, it contains spatial structure; two pixels above and below one another are closely related, even if they are not adjacent in the input vector.
motivation_md: Images have spatial relationships between pixels that models must consider, unlike unstructured input vectors.
recap_md:
- Image inputs are large vectors of concatenated RGB pixel values.
- Pixels vertically adjacent are closely related.
- Spatial structure exists despite non-adjacency in input vectors.

title: variable geometric structure in molecule input
one_liner: Molecules have varying numbers of atoms and connections, requiring models to ingest both geometric structure and constituent atoms.
content: Finally, consider the input for the model that predicts the freezing and boiling points of the molecule. A molecule may contain varying numbers of atoms that can be connected in different ways. In this case, the model must ingest both the geometric structure of the molecule and the constituent atoms to the model.
motivation_md: Molecular inputs vary in size and structure, so models must handle variable geometric and atomic information to make predictions.
recap_md:
- Molecules vary in atom count and connectivity.
- Models must ingest geometric structure and constituent atoms.
- This variability complicates input representation for models.

title: machine learning model
one_liner: A machine learning model maps an input vector to an output vector, such as predicting a child's height from their age.
content: A machine learning model takes a vector and returns an output vector. But what exactly is in this black box? Consider a model to predict the height of a child from their age (figure 1.3). The machine learning model represents a family of equations mapping input to output, and training selects the best equation.
motivation_md: Machine learning models formalize the process of mapping inputs to outputs, enabling predictions such as estimating height from age.
recap_md:
- A model maps input vectors to output vectors.
- Example: predicting child height from age.
- The model represents a family of equations chosen during training.

title: model training as search over family of functions
one_liner: Training a model means searching through a family of equations to find the one that best fits the training data.
content: More precisely, the model represents a family of equations mapping the input to the output (i.e., a family of different cyan curves). The particular equation (curve) is chosen using training data (examples of input/output pairs). In figure 1.3, these pairs are represented by the orange points, and we can see that the model (cyan line) describes these data reasonably. When we talk about training or fitting a model, we mean that we search through the family of possible equations (possible cyan curves) relating input to output to find the one that describes the training data most accurately.
motivation_md: Model training is the process of selecting the best function from a family of possible mappings to accurately represent the training data.
recap_md:
- The model represents a family of input-output equations.
- Training selects the equation that best fits the data.
- This search is done using input/output training pairs.

one_liner: This is known as overfitting when a model describes statistical peculiarities of the training data that are atypical and lead to unusual predictions.
content: A model may describe statistical peculiarities of the training data that are atypical and lead to unusual predictions. This is known as overfitting.

title: Shallow neural networks
one_liner: Shallow neural networks describe piecewise linear functions and are expressive enough to approximate arbitrarily complex relationships between multi-dimensional inputs and outputs.
content: Chapter 2 introduced supervised learning using 1D linear regression. However, this model can only describe the input/output relationship as a line. This chapter introduces shallow neural networks. These describe piecewise linear functions and are expressive enough to approximate arbitrarily complex relationships between multi-dimensional inputs and outputs.
motivation_md: Shallow neural networks extend simple linear models to capture more complex, piecewise linear relationships in multi-dimensional data, enabling better function approximation.
recap_md:
- Shallow neural networks extend 1D linear regression models.
- They describe piecewise linear functions.
- They can approximate complex relationships between multi-dimensional inputs and outputs.

title: universal approximation theorem
one_liner: The universal approximation theorem states that a shallow network with enough hidden units can approximate any continuous 1D function on a compact subset to arbitrary precision.
content:
Universal approximation theorem

In the previous section, we introduced an example neural network with one input, one output, ReLU activation functions, and three hidden units. Let’s now generalize this slightly and consider the case with D hidden units where the dth hidden unit is:
\[ h_d = a[\theta_{d0} + \theta_{d1} x], \]
(3.5)
and these are combined linearly to create the output:
\[ y = \phi_0 + \sum_{d=1}^D \phi_d h_d. \]
(3.6)
The number of hidden units in a shallow network is a measure of the network capacity. With ReLU activation functions, the output of a network with D hidden units has at most D joints and so is a piecewise linear function with at most D + 1 linear regions. As we add more hidden units, the model can approximate more complex functions.
Indeed, with enough capacity (hidden units), a shallow network can describe any continuous 1D function defined on a compact subset of the real line to arbitrary precision. To see this, consider that every time we add a hidden unit, we add another linear region to the function. As these regions become more numerous, they represent smaller sections of the function, which are increasingly well approximated by a line (figure 3.5). The universal approximation theorem proves that for any continuous function, there exists a shallow network that can approximate this function to any specified precision.
motivation_md: The theorem shows shallow networks can approximate any continuous function with enough hidden units, explaining their power in function approximation.
recap_md:
- Shallow networks with D hidden units produce piecewise linear functions with up to D + 1 regions.
- Adding hidden units increases model capacity and function complexity.
- The universal approximation theorem guarantees approximation of any continuous 1D function on a compact set.

title: structure of the book
one_liner: Chapters 2–9 walk through the supervised learning pipeline, describing shallow and deep neural networks, training, and performance measurement.
content: The structure of the book follows the structure of this introduction. Chapters 2–9 walk through the supervised learning pipeline. We describe shallow and deep neural networks and discuss how to train them and measure and improve their performance. Chapters 10–13 describe common architectural variations of deep neural networks, including convolutional networks, residual connections, and transformers. These architectures are used across supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. Chapters 14–18 tackle unsupervised learning using deep neural networks. We devote a chapter each to four modern deep generative models: generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, normalizing flows, and diffusion models. Chapter 19 is a brief introduction to deep reinforcement learning. This is a topic that easily justifies its own book, so the treatment is necessarily superficial. However, this treatment is intended to be a good starting point for readers unfamiliar with this area. Despite the title of this book, some aspects of deep learning remain poorly understood. Chapter 20 poses some fundamental questions. Why are deep networks so easy to train? Why do they generalize so well? Why do they need to be so large? Do they need to be deep? Along the way, we explore unexpected phenomena such as the structure of the loss function, double descent, grokking, and lottery tickets. The book concludes with chapter 21, which discusses ethics and deep learning.
motivation_md: This structure guides readers through the supervised learning pipeline, architectural variations, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and fundamental questions about deep learning, ending with ethics.
recap_md:
- Chapters 2–9 cover supervised learning and neural networks.
- Chapters 10–13 discuss deep network architectures like convolutional and transformer networks.
- Later chapters explore unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and fundamental deep learning questions.

title: recommended books for machine learning and related topics
one_liner: For a broader look at machine learning, the most up-to-date and encyclopedic resource is Probabilistic Machine Learning (Murphy, 2022, 2023).
content: This book is self-contained but is limited to coverage of deep learning. It is intended to be the spiritual successor to Deep Learning (Goodfellow et al., 2016) which is a fantastic resource but does not cover recent advances. For a broader look at machine learning, the most up-to-date and encyclopedic resource is Probabilistic Machine Learning (Murphy, 2022, 2023). However, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Bishop, 2006) is still an excellent and relevant book. If you enjoy this book, then my previous volume, Computer Vision: Models, Learning, and Inference (Prince, 2012), is still worth reading. Some parts have dated badly, but it contains a thorough introduction to probability, including Bayesian methods, and good introductory coverage of latent variable models, geometry for computer vision, Gaussian processes, and graphical models. It uses identical notation to this book and can be found online. A detailed treatment of graphical models can be found in Probabilistic Graphical Models: Principles and Techniques (Koller & Friedman, 2009), and Gaussian processes are covered by Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (Williams & Rasmussen, 2006). For background mathematics, consult Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth et al., 2020). For a more coding-oriented approach, consult Dive into Deep Learning (Zhang et al., 2023). The best overviews for computer vision are Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications (Szeliski, 2022), and Foundations of Computer Vision (Torralba et al., 2024). A good starting point to learn about graph neural networks is Graph Representation Learning (Hamilton, 2020). motivation_md: This list helps readers find comprehensive and specialized resources for deep learning, machine learning, computer vision, and reinforcement learning beyond this book.
recap_md:
- Probabilistic Machine Learning (Murphy, 2022, 2023) is the most up-to-date broad resource.
- Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Bishop, 2006) remains relevant.
- Specialized books cover graphical models, Gaussian processes, and reinforcement learning.

title: Supervised learning model
one_liner: A supervised learning model defines a mapping from one or more inputs to one or more outputs.
content:
Supervised learning
A supervised learning model defines a mapping from one or more inputs to one or more outputs. For example, the input might be the age and mileage of a second-hand Toyota Prius, and the output might be the estimated value of the car in dollars. The model is just a mathematical function (i.e., an equation); when the inputs are passed through this function, it computes the output, and this is termed inference. The model equation also contains parameters. Different parameter values change the outcome of the computation; the model equation describes a family of possible relationships between inputs and outputs, and the parameters specify the particular relationship. When we train or learn a model, we find parameters that describe the true relationship between inputs and outputs. A learning algorithm takes a training set of input/output pairs and manipulates the parameters until the inputs predict their corresponding outputs as closely as possible. If the model works well for these training pairs, then we hope it will make good predictions for new inputs where the true output is unknown.
motivation_md: Supervised learning models formalize how inputs map to outputs, enabling prediction and learning from data pairs.
recap_md:
- A supervised learning model maps inputs to outputs.
- The model is a function with parameters that define the relationship.
- Training adjusts parameters to predict outputs from inputs accurately.

title: inference
one_liner: When the inputs are passed through a model function, it computes the output, and this is termed inference.
content: Passed through this function, it computes the output, and this is termed inference. The model equation also contains parameters. Different parameter values change the outcome of the computation.
motivation_md: Inference is the process of computing outputs from inputs using the model function with given parameters.
recap_md:
- Inference means computing the output by passing inputs through the model function.
- The model function depends on parameters that affect the output.

title: loss
one_liner: We quantify the degree of mismatch in this mapping with the loss L, a scalar summarizing how poorly the model predicts training outputs from inputs for parameters ϕ.
content: As possible. We quantify the degree of mismatch in this mapping with the loss L. This is a scalar value that summarizes how poorly the model predicts the training outputs from their corresponding inputs for parameters ϕ.

content:
A 1D linear regression model describes the relationship between input x and output y as a straight line:
$$
y = f[x, \phi] = \phi_0 + \phi_1 x.
$$
motivation_md: This model captures linear relationships between a single input and output using parameters defining a line.
recap_md:

- The model equation is $y = \phi_0 + \phi_1 x$.

content: Since the best parameters minimize this expression, we call this a least-squares loss. The squaring operation means that the direction of the deviation (i.e., whether the line is

title: model fitting, training, or learning
one_liner: The process of finding parameters that minimize the loss is termed model fitting, training, or learning.
content: The process of finding parameters that minimize the loss is termed model fitting, training, or learning. The basic method is to choose the initial parameters randomly and then improve them by “walking down” the loss function until we reach the bottom (figure 2.4). One way to do this is to measure the gradient of the surface at the current position and take a step in the direction that is most steeply downhill. Then we repeat this process until the gradient is flat and we can improve no further.2
motivation_md: Training adjusts model parameters to minimize loss by iteratively descending the loss surface, improving predictions.
recap_md:
- Model training finds parameters minimizing the loss.
- Gradient descent iteratively updates parameters downhill on the loss surface.
- The process stops when improvements cease (gradient is flat).

title: Line search using the bracketing approach
one_liner: Line search using the bracketing approach involves evaluating the loss function at interior points and eliminating regions to closely bracket the minimum.
content: Figure 6.10 Line search using the bracketing approach. a) The current solution is at position a (orange point), and we wish to search the region [a, d] (gray shaded area). We define two points b, c interior to the search region and evaluate the loss function at these points. Here L[b] > L[c], so we eliminate the range [a, b]. b) We now repeat this procedure in the refined search region and find that L[b] < L[c], so we eliminate the range [c, d]. c) We repeat this process until this minimum is closely bracketed.
motivation_md: This approach helps efficiently narrow down the search for a minimum by iteratively eliminating regions where the loss is higher, focusing the search on promising intervals.
recap_md:
- The method evaluates loss at two interior points in the search region.
- It eliminates the subregion where the loss is higher.
- This process repeats until the minimum is closely bracketed.

title: Adaptive training algorithms
one_liner: Adaptive training algorithms assign different learning rates to parameters and adjust them based on accumulated gradient statistics to improve optimization.
content: Adaptive training algorithms: AdaGrad (Duchi et al., 2011) is an optimization algorithm that addresses the possibility that some parameters may have to move further than others by assigning a different learning rate to each parameter. AdaGrad uses the cumulative squared gradient for each parameter to attenuate its learning rate. This has the disadvantage that the learning rates decrease over time, and learning can halt before the minimum is found. RMSProp (Hinton et al., 2012a) and AdaDelta (Zeiler, 2012) modified this algorithm to help prevent these problems by recursively updating the squared gradient term. By far the most widely used adaptive training algorithm is adaptive moment optimization or Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015). This combines the ideas of momentum (in which the gradient vector is averaged over time) and AdaGrad, AdaDelta, and RMSProp (in which a smoothed squared gradient term is used to modify the learning rate for each parameter). The original paper on the Adam algorithm provided a convergence proof for convex loss functions, but a counterexample was identified by Reddi et al. (2018), who developed a modification of Adam called AMSGrad, which does converge. Of course, in deep learning, the loss functions are non-convex, and Zaheer et al. (2018) subsequently developed an adaptive algorithm called YOGI and proved that it converges in this scenario. Regardless of these theoretical objections, the original Adam algorithm works well in practice and is widely used, not least because it works well over a broad range of hyperparameters and makes rapid initial progress. One potential problem with adaptive training algorithms is that the learning rates are based on accumulated statistics of the observed gradients. At the start of training, when there are few samples, these statistics may be very noisy. This can be remedied by learning rate warm-up (Goyal et al., 2018), in which the learning rates are gradually increased over the first few thousand iterations. An alternative solution is rectified Adam (Liu et al., 2021a), which gradually changes the momentum term over time in a way that helps avoid high variance. Dozat (2016) incorporated Nesterov momentum into the Adam algorithm.
motivation_md: Adaptive training algorithms exist to assign appropriate learning rates to parameters that may require different update scales, improving convergence and stability during training.
recap_md:
- AdaGrad assigns different learning rates per parameter but can cause learning rates to decrease too much.
- RMSProp and AdaDelta modify AdaGrad to prevent learning rate decay.
- Adam combines momentum and adaptive learning rates and is widely used despite some theoretical issues.

title: SGD vs. Adam
one_liner: SGD with momentum can find lower minima than Adam, but Adam often converges faster and performs well with tuned hyperparameters.
content: SGD vs. Adam: There has been a lively discussion about the relative merits of SGD and Adam. Wilson et al. (2017) provided evidence that SGD with momentum can find lower minima than Adam, which generalizes better over a variety of deep learning tasks. However, this is strange since SGD is a special case of Adam (when β = 0, γ →1) once the modification term (equation 6.16) becomes one, which happens quickly. It is hence more likely that SGD outperforms Adam when we use Adam’s default hyperparameters. Loshchilov & Hutter (2019) proposed AdamW, which substantially improves the performance of Adam in the presence of L2 regularization (see section 9.1). Choi et al. (2019) provide evidence that if we search for the best Adam hyperparameters, it performs just as well as SGD and converges faster. Keskar & Socher (2017) proposed a method called SWATS that starts using Adam (to make rapid initial progress) and then switches to SGD (to get better final generalization performance).
motivation_md: Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of SGD and Adam helps select the best optimizer for different deep learning tasks and training goals.
recap_md:
- SGD with momentum can find lower minima and generalize better than Adam.
- Adam is a generalization of SGD and often converges faster.
- Hybrid methods like SWATS combine Adam's speed with SGD's generalization.

title: Exhaustive search
one_liner: Exhaustive search quantizes network parameters and searches the discretized space to find the global minimum, practical only for very small models.
content: Exhaustive search: All the algorithms discussed in this chapter are iterative. A completely different approach is to quantize the network parameters and exhaustively search the resulting discretized parameter space using SAT solvers (Mézard & Mora, 2009). This approach has the potential to find the global minimum and provide a guarantee that there is no lower loss elsewhere but is only practical for very small models.
motivation_md: Exhaustive search provides a guarantee of finding the global minimum by exploring all discretized parameter configurations, useful for small models where iterative methods might fail.
recap_md:
- Exhaustive search quantizes parameters and searches all combinations.
- It can find the global minimum with guarantees.
- Practical only for very small models due to combinatorial explosion.

title: backpropagation algorithm
one_liner: The backpropagation algorithm efficiently computes derivatives needed for training.
content: The batch. The first part of this chapter describes the backpropagation algorithm, which computes these derivatives efficiently.
motivation_md: Efficient computation of derivatives is essential for training neural networks using gradient-based methods.

title: latent variables
one_liner: Some generative models exploit that data can be lower dimensional than the raw number of observed variables suggests.
content: Some (but not all) generative models exploit the fact that data can be lower dimensional than the raw number of observed variables suggests. For example, the number of valid and meaningful English sentences is much smaller than the number of strings created by drawing words at random. Similarly, real-world images are a tiny subset of the images that can be created by drawing random red, green, and blue (RGB) values for every pixel. This is because images are generated by physical processes (see figure 1.9). This leads to the idea that we can describe each data example using a smaller number of underlying latent variables. Here, the role of deep learning is to describe the mapping between these latent variables and the data. The latent variables typically have a simple
motivation_md: Latent variables help represent complex, high-dimensional data with fewer underlying factors, enabling models to capture essential structure more efficiently.
recap_md:
- Latent variables represent lower-dimensional underlying factors in data.
- Real-world data like images and sentences occupy a small subset of possible raw combinations.
- Deep learning maps latent variables to observed high-dimensional data.

title: latent variable sampling and interpolation
one_liner: Many generative models use a deep learning model to describe the relationship between a low-dimensional latent variable and the observed high-dimensional data.
content:
Figure 1.10 Latent variables. Many generative models use a deep learning model to describe the relationship between a low-dimensional “latent” variable and the observed high-dimensional data. The latent variables have a simple probability distribution by design. Hence, new examples can be generated by sampling from the simple distribution over the latent variables and then using the deep learning model to map the sample to the observed data space.
Figure 1.11 Image interpolation. In each row the left and right images are real and the three images in between represent a sequence of interpolations created by a generative model. The generative models that underpin these interpolations have learned that all images can be created by a set of underlying latent variables. By finding these variables for the two real images, interpolating their values, and then using these intermediate variables to create new images, we can generate intermediate results that are both visually plausible and mix the characteristics of the two original images. Top row adapted from Sauer et al. (2022). Bottom row adapted from Ramesh et al. (2022).
motivation_md: Latent variable models enable generating new data by sampling from a simple distribution and mapping to complex observed data, allowing interpolation between examples.
recap_md:
- Latent variables have simple probability distributions.
- New data can be generated by sampling latent variables and mapping them.
- Interpolations between latent variables produce plausible intermediate data.

title: latent variables connecting supervised and unsupervised learning
one_liner: Generative models with latent variables can benefit supervised learning models where the outputs have structure.
content:
Connecting supervised and unsupervised learning
Generative models with latent variables can also benefit supervised learning models where the outputs have structure (figure 1.4). For example, consider learning to predict the images corresponding to a caption. Rather than directly map the text input to an image, we can learn a relation between latent variables that explain the text and the latent variables that explain the image.
This has three advantages. First, we may need fewer text/image pairs to learn this mapping now that the inputs and outputs are lower dimensional. Second, we are more likely to generate a plausible-looking image; any sensible values of the latent variables should produce something that looks like a plausible example. Third, if we introduce randomness to either the mapping between the two sets of latent variables or the mapping from the latent variables to the image, then we can generate multiple images that are all described well by the caption (figure 1.12).
motivation_md: Using latent variables in supervised learning reduces dimensionality, improves plausibility of outputs, and allows generating diverse outputs from the same input.
recap_md:
- Latent variables connect structured inputs and outputs in supervised learning.
- Reduces data needed by lowering dimensionality.
- Enables generating multiple plausible outputs via randomness.

title: reinforcement learning
one_liner: Reinforcement learning involves an agent choosing actions to maximize rewards in a changing environment.
content: The final area of machine learning is reinforcement learning. This paradigm introduces the idea of an agent which lives in a world and can perform certain actions at each time step. The actions change the state of the system but not necessarily in a deterministic way. Taking an action can also produce rewards, and the goal of reinforcement learning is for the agent to learn to choose actions that lead to high rewards on average.
motivation_md: Reinforcement learning models how agents learn to make decisions to maximize rewards in uncertain, changing environments.
recap_md:
- Reinforcement learning involves an agent acting in an environment.
- Actions change the state, often nondeterministically.
- The goal is to learn actions that maximize expected rewards.

title: temporal credit assignment problem
one_liner: The reward may occur some time after the action is taken, so associating a reward with an action is not straightforward.
content: One complication is that the reward may occur some time after the action is taken, so associating a reward with an action is not straightforward. This is known as the temporal credit assignment problem.
motivation_md: Rewards delayed in time make it difficult to identify which actions caused them, complicating learning.
recap_md:
- Rewards can be delayed after actions.
- It is challenging to assign credit to specific actions.
- This challenge is called the temporal credit assignment problem.

title: exploration-exploitation trade-off
one_liner: The agent must trade off exploration and exploitation of what it already knows.
content: Temporal credit assignment problem. As the agent learns, it must trade off exploration and exploitation of what it already knows; perhaps the agent has already learned how to receive modest rewards; should it follow this strategy (exploit what it knows), or should it try different actions to see if it can improve (explore other opportunities)?
motivation_md: Balancing exploration of new actions and exploitation of known rewards is key to effective learning in reinforcement learning.
recap_md:
- Agents face a trade-off between exploration and exploitation.
- Exploitation uses known strategies for rewards.
- Exploration tries new actions to find better rewards.

title: examples illustrating reinforcement learning challenges
one_liner: Examples illustrate challenges like temporal credit assignment and exploration-exploitation trade-off in reinforcement learning.
content:
Two examples
Consider teaching a humanoid robot to locomote. The robot can perform a limited number of actions at a given time (moving various joints), and these change the state of the world (its pose). We might reward the robot for reaching checkpoints in an obstacle course. To reach each checkpoint, it must perform many actions, and it’s unclear which ones contributed to the reward when it is received and which were irrelevant. This is an example of the temporal credit assignment problem.
A second example is learning to play chess. Again, the agent has a set of valid actions (chess moves) at any given time. However, these actions change the state of the system in a non-deterministic way; for any choice of action, the opposing player might respond with many different moves. Here, we might set up a reward structure based on capturing pieces or just have a single reward at the end of the game for winning. In the latter case, the temporal credit assignment problem is extreme; the system must learn which of the many moves it made were instrumental to success or failure.
The exploration-exploitation trade-off is also apparent in these two examples. The robot may have discovered that it can make progress by lying on its side and pushing with one leg. This strategy will move the robot and yields rewards, but much more slowly than the optimal solution: to balance on its legs and walk. So, it faces a choice between exploiting what it already knows (how to slide along the floor awkwardly) and exploring the space of actions (which might result in much faster locomotion). Similarly, in the chess example, the agent may learn a reasonable sequence of opening moves. Should it exploit this knowledge or explore different opening sequences?
motivation_md: These examples demonstrate key reinforcement learning challenges: delayed rewards complicating credit assignment and the need to balance exploration with exploitation.
recap_md:
- Robot locomotion illustrates temporal credit assignment problem.
- Chess shows nondeterministic state changes and delayed rewards.
- Both examples highlight exploration-exploitation trade-offs.

title: policy network
one_liner: This is known as a policy network.
content: There are several possible approaches, but one technique is to use deep networks to build a mapping from the observed world state to an action. This is known as a policy network. In the robot example, the policy network would learn a mapping from its sensor measurements to joint movements. In the chess example, the network would learn a mapping from the current state of the board to the choice of move (figure 1.13).
motivation_md: A policy network provides a way to map observed states directly to actions, enabling systems like robots or game players to decide what to do based on their current situation.
recap_md:
- A policy network maps observed states to actions.
- In robotics, it maps sensor data to joint movements.
- In chess, it maps board states to move choices.

title: ethical concerns in artificial intelligence
one_liner: This potent technology will change the world to at least the same extent as electricity, the internal combustion engine, the transistor, or the internet.
content:
It would be irresponsible to write this book without discussing the ethical implications of artificial intelligence. This potent technology will change the world to at least the same extent as electricity, the internal combustion engine, the transistor, or the internet. The potential benefits in healthcare, design, entertainment, transport, education, and almost every area of commerce are enormous. However, scientists and engineers are often unrealistically optimistic about the outcomes of their work, and the potential for harm is just as great. The following paragraphs highlight five concerns.

Bias and fairness: If we train a system to predict salary levels for individuals based on historical data, then this system will reproduce historical biases; for example, it will probably predict that women should be paid less than men. Several such cases have already become international news stories: an AI system for super-resolving face images made non-white people look more white; a system for generating images produced only pictures of men when asked to synthesize pictures of lawyers. Careless application of algorithmic decision-making using AI has the potential to entrench or aggravate existing biases. See Binns (2018) for further discussion.

Explainability: Deep learning systems make decisions, but we do not usually know exactly how or based on what information. They may be enormous, and there is no way we can understand how they work based on examination. This has led to the sub-field of explainable AI. One moderately successful area is producing local explanations; we cannot explain the entire system, but we can produce an interpretable description of why a particular decision was made. However, it remains unknown whether it is possible to build complex decision-making systems that are fully transparent to their users or even their creators. See Grennan et al. (2022) for further information.

Weaponizing AI: All significant technologies have been applied directly or indirectly toward war. Sadly, violent conflict seems to be an inevitable feature of human behavior. AI is arguably the most powerful technology ever built and will doubtless be deployed extensively in a military context. Indeed, this is already happening (Heikkilä, 2022).

Concentrating power: It is not from a benevolent interest in improving the lot of the human race that the world’s most powerful companies are investing heavily in artificial intelligence. They know that these technologies will allow them to reap enormous profits. Like any advanced technology, deep learning is likely to concentrate power in the hands of the few organizations that control it. Automating jobs that are currently done by humans will change the economic environment and disproportionately affect the livelihoods of lower-paid workers with fewer skills. Optimists argue similar disruptions happened during the industrial revolution and resulted in shorter working hours. The truth is that we simply do not know what effects the large-scale adoption of AI will have on society (see David, 2015).

Existential risk: The major existential risks to the human race all result from technology. Climate change has been driven by industrialization. Nuclear weapons derive from the study of physics. Pandemics are more probable and spread faster because innovations in transport, agriculture, and construction have allowed a larger, denser, and more interconnected population. Artificial intelligence brings new existential risks. We should be very cautious about building systems that are more capable and extensible than human beings. In the most optimistic case, it will put vast power in the hands of the owners. In the most pessimistic case, we will be unable to control it or even understand its motives (see Tegmark, 2018).

This list is far from exhaustive. AI could also enable surveillance, disinformation, violations of privacy, fraud, and manipulation of financial markets, and the energy required to train AI systems contributes to climate change. Moreover, these concerns are not speculative; there are already many examples of ethically dubious applications of AI (consult Dao, 2021, for a partial list). In addition, the recent history of the internet has shown how new technology can cause harm in unexpected ways. The online community of the eighties and early nineties could hardly have predicted the proliferation of fake news, spam, online harassment, fraud, cyberbullying, incel culture, political manipulation, doxxing, online radicalization, and revenge porn.

Everyone studying or researching (or writing books about) AI should contemplate to what degree scientists are accountable for the uses of their technology. We should consider that capitalism primarily drives the development of AI and that legal advances and deployment for social good are likely to lag significantly behind. We should reflect on whether it’s possible, as scientists and engineers, to control progress in this field and to reduce the potential for harm. We should consider what kind of organizations we are prepared to work for. How serious are they in their commitment to reducing the potential harms of AI? Are they simply “ethics-washing” to reduce reputational risk, or do they actually implement mechanisms to halt ethically suspect projects? All readers are encouraged to investigate these issues further.
motivation_md: AI's transformative power raises ethical concerns such as bias, fairness, explainability, weaponization, power concentration, and existential risks, necessitating careful consideration and responsible development.
recap_md:
- AI promises vast benefits but also significant ethical risks.
- Key concerns include bias, explainability, weaponization, power concentration, and existential threats.
- Scientists must consider accountability and the societal impact of AI development.

title: Momentum
one_liner: A common modification to stochastic gradient descent is to add a momentum term, updating parameters with a weighted combination of the current gradient and the previous step's direction.
content:
Momentum
A common modification to stochastic gradient descent is to add a momentum term. We update the parameters with a weighted combination of the gradient computed from the current batch and the direction moved in the previous step:

$$m_{t+1} \leftarrow \beta \cdot m_t + (1 - \beta) \sum_{i \in B_t} \frac{\partial \ell_i[\phi_t]}{\partial \phi}$$
$$\phi_{t+1} \leftarrow \phi_t - \alpha \cdot m_{t+1},$$

where $m_t$ is the momentum (which drives the update at iteration $t$), $\beta \in [0, 1)$ controls the degree to which the gradient is smoothed over time, and $\alpha$ is the learning rate. The recursive formulation of the momentum calculation means that the gradient step is an infinite weighted sum of all the previous gradients, where the weights get smaller as we move back in time.

The effective learning rate increases if all these gradients are aligned over multiple iterations but decreases if the gradient direction repeatedly changes as the terms in the sum cancel out. The overall effect is a smoother trajectory and reduced oscillatory behavior in valleys (figure 6.7).
motivation_md: Momentum smooths the gradient updates by combining current and past gradients, reducing oscillations and speeding convergence in stochastic gradient descent.
recap_md:
- Momentum updates parameters using a weighted sum of current gradient and previous momentum.
- The smoothing factor $\beta \in [0,1)$ controls how past gradients influence updates.
- This reduces oscillations and leads to a smoother optimization path.

title: Nesterov accelerated momentum
one_liner: Nesterov accelerated momentum computes gradients at a predicted future point rather than the current point, correcting the path provided by momentum alone.
content:
Nesterov accelerated momentum
The momentum term can be considered a coarse prediction of where the SGD algorithm will move next. Nesterov accelerated momentum (figure 6.8) computes the gradients at this predicted point rather than at the current point:

$$m_{t+1} \leftarrow \beta \cdot m_t + (1 - \beta) \sum_{i \in B_t} \frac{\partial \ell_i[\phi_t - \alpha \beta \cdot m_t]}{\partial \phi}$$
$$\phi_{t+1} \leftarrow \phi_t - \alpha \cdot m_{t+1},$$

where now the gradients are evaluated at $\phi_t - \alpha \beta \cdot m_t$. One way to think about this is that the gradient term now corrects the path provided by momentum alone.
motivation_md: Nesterov momentum anticipates the next position to compute gradients, improving update accuracy and convergence speed compared to standard momentum.
recap_md:
- Nesterov momentum predicts the next position before computing gradients.
- Gradients are evaluated at $\phi_t - \alpha \beta m_t$ instead of $\phi_t$.
- This corrects the momentum path for better convergence.

title: Adam
one_liner: Adam combines momentum and adaptive normalization of gradients to improve convergence in gradient descent.
content:
Adam
Gradient descent with a fixed step size has the undesirable property of making large adjustments to parameters with large gradients and small adjustments to those with small gradients. When the gradient of the loss surface is much steeper in one direction than another, it is difficult to choose a learning rate that makes good progress in both directions and remains stable (figures 6.9a–b).

A straightforward approach is to normalize the gradients so that we move a fixed distance (governed by the learning rate) in each direction. To do this, we first measure the gradient $m_{t+1}$ and the pointwise squared gradient $v_{t+1}$:

$$m_{t+1} \leftarrow \frac{\partial L[\phi_t]}{\partial \phi}$$
$$v_{t+1} \leftarrow \left( \frac{\partial L[\phi_t]}{\partial \phi} \right)^2.$$ 

Then we apply the update rule:

$$\phi_{t+1} \leftarrow \phi_t - \alpha \cdot \frac{m_{t+1}}{\sqrt{v_{t+1}} + \epsilon},$$

where the square root and division are pointwise, $\alpha$ is the learning rate, and $\epsilon$ is a small constant that prevents division by zero when the gradient magnitude is zero. The term $v_{t+1}$ is the squared gradient, and the positive root of this is used to normalize the gradient itself, so all that remains is the sign in each coordinate direction. The result is that the algorithm moves a fixed distance $\alpha$ along each coordinate, where the direction is determined by whichever way is downhill (figure 6.9c). This simple algorithm makes good progress in both directions but will not converge unless it happens to land exactly at the minimum; instead, it oscillates around it.

Adaptive moment estimation, or Adam, takes this idea and adds momentum to both the estimate of the gradient and the squared gradient:
motivation_md: Adam addresses issues with fixed step size gradient descent by normalizing gradients and adding momentum, enabling stable and efficient convergence in directions with varying curvature.
recap_md:
- Fixed step size gradient descent struggles with varying gradient magnitudes.
- Normalizing gradients to move fixed distances improves progress but causes oscillations.
- Adam adds momentum to both gradients and squared gradients for smoother convergence.

title: Training algorithm hyperparameters
one_liner: The choices of learning algorithm, batch size, learning rate schedule, and momentum coefficients are hyperparameters that directly affect final model performance.
content:
Training algorithm hyperparameters
The choices of learning algorithm, batch size, learning rate schedule, and momentum coefficients are all considered hyperparameters of the training algorithm; these directly affect the final model performance but are distinct from the model parameters. Choosing these can be more art than science, and it’s common to train many models with different hyperparameters and choose the best one. This is known as hyperparameter search.
motivation_md: Hyperparameters control training behavior and performance, so tuning them is essential for optimizing model results.
recap_md:
- Learning algorithm, batch size, learning rate schedule, and momentum coefficients are hyperparameters.
- Hyperparameters affect final model performance but differ from model parameters.
- Hyperparameter search involves training multiple models to find the best settings.

title: Convexity, minima, and saddle points
one_liner: A function is convex if every chord lies above it, which can be tested by the Hessian matrix being positive definite for all parameter values.
content:
Convexity, minima, and saddle points:
A function is convex if every chord (line segment between two points on the surface) lies above the function and does not intersect it. This can be tested algebraically by considering the Hessian matrix (the matrix of second derivatives):

$$H[\phi] = \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_0^2} & 0 & \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_0 \partial \phi_1} & \ldots & \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_0 \partial \phi_N} \\
\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_1 \partial \phi_0} & \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_1^2} & \ldots & \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_1 \partial \phi_N} \\
\vdots & & & & \\
\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_N \partial \phi_0} & \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_N \partial \phi_1} & \ldots & \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \phi_N^2}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If the Hessian matrix is positive definite (has positive eigenvalues) for all possible parameter values, then the function is convex; the loss function will look like a smooth bowl (as in figure 6.1c), so training will be relatively easy. There will be a single global minimum and no local minima or saddle points.

For any loss function, the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix at places where the gradient is zero allow us to classify this position as (i) a minimum (the eigenvalues are all positive), (ii) a maximum (the eigenvalues are all negative), or (iii) a saddle point (positive eigenvalues are associated with directions in which we are at a minimum and negative ones with directions where we are at a maximum).
motivation_md: Understanding convexity and the Hessian matrix helps classify critical points and predict optimization difficulty.
recap_md:
- A function is convex if every chord lies above it, tested via the Hessian matrix.
- Positive definite Hessian means a convex function with a single global minimum.
- Eigenvalues of Hessian at zero-gradient points classify minima, maxima, or saddle points.

title: Line search
one_liner: Gradient descent methods are usually combined with a line search procedure to find the optimal step size along the descent direction.
content:
Line search:
Gradient descent with a fixed step size is inefficient because the distance moved depends entirely on the magnitude of the gradient. It moves a long distance when the function is changing fast (where perhaps it should be more cautious) but a short distance when the function is changing slowly (where perhaps it should explore further). For this reason, gradient descent methods are usually combined with a line search procedure in which we sample the function along the desired direction to try to find the optimal step size. One such approach is bracketing (figure 6.10). Another problem with gradient descent is that it tends to lead to inefficient oscillatory behavior when descending valleys (e.g., path 1 in figure 6.5a).
motivation_md: Line search improves gradient descent by adaptively choosing step sizes, avoiding inefficiency and oscillations.
recap_md:
- Fixed step size gradient descent can be inefficient and oscillatory.
- Line search samples the function along the descent direction to find optimal step size.
- Bracketing is one approach to line search.

title: Newton method
one_liner: The Newton method uses the inverse Hessian matrix to account for curvature, applying more cautious updates and eliminating oscillatory behavior.
content:
Newton method
Most notable is the Newton method, which takes the curvature of the surface into account using the inverse of the Hessian matrix; if the gradient of the function is changing quickly, then it applies a more cautious update. This method eliminates the need for line search and does not suffer from oscillatory behavior. However, it has its own problems; in its simplest form, it moves toward the nearest extremum, but this may be a maximum if we are closer to the top of a hill than we are to the bottom of a valley.

Moreover, computing the inverse Hessian is intractable when the number of parameters is large, as in neural networks.
motivation_md: Newton method improves gradient descent by using curvature information for better updates but is computationally expensive for large models.
recap_md:
- Newton method uses inverse Hessian to incorporate curvature.
- It avoids oscillations and line search but may converge to maxima.
- Computing inverse Hessian is intractable for large parameter spaces.

title: Properties of SGD
one_liner: The limit of SGD as learning rate tends to zero is a stochastic differential equation influenced by the learning-rate to batch size ratio, affecting the width of minima found.
content: The limit of SGD as the learning rate tends to zero is a stochastic differential equation. Jastrzębski et al. (2018) showed that this equation relies on the learning-rate to batch size ratio and that there is a relation between the learning rate to batch size ratio and the width of the minimum found. Wider minima are considered more desirable; if the loss function for test data is similar, then small errors in the parameter estimates will have little effect on test performance. He et al. (2019) prove a generalization bound for SGD that has a positive correlation with the ratio of batch size to learning rate. They train a large number of models on different architectures and datasets and find empirical evidence that test accuracy improves when the ratio of batch size to learning rate is low. Smith et al. (2018) and Goyal et al. (2018) also identified the ratio of batch size to learning rate as being important for generalization (see figure 20.10).
motivation_md: Understanding SGD's behavior and its dependence on learning rate and batch size helps improve generalization and training stability.
recap_md:
- SGD limit as learning rate → 0 is a stochastic differential equation.
- The learning-rate to batch size ratio influences the width of minima found.
- Lower batch size to learning rate ratio correlates with better test accuracy.

title: training data in supervised learning
one_liner: The models require labeled input/output pairs for training, where these pairs act as a teacher or supervisor, giving rise to supervised learning.
content: It follows that the models in figure 1.2 require labeled input/output pairs for training. For example, the music classification model would require a large number of audio clips where a human expert had identified the genre of each. These input/output pairs take the role of a teacher or supervisor for the training process, and this gives rise to the term supervised learning.
motivation_md: Training data with labeled input/output pairs is essential because it provides the supervision needed for models to learn correct mappings in supervised learning.
recap_md:
- Supervised learning requires labeled input/output pairs.
- These pairs act as a teacher or supervisor during training.
- This supervision enables the model to learn correct mappings.

title: deep neural networks
one_liner: Deep neural networks are equations representing broad relationships between input and output, easy to search to fit training data, and can handle large, variable, and structured inputs and outputs.
content: This book concerns deep neural networks, which are a particularly useful type of machine learning model. They are equations that can represent an extremely broad family of relationships between input and output, and where it is particularly easy to search through this family to find the relationship that describes the training data. Deep neural networks can process inputs that are very large, of variable length, and contain various kinds of internal structures. They can output single real numbers (regression), multiple numbers (multivariate regression), or probabilities over two or more classes (binary and multiclass classification, respectively). As we shall see in the next section, their outputs may also be very large, of variable length, and contain internal structure. It is probably hard to imagine equations with these properties, and the reader should endeavor to suspend disbelief for now.
motivation_md: Deep neural networks exist to model complex, structured relationships between inputs and outputs, enabling flexible and powerful learning across diverse data types.
recap_md:
- Deep neural networks represent broad families of input-output relationships.
- They handle large, variable-length, and structured inputs and outputs.
- Outputs can be real numbers, multiple values, or class probabilities.

title: structured outputs
one_liner: Structured outputs are high-dimensional outputs with internal structure closely tied to inputs or with complex internal grammar, such as semantic segmentation or audio transcription.
content:
Figure 1.4a depicts a multivariate binary classification model for semantic segmentation. Here, every pixel of an input image is assigned a binary label that indicates whether it belongs to a cow or the background. Figure 1.4b shows a multivariate regression model where the input is an image of a street scene and the output is the depth at each pixel. In both cases, the output is high-dimensional and structured. However, this structure is closely tied to the input, and this can be exploited; if a pixel is labeled as “cow,” then a neighbor with a similar RGB value probably has the same label. Figures 1.4c–e depict three models where the output has a complex structure that is not so closely tied to the input. Figure 1.4c shows a model where the input is an audio file and the output is the transcribed words from that file. Figure 1.4d is a translation Draft: please send errata to udlbookmail@gmail.com.
