Figure 1.4 Supervised learning tasks with structured outputs. a) This semantic segmentation model maps an RGB image to a binary image indicating whether each pixel belongs to the background or a cow (adapted from Noh et al., 2015). b) This monocular depth estimation model maps an RGB image to an output image where each pixel represents the depth (adapted from Cordts et al., 2016). c) This audio transcription model maps an audio sample to a transcription of the spoken words in the audio. d) This translation model maps an English text string to its French translation. e) This image synthesis model maps a caption to an image (example from https://openai.com/dall-e-2/). In each case, the output has a complex internal structure or grammar. In some cases, many outputs are compatible with the input.
motivation_md: Structured outputs allow models to handle complex, high-dimensional data where outputs have internal structure or grammar, enabling tasks like segmentation, transcription, and translation.
recap_md:
- Structured outputs can be high-dimensional and closely tied to inputs.
- Outputs may have complex internal structures or grammar.
- Examples include semantic segmentation, depth estimation, transcription, translation, and image synthesis.

title: output ambiguity and grammar constraints in structured outputs
one_liner: Output ambiguity and grammar constraints make structured output tasks harder because multiple valid outputs exist and outputs must follow valid structures.
content: In principle, the latter three tasks can be tackled in the standard supervised learning framework, but they are more difficult for two reasons. First, the output may genuinely be ambiguous; there are multiple valid translations from an English sentence to a French one and multiple images that are compatible with any caption. Second, the output contains considerable structure; not all strings of words make valid English and French sentences, and not all collections of RGB values make plausible images. In addition to learning the mapping, we also have to respect the “grammar” of the output. Fortunately, this “grammar” can be learned without the need for output labels. For example, we can learn how to form valid English sentences by learning the statistics of a large corpus of text data. This provides a connection with the next section of the book, which considers unsupervised learning models.
motivation_md: Understanding output ambiguity and grammar constraints is crucial because structured outputs can have multiple valid forms and must adhere to rules, complicating learning.
recap_md:
- Structured outputs can be ambiguous with multiple valid outputs.
- Outputs must respect grammatical or structural constraints.
- Grammar can be learned from data without output labels.

title: unsupervised learning
one_liner: Unsupervised learning constructs a model from input data without output labels to describe or understand data structure.
content: Constructing a model from input data without corresponding output labels is termed unsupervised learning; the absence of output labels means there can be no “supervision.” Rather than learning a mapping from input to output, the goal is to describe or understand the structure of the data. As was the case for supervised learning, the data may have very different characteristics; it may be discrete or continuous, low-dimensional or high-dimensional, and of constant or variable length.
motivation_md: Unsupervised learning exists to model and understand data structure when output labels are unavailable, enabling discovery of patterns and representations.
recap_md:
- Unsupervised learning uses input data without output labels.
- It aims to describe or understand data structure.
- Data can vary widely in type and dimensionality.

title: generative models
one_liner: Generative models learn to synthesize new data examples statistically indistinguishable from training data, either by modeling distributions or generating examples directly.
content: This book focuses on generative unsupervised models, which learn to synthesize new data examples that are statistically indistinguishable from the training data. Some generative models explicitly describe the probability distribution over the input data and here new examples are generated by sampling from this distribution. Others merely learn a mechanism to generate new examples without explicitly describing their distribution. State-of-the-art generative models can synthesize examples that are extremely plausible but distinct from the training examples. They have been particularly successful at generating images (figure 1.5) and text (figure 1.6). They can also synthesize data under the constraint that some outputs are predetermined (termed conditional generation). Examples include image inpainting (figure 1.7) and text completion (figure 1.8). Indeed, modern generative models for text are so powerful that they can appear intelligent. Given a body of text followed by a question, the model can often “fill in” the missing answer by generating the most likely completion of the document. However, in reality, the model only knows about the statistics of language and does not understand the significance of its answers.
motivation_md: Generative models enable creation of new, realistic data examples, advancing applications like image and text synthesis and conditional generation.
recap_md:
- Generative models synthesize new data statistically like training data.
- Some model explicit probability distributions; others generate without them.
- They excel at image and text generation, including conditional tasks.

title: conditional generation
one_liner: Conditional generation synthesizes data under constraints where some outputs are predetermined.
content: Under the constraint that some outputs are predetermined (termed conditional generation). Examples include image inpainting (figure 1.7) and text completion (figure 1.8).
motivation_md: Conditional generation allows generative models to produce outputs that satisfy specific constraints, enabling targeted synthesis like inpainting or text completion.
recap_md:
- Conditional generation produces outputs with predetermined constraints.
- Enables tasks like image inpainting and text completion.
- Extends generative models to controlled synthesis.

title: generative models for images and text
one_liner: Generative models can create realistic images and text by sampling from learned probability distributions, producing novel but plausible outputs.
content:
Figure 1.5 Generative models for images. Left: two images were generated from a model trained on pictures of cats. These are not real cats, but samples from a probability model. Right: two images generated from a model trained on images of buildings. Adapted from Karras et al. (2020b).
The moon had risen by the time I reached the edge of the forest, and the light that filtered through the trees was silver and cold. I shivered, though I was not cold, and quickened my pace. I had never been so far from the village before, and I was not sure what to expect. I had been walking for hours, and I was tired and hungry. I had left in such a hurry that I had not thought to pack any food, and I had not thought to bring a weapon. I was unarmed and alone in a strange place, and I did not know what I was doing.
I had been walking for so long that I had lost all sense of time, and I had no idea how far I had come. I only knew that I had to keep going. I had to find her. I was getting close. I could feel it. She was nearby, and she was in trouble. I had to find her and help her, before it was too late.
Figure 1.6 Short story synthesized from a generative model of text data. The model describes a probability distribution that assigns a probability to every output string. Sampling from the model creates strings that follow the statistics of the training data (here, short stories) but have never been seen before.
Figure 1.7 Inpainting. In the original image (left), the boy is obscured by metal cables. These undesirable regions (center) are removed and the generative model synthesizes a new image (right) under the constraint that the remaining pixels must stay the same. Adapted from Saharia et al. (2022a).
motivation_md: Generative models for images and text demonstrate the ability to create novel, realistic outputs by learning statistical patterns from training data, enabling applications like image synthesis and story generation.
recap_md:
- Generative models produce realistic images by sampling learned distributions.
- They can generate novel text following training data statistics.
- Applications include image inpainting and text story synthesis.

title: Large, structured inputs
one_liner: For large, structured inputs like images, fully connected networks are impractical due to prohibitive parameters and redundant learning across positions.
content:
We have discussed fully connected networks where every element of each layer contributes to every element of the subsequent one. However, these are not practical for large, structured inputs like images, where the input might comprise approximately one million pixels. The number of parameters would be prohibitive, and moreover, we want different parts of the image to be processed similarly; there is no point in independently learning to recognize the same object at every possible position in the image.

The solution is to process local image regions in parallel and then gradually integrate information from increasingly large regions. This kind of local-to-global processing is difficult to specify without using multiple layers (see chapter 10).
motivation_md: Fully connected networks become impractical for large structured inputs like images due to the huge number of parameters and redundant learning of identical features at different positions. Processing local regions in parallel and integrating globally solves this.
recap_md:
- Fully connected networks are impractical for large inputs like images due to parameter explosion.
- Different parts of an image should be processed similarly to avoid redundant learning.
- Local-to-global processing through multiple layers enables efficient handling of large structured inputs.

title: Training and generalization
one_liner: Deep networks are often easier to train than shallow ones and tend to generalize better to new data, with best results achieved using tens or hundreds of layers.
content:
A further possible advantage of deep networks over shallow networks is their ease of fitting; it is usually easier to train moderately deep networks than to train shallow ones (see figure 20.2). It may be that over-parameterized deep models (i.e., those with more parameters than training examples) have a large family of roughly equivalent solutions that are easy to find. However, as we add more hidden layers, training becomes more difficult again. Many methods have been developed to mitigate this problem (see chapter 11).

Deep neural networks also seem to generalize to new data better than shallow ones. In practice, the best results for most tasks have been achieved using networks with tens or hundreds of layers. Neither of these phenomena are well understood, and we return to them in chapter 20.
motivation_md: Deep networks can be easier to train and generalize better than shallow ones, enabling improved performance on many tasks, though the reasons remain not fully understood.
recap_md:
- Deep networks are often easier to train than shallow ones.
- Over-parameterized deep models may have many equivalent solutions.
- Deep networks tend to generalize better, with best results from very deep architectures.

title: Maximum likelihood
one_liner: Maximum likelihood chooses model parameters to maximize the combined probability of observed outputs under predicted conditional distributions.
content:
Consider a model f[x, ϕ] with parameters ϕ that computes an output from input x. Until now, we have implied that the model directly computes a prediction y. We now shift perspective and consider the model as computing a conditional probability distribution Pr(y|x) over possible outputs y given input x. The loss encourages each training output yi to have high probability under the distribution Pr(yi|xi) computed from the corresponding input xi (figure 5.1).

This shift in perspective raises the question of exactly how a model f[x, ϕ] can be adapted to compute a probability distribution. The solution is simple. First, we choose a parametric distribution Pr(y|θ) defined on the output domain y. Then we use the network to compute one or more of the parameters θ of this distribution.

For example, suppose the prediction domain is the set of real numbers, so y ∈ R. Here, we might choose the univariate normal distribution, which is defined on R. This distribution is defined by the mean µ and variance σ², so θ = {µ, σ²}. The machine learning model might predict the mean µ, and the variance σ² could be treated as an unknown constant.

The model now computes different distribution parameters θi = f[xi, ϕ] for each training input xi. Each observed training output yi should have high probability under its corresponding distribution Pr(yi|θi). Hence, we choose the model parameters ϕ so that they maximize the combined probability across all I training examples:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|x_i) = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|\theta_i) = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]).
\]

The combined probability term is the likelihood of the parameters, and hence this equation is known as the maximum likelihood criterion.
motivation_md: This concept provides a principled way to construct loss functions by modeling outputs probabilistically and choosing parameters to maximize the likelihood of observed data.
recap_md:
- Model outputs are treated as conditional probability distributions Pr(y|x).
- Parameters θ of these distributions are predicted by the model.
- Maximum likelihood chooses parameters maximizing the product of output probabilities over training data.

title: loss function derivation from maximum likelihood
one_liner: Maximum likelihood chooses model parameters to maximize the combined probability of observed outputs, assuming identical output distributions and independence across data points.
content:
The model computes different distribution parameters θi = f[xi, ϕ] for each training input xi. Each observed training output yi should have high probability under its corresponding distribution Pr(yi|θi). Hence, we choose the model parameters ϕ so that they maximize the combined probability across all I training examples:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|x_i) = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|\theta_i) = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]).
\]

This combined probability term is the likelihood of the parameters, and hence this equation is known as the maximum likelihood criterion.

Here we are implicitly making two assumptions. First, we assume that the form of the probability distribution over the outputs yi is the same for each data point. Second, we assume that the conditional distributions Pr(yi|xi) of the output given the input are independent, so the total likelihood of the training data decomposes as:

\[
Pr(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_I | x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_I) = \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i | x_i).
\]
motivation_md: This idea formalizes how to derive loss functions from maximum likelihood by assuming identical output distributions and independence, enabling parameter estimation via likelihood maximization.
recap_md:
- Maximum likelihood maximizes the product of output probabilities over training data.
- Assumes identical distribution form for each output.
- Assumes independence of outputs given inputs, so likelihood factorizes as a product.

title: use of log transform in maximum likelihood optimization
one_liner: The log transform converts the product of probabilities into a sum, preserving maxima and improving numerical stability in maximum likelihood optimization.
content:
The log function is monotonically increasing: if z > z′, then log[z] > log[z′]. It follows that the maximum of any function g[z] will be at the same position as the maximum of log[g[z]]. All positions on g[z] with a positive slope retain a positive slope after the log transform, and those with a negative slope retain a negative slope. The position of the maximum remains the same (figure 5.2).

The maximum likelihood criterion is not very practical because each term Pr(yi|f[xi, ϕ]) can be small, so the product of many of these terms can be tiny. It may be difficult to represent this quantity with finite precision arithmetic. Fortunately, we can equivalently maximize the logarithm of the likelihood:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) = \arg\max_{\phi} \log \left( \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) \right) = \arg\max_{\phi} \sum_{i=1}^I \log \left( Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) \right).
\]

This log-likelihood criterion is equivalent because the logarithm is a monotonically increasing function: if z > z′, then log[z] > log[z′] and vice versa. It follows that when we change the model parameters ϕ to improve the log-likelihood criterion, we also improve the original maximum likelihood criterion. Also, the overall maxima of the two criteria must be in the same place, so the best model parameters ˆϕ are the same in both cases. However, the log-likelihood criterion has the practical advantage of using a sum of terms, not a product, so representing it with finite precision isn’t problematic.
motivation_md: Using the log transform turns a product of probabilities into a sum, preserving maxima and avoiding numerical underflow, making maximum likelihood optimization practical and stable.
recap_md:
- Logarithm is monotonically increasing, preserving maxima.
- Log transform converts product of probabilities into a sum.
- Summation improves numerical stability and precision in optimization.

title: log-likelihood criterion
one_liner: The log-likelihood criterion maximizes the sum of log probabilities, equivalent to maximizing the original likelihood but numerically more stable.
content:
The maximum likelihood criterion is not very practical because each term Pr(yi|f[xi, ϕ]) can be small, so the product of many of these terms can be tiny. It may be difficult to represent this quantity with finite precision arithmetic. Fortunately, we can equivalently maximize the logarithm of the likelihood:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\max_{\phi} \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) = \arg\max_{\phi} \log \left( \prod_{i=1}^I Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) \right) = \arg\max_{\phi} \sum_{i=1}^I \log \left( Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) \right).
\]

This log-likelihood criterion is equivalent because the logarithm is a monotonically increasing function: if z > z′, then log[z] > log[z′] and vice versa (figure 5.2). It follows that when we change the model parameters ϕ to improve the log-likelihood criterion, we also improve the original maximum likelihood criterion. It also follows that the overall maxima of the two criteria must be in the same place, so the best model parameters ˆϕ are the same in both cases. However, the log-likelihood criterion has the practical advantage of using a sum of terms, not a product, so representing it with finite precision isn’t problematic.
motivation_md: Maximizing the log-likelihood is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood but avoids numerical issues by summing log probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities.
recap_md:
- Log-likelihood criterion maximizes sum of log probabilities.
- It is equivalent to maximizing original likelihood.
- Summation avoids numerical underflow and precision issues.

title: negative log-likelihood criterion
one_liner: The negative log-likelihood criterion converts maximum log-likelihood maximization into a loss minimization problem by multiplying by minus one.
content:
By convention, model fitting problems are framed in terms of minimizing a loss. To convert the maximum log-likelihood criterion to a minimization problem, we multiply by minus one, which gives us the negative log-likelihood criterion:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\min_{\phi} - \sum_{i=1}^I \log \left( Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) \right) = \arg\min_{\phi} L[\phi],
\]

which forms the final loss function L[ϕ].
motivation_md: Converting maximum likelihood maximization into a minimization problem aligns with standard loss minimization frameworks in model fitting, enabling use of optimization algorithms.
recap_md:
- Negative log-likelihood is the negative of the log-likelihood.
- It converts maximization into a minimization problem.
- This forms the final loss function used for training.

title: conversion of maximum likelihood to minimization problem via negative log-likelihood
one_liner: Maximum log-likelihood is converted to a minimization problem by multiplying by -1, yielding the negative log-likelihood loss function.
content:
By convention, model fitting problems are framed in terms of minimizing a loss. To convert the maximum log-likelihood criterion to a minimization problem, we multiply by minus one, which gives us the negative log-likelihood criterion:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\min_{\phi} - \sum_{i=1}^I \log \left( Pr(y_i|f[x_i, \phi]) \right) = \arg\min_{\phi} L[\phi],
\]

which forms the final loss function L[ϕ].
motivation_md: This conversion allows maximum likelihood estimation to be implemented as a loss minimization problem, compatible with standard optimization methods.
recap_md:
- Maximum log-likelihood maximization is converted to minimization by negation.
- The negative log-likelihood forms the loss function.
- This aligns model fitting with standard loss minimization frameworks.

title: model uncertainty estimation via variance prediction
one_liner: There is nothing to stop us from treating variance σ2 as a learned parameter and minimizing the negative log-likelihood with respect to both model parameters and variance.
content:
To formulate the least squares loss function, we assumed that the network predicted the mean of a normal distribution. The final expression in equation 5.11 does not depend on the variance σ2. However, there is nothing to stop us from treating σ2 as a learned parameter and minimizing equation 5.9 with respect to both the model parameters ϕ and the distribution variance σ2:

ˆϕ, ˆσ2 = argmin_{ϕ,σ2} \left[- \sum_{i=1}^I \log \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp \left(-\frac{(y_i - f[x_i, \phi])^2}{2\sigma^2} \right) \right) \right]. (5.13)
motivation_md: Estimating variance as a learned parameter allows the model to capture uncertainty in predictions, improving robustness beyond assuming constant variance.
recap_md:
- Least squares loss assumes the network predicts the mean of a normal distribution.
- The variance σ2 can be treated as a learned parameter.
- Minimizing negative log-likelihood jointly over model parameters and variance estimates uncertainty.

title: Heteroscedastic regression
one_liner: When the uncertainty of the model varies as a function of the input data, we refer to this as heteroscedastic regression.
content:
The model above assumes that the variance of the data is constant everywhere, which might be unrealistic. When the uncertainty of the model varies as a function of the input data, we refer to this as heteroscedastic (as opposed to homoscedastic, where the uncertainty is constant).

A simple way to model this is to train a neural network f[x, ϕ] that computes both the mean and the variance. For example, consider a shallow network with two outputs. We denote the first output as f_1[x, ϕ] and use this to predict the mean, and the second output as f_2[x, ϕ] to predict the variance.

There is one complication: the variance must be positive, but the network output may not always be positive. To ensure positivity, we pass the second network output through a function that maps any value to a positive one. A suitable choice is the squaring function, giving:

\[
\mu = f_1[x, \phi] \\
\sigma^2 = f_2[x, \phi]^2,
\]

which results in the loss function:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\min_{\phi} \left[- \sum_{i=1}^I \left( \log \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi f_2[x_i, \phi]^2}} \right) - \frac{(y_i - f_1[x_i, \phi])^2}{2 f_2[x_i, \phi]^2} \right) \right].
\] (5.15)
motivation_md: Heteroscedastic regression models varying uncertainty across inputs, capturing more realistic data noise than assuming constant variance.
recap_md:
- Heteroscedastic regression models input-dependent variance.
- A neural network can output both mean and variance predictions.
- Variance output is squared to ensure positivity in the loss function.

title: loss function for heteroscedastic regression
one_liner: A neural network with two outputs predicts both mean and variance, with variance ensured positive by squaring, resulting in a loss function based on the negative log-likelihood of a normal distribution with input-dependent variance.
content:
The model above assumes that the variance of the data is constant everywhere, which might be unrealistic. When the uncertainty of the model varies as a function of the input data, we refer to this as heteroscedastic (as opposed to homoscedastic, where the uncertainty is constant).

A simple way to model this is to train a neural network f[x, ϕ] that computes both the mean and the variance. For example, consider a shallow network with two outputs. We denote the first output as f_1[x, ϕ] and use this to predict the mean, and the second output as f_2[x, ϕ] to predict the variance.

There is one complication: the variance must be positive, but the network output may not always be positive. To ensure positivity, we pass the second network output through a function that maps any value to a positive one. A suitable choice is the squaring function, giving:

\[
\mu = f_1[x, \phi] \\
\sigma^2 = f_2[x, \phi]^2,
\]

which results in the loss function:

\[
\hat{\phi} = \arg\min_{\phi} \left[- \sum_{i=1}^I \left( \log \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi f_2[x_i, \phi]^2}} \right) - \frac{(y_i - f_1[x_i, \phi])^2}{2 f_2[x_i, \phi]^2} \right) \right].
\] (5.15)
motivation_md: Modeling input-dependent variance requires a loss function that accounts for heteroscedasticity, enabling the network to learn both mean and variance effectively.
recap_md:
- Heteroscedastic regression uses a network outputting mean and variance.
- Variance output is squared to ensure positivity.
- The loss function is the negative log-likelihood of a normal distribution with input-dependent variance.

title: heteroscedastic vs. homoscedastic regression
one_liner: Homoscedastic regression predicts a constant variance, while heteroscedastic regression predicts variance as a function of input, making standard deviation input-dependent.
content:
Figure 5.5 illustrates homoscedastic versus heteroscedastic regression.

a) A shallow neural network for homoscedastic regression predicts just the mean \(\mu\) of the output distribution from the input \(x\).

b) The mean (blue line) is a piecewise linear function of the input \(x\), but the variance is constant everywhere (arrows and gray region show ±2 standard deviations).

c) A shallow neural network for heteroscedastic regression also predicts the variance \(\sigma^2\) (or more precisely, computes its square root, which is then squared).

d) The standard deviation becomes a piecewise linear function of the input \(x\).
motivation_md: Comparing homoscedastic and heteroscedastic regression clarifies how modeling input-dependent variance improves uncertainty estimation.
recap_md:
- Homoscedastic regression predicts constant variance across inputs.
- Heteroscedastic regression predicts variance as a function of input.
- Standard deviation in heteroscedastic regression varies piecewise linearly with input.

title: Example 2: binary classification
one_liner: In binary classification, the goal is to assign data x to one of two discrete classes y ∈ {0, 1}.
content:
In binary classification, the goal is to assign the data \(x\) to one of two discrete classes \(y \in \{0, 1\}\). In this context, \(y\) is called a label. Examples include (i) predicting whether a restaurant review is positive (\(y=1\)) or negative (\(y=0\)) from text data \(x\), and (ii) predicting whether a tumor is present (\(y=1\)) or absent (\(y=0\)) from an MRI scan \(x\).

We choose a probability distribution over the output space \(y \in \{0,1\}\). A suitable choice is the Bernoulli distribution, defined on the domain \(\{0,1\}\) with a single parameter \(\lambda \in [0,1]\) representing the probability that \(y=1\):

\[
\Pr(y|\lambda) = \begin{cases} 1 - \lambda & y=0 \\ \lambda & y=1 \end{cases} = (1-\lambda)^{1-y} \lambda^y.
\]

Since \(\lambda\) must lie in \([0,1]\), we pass the network output through a function mapping \(\mathbb{R}\) to \([0,1]\). A suitable choice is the logistic sigmoid function:

\[
\mathrm{sig}[z] = \frac{1}{1 + \exp[-z]}.
\]

Hence, the predicted distribution parameter is \(\lambda = \mathrm{sig}[f[x, \phi]]\). The likelihood is:

\[
\Pr(y|x) = (1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x, \phi]])^{1-y} \cdot \mathrm{sig}[f[x, \phi]]^y.
\]
motivation_md: Binary classification assigns inputs to one of two classes, requiring a probabilistic model to handle uncertainty in predictions.
recap_md:
- Binary classification predicts labels \(y \in \{0,1\}\).
- The Bernoulli distribution models the output with parameter \(\lambda\).
- Logistic sigmoid maps network outputs to valid probabilities \(\lambda \in [0,1]\).

title: loss function for binary classification using Bernoulli distribution
one_liner: The binary cross-entropy loss is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli distribution parameter predicted by a network transformed by the logistic sigmoid.
content:
In binary classification, the goal is to assign data \(x\) to one of two discrete classes \(y \in \{0,1\}\). Examples include predicting whether a restaurant review is positive or negative, or whether a tumor is present or absent from an MRI scan.

The Bernoulli distribution models the output \(y\) with parameter \(\lambda \in [0,1]\), representing the probability that \(y=1\). The probability is:

\[
\Pr(y|\lambda) = (1 - \lambda)^{1-y} \lambda^y.
\]

The machine learning model \(f[x, \phi]\) predicts \(\lambda\) via the logistic sigmoid function:

\[
\mathrm{sig}[z] = \frac{1}{1 + \exp[-z]},
\]

so \(\lambda = \mathrm{sig}[f[x, \phi]]\). The likelihood is:

\[
\Pr(y|x) = (1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x, \phi]])^{1-y} \cdot \mathrm{sig}[f[x, \phi]]^y.
\]

The loss function is the negative log-likelihood of the training set:

\[
\mathcal{L}[\phi] = \sum_{i=1}^I \left[-(1 - y_i) \log \left(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x_i, \phi]] \right) - y_i \log \left( \mathrm{sig}[f[x_i, \phi]] \right) \right].
\]

This is known as the binary cross-entropy loss. The transformed model output \(\mathrm{sig}[f[x, \phi]]\) predicts the Bernoulli parameter \(\lambda\), representing the probability \(y=1\). For inference, a point estimate sets \(y=1\) if \(\lambda > 0.5\) and \(y=0\) otherwise.
motivation_md: The binary cross-entropy loss enables training models to predict probabilities for binary outcomes, matching the Bernoulli likelihood.
recap_md:
- Binary classification uses Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(\lambda\).
- Logistic sigmoid maps network outputs to probabilities.
- Loss is negative log-likelihood, called binary cross-entropy loss.

title: logistic sigmoid
one_liner: The logistic sigmoid function maps the real line to the interval [0, 1].
content:
The logistic sigmoid function is defined as:

\[
\mathrm{sig}[z] = \frac{1}{1 + \exp[-z]}.
\] (5.18)
motivation_md: The logistic sigmoid function is used to transform arbitrary real-valued inputs into probabilities between 0 and 1.
recap_md:
- Logistic sigmoid maps \(\mathbb{R}\) to \([0,1]\).
- Defined as \(\mathrm{sig}[z] = 1 / (1 + e^{-z})\).
- Commonly used to produce probabilities in binary classification.

title: Example 3: multiclass classification
one_liner: Multiclass classification assigns input data to one of K > 2 classes using the categorical distribution and softmax function.
content:
The goal of multiclass classification is to assign an input data example \(x\) to one of \(K > 2\) classes, so \(y \in \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}\). Examples include predicting which of \(K=10\) digits is present in an image or which of \(K\) possible words follows an incomplete sentence.

We choose a distribution over the prediction space \(y\). For \(y \in \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}\), we choose the categorical distribution, defined with parameters \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_K\) that determine the probability of each category:

\[
\Pr(y = k) = \lambda_k.
\] (5.21)

Each \(\lambda_k\) lies in \([0,1]\) and all \(K\) parameters sum to one to ensure a valid probability distribution.

A network \(f[x, \phi]\) with \(K\) outputs computes these parameters from input \(x\). Since the outputs may not satisfy the constraints, we pass them through the softmax function, which ensures positivity and that the outputs sum to one:

\[
\mathrm{softmax}_k[z] = \frac{\exp[z_k]}{\sum_{k'=1}^K \exp[z_{k'}]}.
\] (5.22)

The likelihood that input \(x\) has label \(y=k\) is:

\[
\Pr(y = k | x) = \mathrm{softmax}_k \left(f[x, \phi]\right).
\] (5.23)

The loss function is the negative log-likelihood of the training data.
motivation_md: Multiclass classification generalizes binary classification to multiple classes, requiring a probability distribution over multiple categories and a function to enforce valid probabilities.
recap_md:
- Multiclass classification assigns inputs to one of \(K > 2\) classes.
- Uses categorical distribution with parameters \(\lambda_k\) summing to one.
- Softmax function transforms network outputs to valid probability vectors.

title: point estimate in inference from predicted distribution
one_liner: When we perform inference, we often want a point estimate rather than a distribution, so we return the maximum of the distribution: ˆy = argmax_y Pr(y|f[x, ˆϕ]).
content:
Inference
The network no longer directly predicts the outputs y but instead determines a probability distribution over y. When we perform inference, we often want a point estimate rather than a distribution, so we return the maximum of the distribution:

ˆy = argmax_y Pr(y|f[x, ˆϕ]).
(5.5)
motivation_md: Inference transforms predicted distributions into single point estimates, simplifying decision-making by selecting the most probable output value.
recap_md:
- Inference predicts a probability distribution over outputs y.
- Often, a point estimate is needed instead of the full distribution.
- The point estimate is the value y that maximizes Pr(y|f[x, ˆϕ]).

title: Inference

content:
Inference

ˆy = argmax_y Pr(y|f[x, ˆϕ]).

title: Recipe for constructing loss functions
one_liner: The recipe for constructing loss functions using maximum likelihood is: choose a probability distribution Pr(y|θ), predict parameters θ = f[x, ϕ], minimize negative log-likelihood over training data, then perform inference by returning the distribution or its maximum.
content:
Recipe for constructing loss functions
The recipe for constructing loss functions for training data {x_i, y_i} using the maximum likelihood approach is:

1. Choose a suitable probability distribution Pr(y|θ) defined over the domain of the predictions y with distribution parameters θ.
2. Set the machine learning model f[x, ϕ] to predict one or more of these parameters, so θ = f[x, ϕ] and Pr(y|θ) = Pr(y|f[x, ϕ]).
3. To train the model, find the network parameters ˆϕ that minimize the negative log-likelihood loss function over the training dataset pairs {x_i, y_i}:

ˆϕ = argmin_ϕ L[ϕ] = argmin_ϕ 
  - ∑_{i=1}^I log Pr(y_i|f[x_i, ϕ]).
(5.6)

4. To perform inference for a new test example x, return either the full distribution Pr(y|f[x, ˆϕ]) or the value where this distribution is maximized.

We devote most of the rest of this chapter to constructing loss functions for common prediction types using this recipe.
motivation_md: This recipe provides a systematic way to construct loss functions by modeling outputs probabilistically and optimizing parameters to maximize data likelihood.
recap_md:
- Choose a probability distribution Pr(y|θ) over outputs.
- Predict distribution parameters θ = f[x, ϕ].
- Train by minimizing negative log-likelihood over training data.
- Perform inference by returning the full distribution or its maximum.

title: Example 1: univariate regression
one_liner: In univariate regression, the goal is to predict a scalar output y ∈ R from input x using a model f[x, ϕ], choosing a univariate normal distribution with parameters µ and σ² to model output uncertainty.
content:
Example 1: univariate regression

Figure 5.3 The univariate normal distribution (also known as the Gaussian distribution) is defined on the real line z ∈ R and has parameters µ and σ². The mean µ determines the position of the peak. The positive root of the variance σ² (the standard deviation) determines the width of the distribution. Since the total probability density sums to one, the peak becomes higher as the variance decreases and the distribution becomes narrower.

We start by considering univariate regression models. Here the goal is to predict a single scalar output y ∈ R from input x using a model f[x, ϕ] with parameters ϕ. Following the recipe, we choose a probability distribution over the output domain y. We select the univariate normal distribution (figure 5.3), which is defined over y ∈ R. This has two parameters (mean µ and variance σ²) and has a probability density function:

Pr(y|µ, σ²) = (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(y - µ)² / (2σ²)).
(5.7)

Second, we set the machine learning model f[x, ϕ] to compute one or more of the parameters of this distribution. Here, we just compute the mean so µ = f[x, ϕ]:

Pr(y|f[x, ϕ], σ²) = (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(y - f[x, ϕ])² / (2σ²)).
(5.8)

We aim to find the parameters ϕ that make the training data {x_i, y_i} most probable under this distribution (figure 5.4). To accomplish this, we choose a loss function L[ϕ] based on the negative log-likelihood:

L[ϕ] = - ∑_{i=1}^I log Pr(y_i|f[x_i, ϕ], σ²) = - ∑_{i=1}^I log (1 / √(2πσ²) exp(-(y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²))).
(5.9)

When we train the model, we seek parameters ˆϕ that minimize this loss.
motivation_md: Modeling outputs with a normal distribution in univariate regression allows capturing uncertainty and leads to a principled loss function based on likelihood.
recap_md:
- Univariate regression predicts scalar output y from input x.
- Use a normal distribution with mean µ and variance σ² to model outputs.
- Train by minimizing negative log-likelihood of the data under this distribution.

title: loss function for univariate regression using normal distribution
one_liner: The least squares loss function for univariate regression arises by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of a normal distribution with fixed variance, leading to minimizing the sum of squared errors.
content:
Example 1: univariate regression

Figure 5.3 The univariate normal distribution (also known as the Gaussian distribution) is defined on the real line z ∈ R and has parameters µ and σ². The mean µ determines the position of the peak. The positive root of the variance σ² (the standard deviation) determines the width of the distribution. Since the total probability density sums to one, the peak becomes higher as the variance decreases and the distribution becomes narrower.

We start by considering univariate regression models. Here the goal is to predict a single scalar output y ∈ R from input x using a model f[x, ϕ] with parameters ϕ. Following the recipe, we choose a probability distribution over the output domain y. We select the univariate normal distribution (figure 5.3), which is defined over y ∈ R. This has two parameters (mean µ and variance σ²) and has a probability density function:

Pr(y|µ, σ²) = (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(y - µ)² / (2σ²)).
(5.7)

Second, we set the machine learning model f[x, ϕ] to compute one or more of the parameters of this distribution. Here, we just compute the mean so µ = f[x, ϕ]:

Pr(y|f[x, ϕ], σ²) = (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(y - f[x, ϕ])² / (2σ²)).
(5.8)

We aim to find the parameters ϕ that make the training data {x_i, y_i} most probable under this distribution (figure 5.4). To accomplish this, we choose a loss function L[ϕ] based on the negative log-likelihood:

L[ϕ] = - ∑_{i=1}^I log Pr(y_i|f[x_i, ϕ], σ²) = - ∑_{i=1}^I log (1 / √(2πσ²) exp(-(y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²))).
(5.9)

When we train the model, we seek parameters ˆϕ that minimize this loss.

Least squares loss function

Now let’s perform some algebraic manipulations on the loss function. We seek:

ˆϕ = argmin_ϕ - ∑_{i=1}^I log (1 / √(2πσ²) exp(-(y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²)))

= argmin_ϕ - ∑_{i=1}^I (log (1 / √(2πσ²)) - (y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²))

= argmin_ϕ - ∑_{i=1}^I (-(y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²))

= argmin_ϕ ∑_{i=1}^I (y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])²,

where terms independent of ϕ are removed. This recovers the least squares loss function:

L[ϕ] = ∑_{i=1}^I (y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])².

motivation_md: Minimizing the negative log-likelihood of a normal distribution with fixed variance leads to the familiar least squares loss, connecting probabilistic modeling with classical regression.
recap_md:
- The normal distribution models output uncertainty with mean and variance.
- Minimizing negative log-likelihood yields the least squares loss.
- Least squares loss sums squared differences between true and predicted values.

title: Least squares loss function
one_liner: The least squares loss function is derived by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of a normal distribution, resulting in minimizing the sum of squared errors between observed and predicted values.
content:
Least squares loss function

Now let’s perform some algebraic manipulations on the loss function. We seek:

ˆϕ = argmin_ϕ - ∑_{i=1}^I log (1 / √(2πσ²) exp(-(y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²)))

= argmin_ϕ - ∑_{i=1}^I (log (1 / √(2πσ²)) - (y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²))

= argmin_ϕ - ∑_{i=1}^I (-(y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²))

= argmin_ϕ ∑_{i=1}^I (y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])²,

where we removed the first term because it doesn’t depend on ϕ and the denominator as it is a positive constant scaling factor that does not affect the position of the minimum.

The result of these manipulations is the least squares loss function originally introduced in chapter 2:

L[ϕ] = ∑_{i=1}^I (y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])².
(5.11)
motivation_md: Deriving the least squares loss from a probabilistic perspective shows its foundation in maximum likelihood estimation with a normal distribution.
recap_md:
- The loss function is the negative log-likelihood of a normal distribution.
- Terms independent of parameters are removed to simplify.
- The resulting loss sums squared errors between observed and predicted values.

title: Estimating variance
one_liner: We can treat the variance σ² as a learned parameter and minimize the negative log-likelihood loss with respect to both model parameters ϕ and variance σ².
content:
Estimating variance

To formulate the least squares loss function, we assumed that the network predicted the mean of a normal distribution. The final expression in equation 5.11 (perhaps surprisingly) does not depend on the variance σ². However, there is nothing to stop us from treating σ² as a learned parameter and minimizing equation 5.9 with respect to both the model parameters ϕ and the distribution variance σ²:

ˆϕ, ˆσ² = argmin_{ϕ, σ²} - ∑_{i=1}^I log (1 / √(2πσ²) exp(-(y_i - f[x_i, ϕ])² / (2σ²))).
(5.13)
motivation_md: Learning the variance parameter allows the model to capture output uncertainty more flexibly rather than assuming a fixed variance.
recap_md:
- Least squares loss assumes a fixed variance σ².
- The variance σ² can be treated as a learnable parameter.
- Minimize negative log-likelihood jointly over ϕ and σ².

title: universal approximation theorem for multivariate inputs and outputs
one_liner: The universal approximation theorem also holds for networks mapping multivariate inputs to multivariate outputs.
content: In the above example, the network has a single scalar input x and a single scalar output y. However, the universal approximation theorem also holds for the more general case where the network maps multivariate inputs x = [x1, x2, . . . , xDi]^T to multivariate output predictions y = [y1, y2, . . . , yDo]^T. We first explore how to extend the model to predict multivariate outputs. Then we consider multivariate inputs. Finally, in section 3.4, we ...
motivation_md: Extending the universal approximation theorem to multivariate inputs and outputs allows neural networks to model complex, high-dimensional data and predict multiple outputs simultaneously.
recap_md:
- The universal approximation theorem applies beyond scalar inputs and outputs.
- Networks can map vectors x ∈ R^{Di} to vectors y ∈ R^{Do}.
- This extension enables modeling of complex multivariate relationships.

title: Visualizing multivariate inputs
one_liner: To cope with multivariate inputs x, we extend the linear relations between the input and the hidden units.
content:
To cope with multivariate inputs x, we extend the linear relations between the input and the hidden units. So a network with two inputs x = [x1, x2]^T and a scalar output y (figure 3.7) might have three hidden units defined by:

h_1 = a[\theta_{10} + \theta_{11}x_1 + \theta_{12}x_2]

h_2 = a[\theta_{20} + \theta_{21}x_1 + \theta_{22}x_2]

h_3 = a[\theta_{30} + \theta_{31}x_1 + \theta_{32}x_2],

where there is now one slope parameter for each input. The hidden units are combined to form the output in the usual way:

y = \phi_0 + \phi_1 h_1 + \phi_2 h_2 + \phi_3 h_3.

Figure 3.8 illustrates the processing of this network. Each hidden unit receives a linear combination of the two inputs, which forms an oriented plane in the 3D input/output space. The activation function clips the negative values of these planes to zero. The clipped planes are then recombined in a second linear function (equation 3.10) to create a continuous piecewise linear surface consisting of convex polygonal regions (figure 3.8j).

Each region corresponds to a different activation pattern. For example, in the central triangular region, the first and third hidden units are active, and the second is inactive. When there are more than two inputs to the model, it becomes difficult to visualize. However, the interpretation is similar. The output will be a continuous piecewise linear function of the input, where the linear regions are now convex polytopes in the multidimensional input space.

Note that as the input dimensions grow, the number of linear regions increases rapidly (figure 3.9). To get a feeling for how rapidly, consider that each hidden unit defines a hyperplane that delineates the part of space where this unit is active from the part where it is not (cyan lines in 3.8d–f). If we had the same number of hidden units as input dimensions D_i, we could align each hyperplane with one of the coordinate axes (figure 3.10). For two input dimensions, this would divide the space into four quadrants. For three dimensions, this would create eight octants, and for D_i dimensions, this would create 2^{D_i} orthants. Shallow neural networks usually have more hidden units than input dimensions, so they typically create more than 2^{D_i} linear regions.
motivation_md: Multivariate inputs require extending the linear relations in neural networks to handle multiple input dimensions, enabling the network to form complex piecewise linear functions over multidimensional input spaces.
recap_md:
- Multivariate inputs extend linear relations between inputs and hidden units.
- Hidden units receive linear combinations forming oriented planes.
- Activation functions clip these planes, creating piecewise linear convex regions.

title: Shallow neural networks: general case
one_liner: A general shallow neural network maps multi-dimensional inputs to multi-dimensional outputs using hidden units computed by nonlinear activations on linear combinations of inputs.
content:
A shallow neural network with two inputs x = [x_1, x_2]^T and three hidden units h_1, h_2, h_3 is defined by:

h_1 = a[\theta_{10} + \theta_{11} x_1 + \theta_{12} x_2]

h_2 = a[\theta_{20} + \theta_{21} x_1 + \theta_{22} x_2]

h_3 = a[\theta_{30} + \theta_{31} x_1 + \theta_{32} x_2],

where each hidden unit has one slope parameter per input. The hidden units combine linearly to form the output:

y = \phi_0 + \phi_1 h_1 + \phi_2 h_2 + \phi_3 h_3.

Each hidden unit receives a linear combination of inputs, forming an oriented plane in the 3D input/output space. The activation function clips negative values to zero, and the clipped planes combine linearly to create a continuous piecewise linear surface of convex polygonal regions (figure 3.8j). Each region corresponds to a different activation pattern.

For more than two inputs, visualization is difficult, but the output remains a continuous piecewise linear function where linear regions are convex polytopes in multidimensional input space. As input dimensions grow, the number of linear regions increases rapidly (figure 3.9). Each hidden unit defines a hyperplane separating active and inactive regions; with D_i input dimensions and D hidden units, the network can create more than 2^{D_i} linear regions.

More generally, a shallow neural network y = f[x, \phi] maps multi-dimensional input x ∈ R^{D_i} to output y ∈ R^{D_o} using D hidden units, each computed as:

h_d = a\left(\theta_{d0} + \sum_{i=1}^{D_i} \theta_{di} x_i \right),

and combined linearly to produce output:

y_j = \phi_{j0} + \sum_{d=1}^D \phi_{jd} h_d,

where a[\cdot] is a nonlinear activation function and the model parameters are \phi = \{\theta_{\cdot\cdot}, \phi_{\cdot\cdot}\}.
motivation_md: This general formulation extends shallow neural networks to handle multi-dimensional inputs and outputs, enabling flexible function approximation in high-dimensional spaces.
recap_md:
- Hidden units apply nonlinear activations to linear combinations of inputs.
- Outputs are linear combinations of hidden unit activations.
- The network partitions input space into convex polytopes with piecewise linear functions.

title: Terminology
one_liner: Neural networks are described in terms of layers, units, weights, biases, and activations, with various terms like MLP, shallow, deep, feed-forward, and fully connected networks.
content:
The model has parameters \phi = \{\theta_{\cdot\cdot}, \phi_{\cdot\cdot}\}. Figure 3.11 shows an example with three inputs, three hidden units, and two outputs. The activation function permits the model to describe nonlinear relations between input and output, and as such, it must be nonlinear; with no activation function or a linear activation function, the overall mapping would be linear. Many activation functions have been tried, but the most common is the ReLU, which is easily interpretable.

With ReLU activations, the network divides the input space into convex polytopes defined by intersections of hyperplanes computed by the "joints" in the ReLU functions. Each convex polytope contains a different linear function. The polytopes are the same for each output, but the linear functions they contain can differ.

Neural networks have much jargon. They are often described in terms of layers: the input layer, hidden layer(s), and output layer. For example, a network with one hidden layer containing four hidden units is called a shallow neural network. Hidden units are sometimes called neurons. The values before activation functions are pre-activations; after activation, they are activations.

Any neural network with at least one hidden layer is called a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Networks with one hidden layer are shallow neural networks; those with multiple hidden layers are deep neural networks. Networks with acyclic connections are feed-forward networks. If every unit in one layer connects to every unit in the next, the network is fully connected.

Connections represent slope parameters called weights. Offset parameters are called biases. The variables in the hidden layer are neurons or hidden units. Values feeding into hidden units are pre-activations; values after activation are activations.
motivation_md: Understanding the terminology clarifies the structure and components of neural networks, facilitating communication and comprehension of their architecture and function.
recap_md:
- Neural networks have layers: input, hidden, and output.
- Hidden units (neurons) have pre-activations and activations.
- Networks are described as MLPs, shallow/deep, feed-forward, and fully connected.

title: Activation functions
one_liner: ReLU is the most common activation function, dividing input space into convex polytopes with piecewise linear functions.
content:
Activation functions are nonlinear functions applied to the outputs of linear combinations in neural networks. The ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation function is the most common choice due to its interpretability and effectiveness. With ReLU activations, the network divides the input space into convex polytopes defined by intersections of hyperplanes computed by the "joints" in the ReLU functions. Each convex polytope contains a different linear function. The polytopes are the same for each output, but the linear functions they contain can differ.

Neural networks have a lot of associated jargon. They are often described in terms of layers: input, hidden, and output layers. A network with one hidden layer containing four hidden units is a shallow neural network; multiple hidden layers form a deep neural network. Networks with acyclic connections are feed-forward networks. If every element in one layer connects to every element in the next, the network is fully connected.

Connections represent slope parameters called weights; offset parameters are called biases. The values feeding into hidden units before activation are pre-activations; after activation, they are activations.

Shallow neural networks compute several linear functions of the input, pass each result through an activation function, then take a linear combination of these activations to form outputs. With enough hidden units, shallow neural networks can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary precision.

Historically, activation functions included logistic sigmoid and tanh. The ReLU was re-popularized in the 2000s and has the advantage that its derivative is one for positive inputs, aiding training stability and efficiency. However, ReLU's derivative is zero for negative inputs, leading to the "dying ReLU" problem where some units never activate during training.

Variations like leaky ReLU, parametric ReLU, and concatenated ReLU address this problem. Smooth functions such as SoftPlus, Gaussian error linear unit, sigmoid linear unit, and exponential linear unit have also been proposed. The scaled exponential linear unit helps stabilize activation variance. The Swish function, discovered empirically, and its approximation HardSwish are other notable activation functions.

No definitive best activation function exists, but leaky ReLU and parametric ReLU can provide minor gains. This book focuses on the basic ReLU due to its ease of characterization in terms of linear regions.
motivation_md: Activation functions introduce nonlinearity essential for neural networks to model complex functions; ReLU is popular for its simplicity and training benefits despite some limitations.
recap_md:
- Activation functions add nonlinearity; ReLU is most common.
- ReLU divides input space into convex polytopes with piecewise linear functions.
- Variants like leaky ReLU address the dying ReLU problem.

title: Universal approximation theorem
one_liner: The width version of the universal approximation theorem states that a network with one hidden layer and finite hidden units can approximate any continuous function on a compact subset of R^n.
content: Universal approximation theorem: The width version of this theorem states that for any continuous function on a compact subset of \mathbb{R}^n and for an arbitrary specified accuracy, there exists a network with one hidden layer containing a finite number of hidden units that can approximate the given function to that accuracy. This was proved by Cybenko (1989) for a class of sigmoid activations and was later shown to be true for a larger class of nonlinear activation functions (Hornik, 1991).
motivation_md: This theorem guarantees that shallow neural networks with sufficient width can approximate any continuous function, justifying their use as universal function approximators.
recap_md:
- Any continuous function on a compact subset of \mathbb{R}^n can be approximated.
- Approximation achieved by a network with one hidden layer and finite units.
- Proven for sigmoid and other nonlinear activation functions.

title: Binomial coeﬀicient
one_liner: The number of regions created by D hyperplanes in Di-dimensional input space is at most the sum of binomial coefficients from j=0 to Di of (D choose j).
content: The number of regions created by D hyperplanes in the D_i \le D-dimensional input space was shown by Zaslavsky (1975) to be at most \sum_{j=0}^{D_i} \binom{D}{j} (i.e., a sum of binomial coefficients). As a rule of thumb, shallow neural networks almost always have a larger number D of hidden units than input dimensions D_i and create between 2^{D_i} and 2^D linear regions.
motivation_md: Understanding the maximum number of linear regions formed by hyperplanes helps characterize the complexity and expressive power of shallow neural networks.
recap_md:
- Maximum regions formed by D hyperplanes in D_i-dimensional space is \sum_{j=0}^{D_i} \binom{D}{j}.
- Shallow networks typically have more hidden units than input dimensions.
- They create between 2^{D_i} and 2^D linear regions.

title: Linear, aﬀine, and nonlinear functions
one_liner: A linear function obeys superposition, but adding an offset makes it affine; both are often called linear in machine learning.
content: Linear, affine, and nonlinear functions: Technically, a linear transformation f[\cdot] is any function that obeys the principle of superposition, so f[a+b] = f[a] + f[b]. This definition implies that f[2a] = 2f[a]. The weighted sum f[h_1, h_2, h_3] = \phi_1 h_1 + \phi_2 h_2 + \phi_3 h_3 is linear, but once the offset (bias) is added so f[h_1, h_2, h_3] = \phi_0 + \phi_1 h_1 + \phi_2 h_2 + \phi_3 h_3, this is no longer true. To see this, consider that the output is doubled when we double the arguments of the former function. This is not the case for the latter function, which is more properly termed an affine function. However, it is common in machine learning to conflate these terms. We follow this convention in this book and refer to both as linear. All other functions we will encounter are nonlinear.
motivation_md: Distinguishing linear and affine functions clarifies the role of offsets (biases) in models, though machine learning often treats both as linear for simplicity.
recap_md:
- Linear functions obey superposition: f[a+b] = f[a] + f[b].
- Adding an offset creates an affine function, not strictly linear.
- Machine learning often calls both linear for convenience.

title: Regularizer
one_liner: Any factor that biases a solution toward a subset of equivalent solutions is known as a regularizer.
content: A subset of the solutions with a similar training loss is known as a regularizer. It is thought that the initialization and/or fitting of neural networks have an implicit regularizing effect. Consequently, in the over-parameterized regime, more reasonable solutions, such as that in panel (a), are encouraged. The answer to this question is uncertain, but there are two likely possibilities. First, the network initialization may encourage smoothness, and the model never departs from the sub-domain of smooth function during the training process. Second, the training algorithm may somehow “prefer” to converge to smooth functions. Any factor that biases a solution toward a subset of equivalent solutions is known as a regularizer, so one possibility is that the training algorithm acts as an implicit regularizer (see section 9.2).
motivation_md: Regularizers help bias solutions toward more reasonable or smooth functions, especially in over-parameterized neural networks, improving model behavior and generalization.
recap_md:
- A regularizer biases solutions toward a subset of equivalent solutions.
- Neural network initialization and training may implicitly regularize toward smoothness.
- Training algorithms can act as implicit regularizers.

title: Implicit regularization
one_liner: It is thought that the initialization and/or fitting of neural networks have an implicit regularizing effect.
content: It is thought that the initialization and/or fitting of neural networks have an implicit regularizing effect. Consequently, in the over-parameterized regime, more reasonable solutions, such as that in panel (a), are encouraged. The answer to this question is uncertain, but there are two likely possibilities. First, the network initialization may encourage smoothness, and the model never departs from the sub-domain of smooth function during the training process. Second, the training algorithm may somehow “prefer” to converge to smooth functions. Any factor that biases a solution toward a subset of equivalent solutions is known as a regularizer, so one possibility is that the training algorithm acts as an implicit regularizer (see section 9.2).
motivation_md: Implicit regularization explains why neural networks trained with standard methods tend to find smooth, reasonable solutions despite over-parameterization.
recap_md:
- Neural network initialization and fitting may implicitly regularize solutions.
- This encourages smooth functions during training.
- Training algorithms may prefer convergence to smooth functions.

title: Hyperparameters
one_liner: The process of finding the best hyperparameters is termed hyperparameter search or neural architecture search when focused on network structure.
content: These are termed hyperparameters. The process of finding the best hyperparameters is termed hyperparameter search or (when focused on network structure) neural architecture search.
motivation_md: Hyperparameters control model behavior and must be tuned to optimize performance, motivating hyperparameter search methods.
recap_md:
- Hyperparameters are parameters set before training.
- Finding the best hyperparameters is called hyperparameter search.
- Neural architecture search focuses on network structure hyperparameters.

title: Hyperparameter search
one_liner: Hyperparameter search is the process of finding the best hyperparameters or neural architecture.
content: Hyperparameter search or (when focused on network structure) neural architecture search.
motivation_md: Hyperparameter search systematically identifies the best hyperparameters to improve model performance.
recap_md:
- Hyperparameter search finds the best hyperparameters.
- Neural architecture search focuses on network structure.
- Both optimize model performance.

title: Validation set
one_liner: For every choice of hyperparameters, we train the associated model using the training set and evaluate performance on the validation set.
content: As a validation set, for every choice of hyperparameters, we train the associated model using the training set and evaluate performance on the validation set. Finally, we select the model that worked best on the validation set and measure its performance on the test set.
motivation_md: Validation sets help select the best hyperparameters by evaluating model performance on unseen data before final testing.
recap_md:
- Validation sets evaluate model performance for hyperparameter choices.
- Models are trained on the training set.
- The best model on the validation set is selected for final testing.

title: Generalization
one_liner: To measure performance, we use a separate test set.
content: To measure performance, we use a separate test set. The degree to which performance is good on this test set reflects the model's ability to generalize beyond the training data.
motivation_md: Generalization measures how well a model performs on unseen data, indicating its real-world effectiveness.
recap_md:
- Performance is measured on a separate test set.
- Good test performance indicates strong generalization.
- Generalization reflects model ability beyond training data.

title: Bias-variance trade-off
one_liner: This is known as the bias-variance trade-off, and there is a capacity where the trade-off is optimal.
content: Bias but increases variance. This is known as the bias-variance trade-off, and there is a capacity where the trade-off is optimal.
motivation_md: The bias-variance trade-off balances underfitting and overfitting to optimize model capacity and performance.
recap_md:
- Increasing capacity reduces bias but increases variance.
- The bias-variance trade-off balances these effects.
- There is an optimal capacity for this trade-off.

title: Double descent curve
one_liner: Together, these two phenomena create the double descent curve.
content: Capacity, even when the parameters exceed the training examples. Together, these two phenomena create the double descent curve. It is thought that the model interpolates.
motivation_md: The double descent curve explains how model performance can improve even beyond traditional overfitting points as capacity increases.
recap_md:
- Model capacity can exceed the number of training examples.
- This leads to the double descent curve phenomenon.
- The model is thought to interpolate training data in this regime.

title: interpretation of cross-entropy as uncertainty measure
one_liner: The cross-entropy can be interpreted as the amount of uncertainty that remains in one distribution after taking into account what we already know from the other.
content:
The first term disappears, as it has no dependence on \(\theta\). The remaining second term is known as the cross-entropy. It can be interpreted as the amount of uncertainty that remains in one distribution after taking into account what we already know from the other. Now, we substitute in the definition of \(q(y)\) from equation 5.28:

\[
\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \left[- \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I \delta[y - y_i] \right) \log \left( \Pr(y|\theta) \right) dy \right] = \arg\min_{\theta} \left[-\frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I \log \left( \Pr(y_i|\theta) \right) \right] = \arg\min_{\theta} \left[- \sum_{i=1}^I \log \left( \Pr(y_i|\theta) \right) \right].
\]
motivation_md: Cross-entropy quantifies the remaining uncertainty in one distribution after considering another, providing a principled way to measure how well a model distribution matches empirical data.
recap_md:
- Cross-entropy measures uncertainty remaining in one distribution after accounting for another.
- It is computed as the negative expected log-probability of data under the model.
- Minimizing cross-entropy corresponds to maximizing data likelihood.

title: equivalence of negative log-likelihood and cross-entropy loss
aliases: equivalence of negative log-likelihood and cross-entropy loss
one_liner: The negative log-likelihood criterion and the cross-entropy criterion are equivalent.
content: It follows that the negative log-likelihood criterion (from maximizing the data likelihood) and the cross-entropy criterion (from minimizing the distance between the model and empirical data distributions) are equivalent.
motivation_md: Understanding this equivalence clarifies why minimizing cross-entropy loss is a principled approach to fitting probabilistic models to data.
recap_md:
- Negative log-likelihood and cross-entropy loss are equivalent criteria.
- Both arise from fitting model distributions to data.
- This equivalence underpins many loss functions in probabilistic modeling.

title: summary of loss functions and modeling approach
one_liner: Neural networks compute parameters of probability distributions over outputs, leading to principled loss functions based on maximizing data likelihood or minimizing negative log-likelihood.
content:
We previously considered neural networks as directly predicting outputs \(y\) from data \(x\). In this chapter, we shifted perspective to think about neural networks as computing the parameters \(\theta\) of probability distributions \(\Pr(y|\theta)\) over the output space. This led to a principled approach to building loss functions. We selected model parameters \(\phi\) that maximized the likelihood of the observed data under these distributions. We saw that this is equivalent to minimizing the negative log-likelihood.

The least squares criterion for regression is a natural consequence of this approach; it follows from the assumption that \(y\) is normally distributed and that we are predicting the mean. We also saw how the regression model could be (i) extended to estimate the uncertainty over the prediction and (ii) extended to make that uncertainty dependent on the input (the heteroscedastic model). We applied the same approach to both binary and multiclass classification and derived loss functions for each.

We discussed how to tackle more complex data types and how to deal with multiple outputs. Finally, we argued that cross-entropy is an equivalent way to think about fitting models.
motivation_md: This approach provides a unified framework for designing loss functions by modeling outputs probabilistically, allowing principled training of neural networks for various tasks.
recap_md:
- Neural networks model parameters \(\theta\) of output distributions \(\Pr(y|\theta)\).
- Loss functions arise from maximizing likelihood or minimizing negative log-likelihood.
- Extensions include uncertainty estimation and classification loss functions.

title: notes on loss functions and related research
one_liner: Loss functions can be designed for complex data types, multiple outputs, and various modeling goals, with extensive related research on robust regression, quantile estimation, class imbalance, and ranking.
content:
In previous chapters, we developed neural network models. In this chapter, we developed loss functions for deciding how well a model describes the training data for a given set of parameters. The next chapter considers model training, in which we aim to find the model parameters that minimize this loss.

Losses based on the normal distribution: Nix & Weigend (1994) and Williams (1996) investigated heteroscedastic nonlinear regression in which both the mean and the variance of the output are functions of the input. In the context of unsupervised learning, Burda et al. (2016) use a loss function based on a multivariate normal distribution with diagonal covariance, and Dorta et al. (2018) use a loss function based on a normal distribution with full covariance.

Robust regression: Qi et al. (2020) investigate the properties of regression models that minimize mean absolute error rather than mean squared error. This loss function follows from assuming a Laplace distribution over the outputs and estimates the median output for a given input rather than the mean. Barron (2019) presents a loss function that parameterizes the degree of robustness. When interpreted in a probabilistic context, it yields a family of univariate probability distributions that includes the normal and Cauchy distributions as special cases.

Estimating quantiles: Sometimes, we may not want to estimate the mean or median in a regression task but may instead want to predict a quantile. For example, this is useful for risk models, where we want to know that the true value will be less than the predicted value 90% of the time. This is known as quantile regression (Koenker & Hallock, 2001). This could be done by fitting a heteroscedastic regression model and then estimating the quantile based on the predicted normal distribution. Alternatively, the quantiles can be estimated directly using quantile loss (also known as pinball loss). In practice, this minimizes the absolute deviations of the data from the model but weights the deviations in one direction more than the other. Recent work has investigated simultaneously predicting multiple quantiles to get an idea of the overall distribution shape (Rodrigues & Pereira, 2020).

Class imbalance and focal loss: Lin et al. (2017c) address data imbalance in classification problems. If the number of examples for some classes is much greater than for others, then the standard maximum likelihood loss does not work well; the model may concentrate on becoming more confident about well-classified examples from the dominant classes and classify less well-represented classes poorly. Lin et al. (2017c) introduce focal loss, which adds a single extra parameter that down-weights the effect of well-classified examples to improve performance.

Learning to rank: Cao et al. (2007), Xia et al. (2008), and Chen et al. (2009) all used the Plackett-Luce model in loss functions for learning to rank data. This is the listwise approach to learning to rank as the model ingests an entire list of objects to be ranked at once. Alternative approaches are the pointwise approach, in which the model ingests a single object, and the pairwise approach, where the model ingests pairs of objects. Chen et al. (2009) summarize different approaches for learning to rank.

Other data types: Fan et al. (2020) use a loss based on the beta distribution for predicting values between zero and one. Jacobs et al. (1991) and Bishop (1994) investigated mixture density networks for multimodal data. These model the output as a mixture of Gaussians.
motivation_md: Loss functions must adapt to diverse data types, modeling goals, and challenges like class imbalance, motivating extensive research on robust, quantile, and ranking losses.
recap_md:
- Loss functions extend to heteroscedastic regression, robust regression, and quantile estimation.
- Focal loss addresses class imbalance by down-weighting well-classified examples.
- Learning to rank uses listwise, pointwise, and pairwise approaches with specialized loss functions.

title: von Mises distribution
one_liner: The von Mises distribution is defined over the circular domain (−π, π] with mean µ and concentration κ > 0.
content: The von Mises distribution is defined over the circular domain \((-\pi, \pi]\). It has two parameters. The mean \(\mu\) determines the position of the peak. The concentration \(\kappa > 0\) acts like the inverse of the variance. Hence \(1/\sqrt{\kappa}\) is roughly equivalent to the standard deviation in a normal distribution.
motivation_md: The von Mises distribution models data on a circle, such as angles, with parameters controlling peak location and concentration, analogous to mean and variance in normal distributions.
recap_md:
- Defined on the circular domain \((-\pi, \pi]\).
- Mean \(\mu\) locates the peak.
- Concentration \(\kappa > 0\) inversely relates to variance.

title: Non-probabilistic approaches
one_liner: Non-probabilistic loss functions, such as hinge loss and exponential loss, can be used instead of probabilistic approaches.
content: It is not strictly necessary to adopt the probabilistic approach discussed in this chapter, but this has become the default in recent years; any loss function that aims to reduce the distance between the model output and the training outputs will suffice, and distance can be defined in any way that seems sensible. There are several well-known non-probabilistic machine learning models for classification, including support vector machines (Vapnik, 1995; Cristianini & Shawe-Taylor, 2000), which use hinge loss, and AdaBoost (Freund & Schapire, 1997), which uses exponential loss.
motivation_md: While probabilistic loss functions are common, alternative non-probabilistic losses provide flexibility and have been successful in classification tasks.
recap_md:
- Probabilistic loss functions are common but not mandatory.
- Non-probabilistic losses include hinge loss and exponential loss.
- Support vector machines and AdaBoost use these non-probabilistic losses.

title: Local minima and saddle points
one_liner: Loss functions can have many local minima and saddle points, making it challenging to find the global minimum.
content:
Figure 6.4 depicts the loss function associated with the Gabor model for this dataset. There are numerous local minima (cyan circles). Here the gradient is zero, and the loss increases if we move in any direction, but we are not at the overall minimum of the function. The point with the lowest loss is known as the global minimum and is depicted by the gray circle.

If we start in a random position and use gradient descent to go downhill, there is no guarantee that we will wind up at the global minimum and find the best parameters (figure 6.5a). It’s equally or even more likely that the algorithm will terminate in one of the local minima. Furthermore, there is no way of knowing whether there is a better solution elsewhere.

In addition, the loss function contains saddle points where the gradient is locally zero, but the function increases in some directions and decreases in others. The blue cross in figure 6.4 is an example of a saddle point; the function decreases as we move horizontally in either direction but increases as we move vertically. If the current parameters are not exactly at the saddle point, then gradient descent can escape by moving downhill. However, the surface near the saddle point is flat, so it’s hard to be sure that training hasn’t converged; if we terminate the algorithm when the gradient is small, we may erroneously stop near a saddle point.
motivation_md: Understanding local minima and saddle points explains why optimization algorithms may get stuck and why finding the global minimum is challenging.
recap_md:
- Loss functions can have many local minima where gradient is zero but not minimal.
- Gradient descent may converge to local minima instead of the global minimum.
- Saddle points have zero gradient but mixed curvature, complicating convergence detection.

title: Stochastic gradient descent
one_liner: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) adds noise to gradient descent by using random subsets of data to help escape local minima and saddle points.
content:
The Gabor model has two parameters, so we could find the global minimum by either (i) exhaustively searching the parameter space or (ii) repeatedly starting gradient descent from different positions and choosing the result with the lowest loss. However, neural network models can have millions of parameters, so neither approach is practical. In short, using gradient descent to find the global optimum of a high-dimensional loss function is challenging. We can find a minimum, but there is no way to tell whether this is the global minimum or even a good one.

One of the main problems is that the final destination of a gradient descent algorithm is entirely determined by the starting point. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) attempts to remedy this problem by adding some noise to the gradient at each step. The solution still moves downhill on average, but at any given iteration, the direction chosen is not necessarily in the steepest downhill direction. Indeed, it might not be downhill at all. The SGD algorithm has the possibility of moving temporarily uphill and hence jumping from one “valley” of the loss function to another (figure 6.5b).

The mechanism for introducing randomness is simple. At each iteration, the algorithm chooses a random subset of the training data and computes the gradient from these examples alone.
