This subset is known as a minibatch or batch for short. The update rule for the model parameters \(\phi_t\) at iteration \(t\) is hence:

\[
\phi_{t+1} \leftarrow \phi_t - \alpha \cdot \sum_{i \in B_t} \frac{\partial \ell_i[\phi_t]}{\partial \phi},
\]

where \(B_t\) is a set containing the indices of the input/output pairs in the current batch and, as before, \(\ell_i\) is the loss due to the \(i\)th pair. The term \(\alpha\) is the learning rate, and together with the gradient magnitude, determines the distance moved at each iteration. The learning rate is chosen at the start of the procedure and does not depend on the local properties of the function.

The batches are usually drawn from the dataset without replacement. The algorithm works through the training examples until it has used all the data, at which point it starts sampling from the full training dataset again. A single pass through the entire training dataset is referred to as an epoch. A batch may be as small as a single example or as large as the whole dataset. The latter case is called full-batch gradient descent and is identical to regular (non-stochastic) gradient descent.

An alternative interpretation of SGD is that it computes the gradient of a different loss function at each iteration; the loss function depends on both the model and the training data and hence will differ for each randomly selected batch. In this view, SGD performs deterministic gradient descent on a constantly changing loss function (figure 6.6). However, despite this variability, the expected loss and expected gradients at any point remain the same as for gradient descent.

SGD has several attractive features. First, although it adds noise to the trajectory, it still improves the fit to a subset of the data at each iteration. Hence, the updates tend to be sensible even if they are not optimal. Second, because it draws training examples without replacement and iterates through the dataset, the training examples all still contribute equally. Third, it is less computationally expensive to compute the gradient from just a subset of the training data. Fourth, it can (in principle) escape local minima. Fifth, it reduces the chances of getting stuck near saddle points; it is likely that at least some of the possible batches will have a significant gradient at any point on the loss function. Finally, there is some evidence that SGD finds parameters for neural networks that cause them to generalize well to new data in practice (see section 9.2).

SGD does not necessarily “converge” in the traditional sense. However, the hope is that when we are close to the global minimum, all the data points will be well described by the model. Consequently, the gradient will be small, whichever batch is chosen, and the parameters will cease to change much. In practice, SGD is often applied with a learning rate schedule. The learning rate \(\alpha\) starts at a high value and is decreased by a constant factor every \(N\) epochs. The logic is that in the early stages of training, we want the algorithm to explore the parameter space, jumping from valley to valley to find a sensible region. In later stages, we are roughly in the right place and are more concerned with fine-tuning the parameters, so we decrease \(\alpha\) to make smaller changes.
motivation_md: SGD introduces randomness to help escape local minima and saddle points, enabling training of high-dimensional models like neural networks.
recap_md:
- SGD uses random subsets (batches) of data to compute gradients.
- It can escape local minima and saddle points by adding noise.
- Learning rate schedules help balance exploration and fine-tuning.

title: loss function for multiclass classification using categorical distribution
one_liner: The loss function is the negative log-likelihood of the training data for multiclass classification using the categorical distribution.
content:
The goal of multiclass classification is to assign an input data example x to one of K > 2 classes, so y ∈ {1, 2, ..., K}. Real-world examples include predicting which of K = 10 digits y is present in an image x of a handwritten number or predicting which of K possible words y follows an incomplete sentence x.

We choose a distribution over the prediction space y. Since y ∈ {1, 2, ..., K}, we select the categorical distribution, which has K parameters λ1, λ2, ..., λK that determine the probability of each category: Pr(y = k) = λk. These parameters must lie in the range [0, 1] and collectively sum to one to ensure a valid probability distribution.

A network f[x, ϕ] with K outputs computes these K parameters from the input x. Because the network outputs may not obey the constraints, we pass them through the softmax function, which converts an arbitrary vector of length K into a vector with elements in [0, 1] summing to one. The kth output of the softmax function is:

softmax_k[z] = exp[z_k] / \sum_{k'=1}^K exp[z_{k'}],

where the exponentials ensure positivity, and the denominator ensures the sum is one.

The likelihood that input x has label y = k is:

Pr(y = k | x) = softmax_k(f[x, ϕ]).

The loss function is the negative log-likelihood of the training data:

L[ϕ] = - \sum_{i=1}^I \log(softmax_{y_i}(f[x_i, ϕ])) = - \sum_{i=1}^I \left(f_{y_i}[x_i, ϕ] - \log \sum_{k'=1}^K \exp(f_{k'}[x_i, ϕ])\right),

where f_{y_i}[x, ϕ] and f_{k'}[x, ϕ] denote the y_i-th and k'-th outputs of the network, respectively. This is known as the multiclass cross-entropy loss.
motivation_md: Multiclass classification requires assigning inputs to one of multiple classes, so we need a loss function that models probabilities over these classes and guides the model to predict correct class probabilities.
recap_md:
- Multiclass classification assigns inputs to one of K > 2 classes using the categorical distribution.
- The softmax function converts arbitrary network outputs into valid probability parameters for the categorical distribution.
- The loss function is the negative log-likelihood (multiclass cross-entropy) of the training data under the model.

title: softmax function
one_liner: The softmax function takes an arbitrary vector of length K and returns a vector with elements in [0, 1] that sum to one.
content:
The softmax function takes an arbitrary vector of length K and returns a vector of the same length where the elements are in the range [0, 1] and sum to one. The kth output of the softmax function is:

softmax_k[z] = \frac{\exp[z_k]}{\sum_{k'=1}^K \exp[z_{k'}]},

where the exponential functions ensure positivity, and the sum in the denominator ensures the K numbers sum to one.
motivation_md: The softmax function is used to convert arbitrary real-valued outputs from a network into valid probability distributions over multiple classes.
recap_md:
- Softmax converts any vector into a probability distribution with non-negative elements summing to one.
- Each output is computed as the exponential of the input element divided by the sum of exponentials.
- This ensures positivity and normalization of outputs.

title: Multiple outputs
one_liner: Multiple outputs involve predicting vector-valued targets by treating each prediction as independent and modeling each element's distribution separately.
content:
Often, we wish to make more than one prediction with the same model, so the target output y is a vector. For example, predicting a molecule’s melting and boiling points (multivariate regression) or the object class at every point in an image (multivariate classification).

While it is possible to define multivariate probability distributions and model their parameters as a function of the input, it is more usual to treat each prediction as independent. Independence implies that the probability Pr(y | f[x, ϕ]) is treated as a product of univariate terms for each element y_d ∈ y:

Pr(y | f[x, ϕ]) = \prod_d Pr(y_d | f_d[x, ϕ]),

where f_d[x, ϕ] is the d-th set of network outputs describing the parameters of the distribution over y_d.

For example, to predict multiple continuous variables y_d ∈ ℝ, we use a normal distribution for each y_d, and the network outputs f_d[x, ϕ] predict the means of these distributions. To predict multiple discrete variables y_d ∈ {1, 2, ..., K}, we use a categorical distribution for each y_d, where each set of network outputs f_d[x, ϕ] predicts the K values that contribute to the categorical distribution for y_d.

When minimizing the negative log probability, the product becomes a sum of terms:

L[ϕ] = - \sum_{i=1}^I \log Pr(y_i | f[x_i, ϕ]) = - \sum_{i=1}^I \sum_d \log Pr(y_{id} | f_d[x_i, ϕ]).
motivation_md: Predicting multiple outputs simultaneously requires modeling each output's distribution; assuming independence simplifies this by treating the joint probability as a product of individual probabilities.
recap_md:
- Multiple outputs predict vector-valued targets, often treating each output independently.
- The joint probability is modeled as a product of univariate distributions for each output element.
- Loss functions sum the negative log-probabilities over all outputs and data points.

title: loss function for multiple outputs assuming independence
one_liner: The loss function for multiple outputs assuming independence sums the negative log probabilities of each output's predicted distribution.
content:
Often, we wish to make more than one prediction with the same model, so the target output y is a vector. For example, predicting a molecule’s melting and boiling point (multivariate regression) or the object class at every point in an image (multivariate classification).

While it is possible to define multivariate probability distributions and use a neural network to model their parameters as a function of the input, it is more usual to treat each prediction as independent. Independence implies that we treat the probability Pr(y | f[x, ϕ]) as a product of univariate terms for each element y_d ∈ y:

Pr(y | f[x, ϕ]) = \prod_d Pr(y_d | f_d[x, ϕ]),

where f_d[x, ϕ] is the d-th set of network outputs describing the parameters of the distribution over y_d.

For example, to predict multiple continuous variables y_d ∈ ℝ, we use a normal distribution for each y_d, and the network outputs f_d[x, ϕ] predict the means of these distributions. To predict multiple discrete variables y_d ∈ {1, 2, ..., K}, we use a categorical distribution for each y_d, where each set of network outputs f_d[x, ϕ] predicts the K values that contribute to the categorical distribution for y_d.

When minimizing the negative log probability, this product becomes a sum of terms:

L[ϕ] = - \sum_{i=1}^I \log Pr(y_i | f[x_i, ϕ]) = - \sum_{i=1}^I \sum_d \log Pr(y_{id} | f_d[x_i, ϕ]).
motivation_md: Modeling multiple outputs simultaneously is common, and assuming independence simplifies the loss function to a sum over individual output losses, making training tractable.
recap_md:
- Multiple outputs are modeled by assuming independence between each output element.
- The joint probability is a product of individual output probabilities.
- The loss function sums negative log probabilities over all outputs and data points.

title: loss functions for various data types
one_liner: To make different types of predictions, we choose an appropriate distribution over that domain and apply the recipe in section 5.2.
content: In this chapter, we have focused on regression and classification because these problems are widespread. However, to make different types of predictions, we simply choose an appropriate distribution over that domain and apply the recipe in section 5.2. Figure 5.11 enumerates a series of probability distributions and their prediction domains. Some of these are explored in the problems at the end of the chapter.
motivation_md: Different prediction problems require different probability distributions and corresponding loss functions; this concept guides choosing the right distribution for the task.
recap_md:
- Regression and classification are common prediction problems.
- Different prediction types require choosing suitable probability distributions.
- The recipe from section 5.2 applies generally to these distributions.

title: loss functions for various prediction types
one_liner: To make different types of predictions, we choose an appropriate distribution over that domain and apply the recipe in section 5.2.
content: In this chapter, we have focused on regression and classification because these problems are widespread. However, to make different types of predictions, we simply choose an appropriate distribution over that domain and apply the recipe in section 5.2. Figure 5.11 enumerates a series of probability distributions and their prediction domains. Some of these are explored in the problems at the end of the chapter.
motivation_md: Choosing the correct probability distribution for the prediction domain allows effective modeling and loss function design for diverse prediction tasks.
recap_md:
- Regression and classification are common prediction problems.
- Different prediction types require suitable probability distributions.
- The recipe from section 5.2 generalizes to these distributions.

title: independence assumption for multiple outputs
one_liner: The independence assumption treats multiple output predictions as independent, modeling the joint probability as a product of individual output probabilities.
content:
Often, we wish to make more than one prediction with the same model, so the target output y is a vector. For example, predicting a molecule’s melting and boiling point (a multivariate regression problem) or the object class at every point in an image (a multivariate classification problem).

While it is possible to define multivariate probability distributions and use a neural network to model their parameters as a function of the input, it is more usual to treat each prediction as independent. Independence implies that we treat the probability Pr(y | f[x, ϕ]) as a product of univariate terms for each element y_d ∈ y:

Pr(y | f[x, ϕ]) = \prod_d Pr(y_d | f_d[x, ϕ]),

where f_d[x, ϕ] is the d-th set of network outputs describing the parameters of the distribution over y_d.

For example, to predict multiple continuous variables y_d ∈ ℝ, we use a normal distribution for each y_d, and the network outputs f_d[x, ϕ] predict the means of these distributions. To predict multiple discrete variables y_d ∈ {1, 2, ..., K}, we use a categorical distribution for each y_d, where each set of network outputs f_d[x, ϕ] predicts the K values that contribute to the categorical distribution for y_d.

When we minimize the negative log probability, this product becomes a sum of terms:

L[ϕ] = - \sum_{i=1}^I \log Pr(y_i | f[x_i, ϕ]) = - \sum_{i=1}^I \sum_d \log Pr(y_{id} | f_d[x_i, ϕ]).
motivation_md: Assuming independence between multiple outputs simplifies modeling and loss computation by allowing the joint probability to factor into individual probabilities.
recap_md:
- Multiple outputs are often modeled as independent predictions.
- The joint probability is the product of individual output probabilities.
- This assumption simplifies the loss function to a sum over outputs.

title: Cross-entropy loss
one_liner: The cross-entropy loss is equivalent to the negative log-likelihood and measures the distance between the empirical data distribution and the model distribution.
content:
The cross-entropy loss is based on finding parameters θ that minimize the distance between the empirical distribution q(y) of observed data y and a model distribution Pr(y | θ). The distance between two probability distributions q(z) and p(z) can be evaluated using the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence:

D_{KL}(q || p) = \int q(z) \log q(z) dz - \int q(z) \log p(z) dz.

Considering the empirical data distribution at points {y_i}_{i=1}^I described as a weighted sum of point masses:

q(y) = \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I \delta[y - y_i],

where δ[•] is the Dirac delta function, we want to minimize the KL divergence between the model distribution Pr(y | θ) and this empirical distribution:

\hat{θ} = \arg\min_θ \left( \int q(y) \log q(y) dy - \int q(y) \log Pr(y | θ) dy \right) = \arg\min_θ \left( - \int q(y) \log Pr(y | θ) dy \right).

The first term disappears as it has no dependence on θ. Substituting q(y) and simplifying gives:

\hat{θ} = \arg\min_θ \left( - \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I \log Pr(y_i | θ) \right) = \arg\min_θ \left( - \sum_{i=1}^I \log Pr(y_i | θ) \right),

where the constant scaling factor 1/I is dropped as it does not affect the minimum position.

In machine learning, the distribution parameters θ are computed by the model f[x_i, ϕ], so:

\hat{ϕ} = \arg\min_ϕ \left( - \sum_{i=1}^I \log Pr(y_i | f[x_i, ϕ]) \right).

Thus, the negative log-likelihood criterion and the cross-entropy criterion are equivalent.
motivation_md: Cross-entropy loss measures how well the model distribution matches the empirical data distribution by minimizing their KL divergence, providing a principled loss function for training probabilistic models.
recap_md:
- Cross-entropy loss minimizes the KL divergence between empirical and model distributions.
- It is equivalent to minimizing the negative log-likelihood of observed data.
- Model parameters are optimized to reduce the cross-entropy loss.

title: Smooth function interpolation in over-parameterized regime
one_liner: More smoothly between the training data points in the over-parameterized “modern regime,” although it is unclear what drives this.
content: More smoothly between the training data points in the over-parameterized “modern regime,” although it is unclear what drives this. To choose the capacity and other model parameters, further investigation is needed.
motivation_md: Understanding smooth interpolation in over-parameterized models is important because it affects how models generalize between training points, though the underlying causes remain unclear.
recap_md:
- Over-parameterized models interpolate more smoothly between training points.
- The reasons for this smoothness are not yet fully understood.
- Choosing model capacity and parameters remains a challenge in this regime.

title: Cross-validation
one_liner: Cross-validation partitions training and validation data into K disjoint subsets to reduce variance and improve hyperparameter selection.
content:
Cross-validation: It is typical to divide the data into three parts: training data (to learn the model parameters), validation data (to choose the hyperparameters), and test data (to estimate the final performance). However, this division may cause problems when the total number of data examples is limited; if the number of training examples is comparable to the model capacity, then the variance will be large.

One way to mitigate this problem is to use k-fold cross-validation. The training and validation data are partitioned into K disjoint subsets. For example, we might divide these data into five parts. We train with four and validate with the fifth for each of the five permutations and choose the hyperparameters based on the average validation performance. The final test performance is assessed using the average of the predictions from the five models with the best hyperparameters on an entirely different test set. There are many variations of this idea, but all share the general goal of using a larger proportion of the data to train the model, thereby reducing variance.
motivation_md: Cross-validation exists to reduce variance in model evaluation and hyperparameter tuning when data is limited, enabling more reliable model selection.
recap_md:
- Data is split into training, validation, and test sets for model learning and evaluation.
- K-fold cross-validation partitions data into K subsets, training on K-1 and validating on the remaining one.
- This approach reduces variance by using more data for training and averaging validation results.

title: Capacity
one_liner: The representational capacity of a model describes the space of possible functions it can construct when we consider all possible parameter values.
content: We have used the term capacity informally to mean the number of parameters or hidden units in the model (and hence indirectly, the ability of the model to fit functions of increasing complexity). The representational capacity of a model describes the space of possible functions it can construct when we consider all possible parameter values. When we take into account the fact that an optimization algorithm may not be able to reach all of these solutions, what is left is the effective capacity.
motivation_md: Capacity measures a model's ability to represent complex functions, which is crucial for understanding its potential to fit data and generalize.
recap_md:
- Capacity often refers to the number of parameters or hidden units in a model.
- Representational capacity is the set of all functions a model can represent with any parameter values.
- Effective capacity accounts for limitations of optimization algorithms in reaching all possible solutions.

title: Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension
one_liner: The Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension is the largest number of training examples that a binary classifier can label arbitrarily.
content: The Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension (Vapnik & Chervonenkis, 1971) is a more formal measure of capacity. It is the largest number of training examples that a binary classifier can label arbitrarily. Bartlett et al. (2019) derive upper and lower bounds for the VC dimension in terms of the number of layers and weights.
motivation_md: The VC dimension provides a formal way to measure a model's capacity by quantifying its ability to fit arbitrary labels, helping to understand generalization limits.
recap_md:
- VC dimension measures capacity as the largest set of points a classifier can label arbitrarily.
- It is a formal, theoretical measure of model complexity.
- Bounds on VC dimension relate to network layers and weights.

title: Rademacher complexity
one_liner: Rademacher complexity is the expected empirical performance of a classification model with optimal parameters on data with random labels.
content: An alternative measure of capacity is the Rademacher complexity, which is the expected empirical performance of a classification model (with optimal parameters) for data with random labels. Neyshabur et al. (2017) derive a lower bound on the generalization error in terms of the Rademacher complexity.
motivation_md: Rademacher complexity quantifies model capacity by measuring how well a model can fit random noise, providing insights into generalization error bounds.
recap_md:
- Rademacher complexity measures expected performance on data with random labels.
- It serves as an alternative capacity measure to VC dimension.
- It provides lower bounds on generalization error.

title: Double descent
one_liner: Double descent describes test error decreasing again in the over-parameterized regime for certain neural networks and models.
content: The term “double descent” was coined by Belkin et al. (2019), who demonstrated that the test error decreases again in the over-parameterized regime for two-layer neural networks and random features. They also claimed that this occurs in decision trees, although Buschjäger & Morik (2021) subsequently provided evidence to the contrary. Nakkiran et al. (2021) show that double descent occurs for various modern datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, IWSLT’14 de-en), architectures (CNNs, ResNets, transformers), and optimizers (SGD, Adam). The phenomenon is more pronounced when noise is added to the target labels (Nakkiran et al., 2021) and when some regularization techniques are used (Ishida et al., 2020).
motivation_md: Double descent challenges traditional views by showing that test error can decrease again with more parameters, highlighting complex generalization behavior in modern models.
recap_md:
- Double descent is a phenomenon where test error decreases again in over-parameterized models.
- It has been observed in neural networks, random features, and various architectures.
- Noise in labels and regularization can accentuate this effect.

title: Epoch-wise double descent
one_liner: Epoch-wise double descent occurs by fixing capacity and increasing training iterations, showing a double descent pattern over epochs.
content: Epoch-wise double descent occurs when we fix capacity and increase the number of training iterations. They term this epoch-wise double descent. This phenomenon has been modeled by Pezeshki et al. (2022) in terms of different learning dynamics.
motivation_md: Epoch-wise double descent reveals how increasing training time at fixed capacity can cause test error to decrease, then increase, then decrease again, informing training strategies.
recap_md:
- Fix model capacity and increase training iterations to observe epoch-wise double descent.
- Test error shows a double descent pattern over epochs.
- This phenomenon has been modeled to understand learning dynamics.

title: Double descent and training data size effect
one_liner: Double descent predicts that adding training data can sometimes worsen test performance.
content: Double descent makes the rather strange prediction that adding training data can sometimes worsen test performance. Consider an over-parameterized model in the second descending part of the curve. If we increase the training data to match the model capacity, we will now be in the critical region of the new test error curve, and the test loss may increase.
motivation_md: This concept highlights the counterintuitive effect where increasing training data can degrade test performance due to the double descent phenomenon, challenging traditional assumptions.
recap_md:
- Double descent predicts that adding training data can worsen test performance.
- Increasing training data to match model capacity can move the model into a critical region.
- This can cause an increase in test loss despite more data.

title: Noise, bias, and variance
one_liner: There are three possible sources of error, which are known as noise, bias, and variance respectively.
content:
There are three possible sources of error, which are known as noise, bias, and variance respectively (figure 8.5):

Noise
The data generation process includes the addition of noise, so there are multiple possible valid outputs y for each input x (figure 8.5a). This source of error is insurmountable for the test data. Note that it does not necessarily limit the training performance; we will likely never see the same input x twice during training, so it is still possible to fit the training data perfectly.

Noise may arise because there is a genuine stochastic element to the data generation process, because some of the data are mislabeled, or because there are further explanatory variables that were not observed. In rare cases, noise may be absent; for example, a network might approximate a function that is deterministic but requires significant computation to evaluate. However, noise is usually a fundamental limitation on the possible test performance.

Bias
A second potential source of error may occur because the model is not flexible enough to fit the true function perfectly. For example, the three-region neural network model cannot exactly describe the quasi-sinusoidal function, even when the parameters are chosen optimally (figure 8.5b). This is known as bias.

Variance
We have limited training examples, and there is no way to distinguish systematic changes in the underlying function from noise in the underlying data. When we fit a model, we do not get the closest possible approximation to the true underlying function. Indeed, for different training datasets, the result will be slightly different each time. This additional source of variability in the fitted function is termed variance (figure 8.5c). In practice, there might also be additional variance due to the stochastic learning algorithm, which does not necessarily converge to the same solution each time.
motivation_md: Understanding noise, bias, and variance helps identify different sources of error in model predictions, guiding improvements in model design and training.
recap_md:
- Noise arises from randomness or unobserved factors in data generation.
- Bias occurs when the model is too simple to capture the true function.
- Variance reflects variability in model fitting due to limited training data.

title: Bias-variance trade-off
one_liner: Increasing the model capacity does not necessarily reduce the test error; this is known as the bias-variance trade-off.
content:
However, figures 8.7d–f show an unexpected side-effect of increasing the model capacity. For a fixed-size training dataset, the variance term typically increases as the model capacity increases. Consequently, increasing the model capacity does not necessarily reduce the test error. This is known as the bias-variance trade-off.

Figure 8.8 explores this phenomenon. In panels a–c), we fit the simplified three-region model to three different datasets of fifteen points. Although the datasets differ, the final model is much the same; the noise in the dataset roughly averages out in each linear region. In panels d–f), we fit a model with ten regions to the same three datasets. This model has more flexibility, but this is disadvantageous; the model certainly fits the data better, and the training error will be lower, but much of the extra descriptive power is devoted to modeling the noise. This phenomenon is known as overfitting.

We’ve seen that as we add capacity to the model, the bias decreases, but the variance increases for a fixed-size training dataset. This suggests that there is an optimal capacity.
motivation_md: The bias-variance trade-off explains why increasing model complexity can reduce bias but increase variance, affecting test error and leading to overfitting.
recap_md:
- Increasing model capacity reduces bias but increases variance.
- Overfitting occurs when the model fits noise in the training data.
- There is an optimal model capacity balancing bias and variance.

title: Double descent
one_liner: The test error decreases as we add model capacity but does not increase as predicted by the bias-variance trade-off curve; it keeps decreasing.
content:
In the previous section, we examined the bias-variance trade-off as we increased the capacity of a model. Let’s now return to the MNIST-1D dataset and see whether this happens in practice. We use 10,000 training examples, test with another 5,000 examples and examine the training and test performance as we increase the capacity (number of parameters) in the model. We train the model with Adam and a step size of 0.005 using a full batch of 10,000 examples for 4000 steps.

Figure 8.10a shows the training and test error for a neural network with two hidden layers as the number of hidden units increases. The training error decreases as the capacity grows and quickly becomes close to zero. The vertical dashed line represents the capacity where the model has the same number of parameters as there are training examples, but the model memorizes the dataset before this point. The test error decreases as we add model capacity but does not increase as predicted by the bias-variance trade-off curve; it keeps decreasing.
motivation_md: Double descent challenges the traditional bias-variance trade-off by showing test error can keep decreasing even as model capacity grows beyond the number of training examples.
recap_md:
- Training error decreases as model capacity increases.
- Test error does not increase at the interpolation threshold but keeps decreasing.
- This behavior contradicts the classic bias-variance trade-off prediction.

title: Double descent
one_liner: Double descent is a phenomenon where test error decreases again after initially increasing as model capacity grows beyond fitting the training data exactly.
content:
Once more, the training error decreases to zero. This time, there is more randomness, and the model requires almost as many parameters as there are data points to memorize the data. The test error does show the typical bias-variance trade-off as we increase the capacity to the point where the model fits the training data exactly. However, then it does something unexpected; it starts to decrease again. Indeed, if we add enough capacity, the test loss reduces to below the minimal level that we achieved in the first part of the curve.

This phenomenon is known as double descent. For some datasets like MNIST, it is present with the original data (figure 8.10c). For others, like MNIST-1D and CIFAR-100 (figure 8.10d), it emerges or becomes more prominent when we add noise to the labels.
motivation_md: Double descent reveals that increasing model capacity beyond the interpolation point can improve test performance, challenging traditional error trade-offs.
recap_md:
- Test error initially increases then decreases as model capacity grows beyond fitting training data.
- Double descent occurs in datasets like MNIST and CIFAR-100.
- Adding noise to labels can make double descent more prominent.

title: Classical and modern regimes of double descent
one_liner: The first part of the curve is the classical (under-parameterized) regime, the second is the modern (over-parameterized) regime, and the central part is the critical regime.
content: The first part of the curve is referred to as the classical or under-parameterized regime, and the second part as the modern or over-parameterized regime. The central part where the error increases is termed the critical regime.
motivation_md: Understanding these regimes helps interpret model behavior as capacity changes, especially in double descent phenomena.
recap_md:
- Classical regime: model under-parameterized.
- Critical regime: error increases.
- Modern regime: model over-parameterized.

title: Inductive bias
one_liner: Between data points is known as its inductive bias.
content: between data points is known as its inductive bias.
motivation_md: Inductive bias refers to assumptions a model makes to generalize beyond observed data points, guiding learning and predictions.
recap_md:
- Inductive bias is the assumption about data behavior between points.
- It influences model generalization.
- It is essential for learning from limited data.

title: Curse of dimensionality
one_liner: High-dimensional space overwhelming the number of training points is termed the curse of dimensionality.
content: high-dimensional space to overwhelm the number of training points is termed the curse of dimensionality.
motivation_md: The curse of dimensionality describes how high-dimensional data can make learning difficult due to sparse training points relative to space volume.
recap_md:
- Curse of dimensionality arises in high-dimensional spaces.
- It overwhelms the number of training points.
- It complicates learning and generalization.

title: Smooth interpolation between sparse data points
one_liner: As we add capacity to the model, it interpolates between the nearest data points increasingly smoothly.
content: Between them. The putative explanation for double descent is that as we add capacity to the model, it interpolates between the nearest data points increasingly smoothly. In the absence of information about what happens between the training points, assuming smoothness is sensible and will probably generalize reasonably to new data.
motivation_md: Smooth interpolation helps models generalize well between sparse training points, explaining improved performance with increased capacity.
recap_md:
- Increasing capacity leads to smoother interpolation between data points.
- Smoothness assumption aids generalization.
- This explains the double descent phenomenon.

title: vanishing and exploding gradient problems summary
one_liner: The magnitudes of hidden unit activations and gradients can exponentially decrease or increase, causing vanishing or exploding gradient problems that impede training but can be avoided with proper initialization.
content: Careful parameter initialization is critical. The magnitudes of the hidden unit activations can either decrease or increase exponentially in the forward pass. The same is true of the gradient magnitudes in the backward pass, where these behaviors are known as the vanishing gradient and exploding gradient problems. Both impede training but can be avoided with appropriate initialization.
motivation_md: Vanishing and exploding gradients cause training difficulties by making gradients too small or too large, so understanding and addressing these problems ensures stable and efficient neural network training.
recap_md:
- Hidden unit activations can exponentially decrease or increase in forward pass.
- Gradient magnitudes can similarly vanish or explode in backward pass.
- Proper parameter initialization helps avoid these problems and improves training.

title: history and implementation notes on backpropagation
one_liner: Backpropagation, efficiently reusing partial computations to calculate gradients, was popularized by Rumelhart et al. (1985) and is implemented as reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation in modern frameworks.
content:
Backpropagation: Efficient reuse of partial computations while calculating gradients in computational graphs has been repeatedly discovered, including by Werbos (1974), Bryson et al. (1979), LeCun (1985), and Parker (1985). However, the most celebrated description of this idea was by Rumelhart et al. (1985) and Rumelhart et al. (1986), who also coined the term “backpropagation.” This latter work kick-started a new phase of neural network research in the eighties and nineties; for the first time, it was practical to train networks with hidden layers. However, progress stalled due (in retrospect) to a lack of training data, limited computational power, and the use of sigmoid activations. Areas such as natural language processing and computer vision did not rely on neural network models until the remarkable image classification results of Krizhevsky et al. (2012) ushered in the modern era of deep learning.

The implementation of backpropagation in modern deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow is an example of reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation. This is distinguished from forward-mode algorithmic differentiation in which the derivatives from the chain rule are accumulated while moving forward through the computational graph (see problem 7.13).
motivation_md: Backpropagation enables efficient gradient computation in neural networks, making training of deep models with hidden layers practical and effective, which was crucial for the development of modern deep learning.
recap_md:
- Backpropagation efficiently reuses partial computations to calculate gradients.
- Popularized by Rumelhart et al. (1985), enabling training of networks with hidden layers.
- Implemented as reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation in frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow.

title: Backpropagation
one_liner: Backpropagation efficiently reuses partial computations to calculate gradients in computational graphs, popularized by Rumelhart et al. (1985), and is implemented as reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation.
content:
Backpropagation: Efficient reuse of partial computations while calculating gradients in computational graphs has been repeatedly discovered, including by Werbos (1974), Bryson et al. (1979), LeCun (1985), and Parker (1985). However, the most celebrated description of this idea was by Rumelhart et al. (1985) and Rumelhart et al. (1986), who also coined the term “backpropagation.” This latter work kick-started a new phase of neural network research in the eighties and nineties; for the first time, it was practical to train networks with hidden layers. However, progress stalled due (in retrospect) to a lack of training data, limited computational power, and the use of sigmoid activations. Areas such as natural language processing and computer vision did not rely on neural network models until the remarkable image classification results of Krizhevsky et al. (2012) ushered in the modern era of deep learning.

The implementation of backpropagation in modern deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow is an example of reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation. This is distinguished from forward-mode algorithmic differentiation in which the derivatives from the chain rule are accumulated while moving forward through the computational graph (see problem 7.13).
motivation_md: Backpropagation solves the problem of efficiently computing gradients for training neural networks, enabling practical training of deep models with hidden layers.
recap_md:
- Backpropagation reuses partial computations to efficiently calculate gradients.
- Coined and popularized by Rumelhart et al. (1985).
- Implemented as reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation in modern frameworks.

title: notes on weight initialization methods
one_liner: He initialization, based on Glorot/Xavier initialization, and other methods like SeLU and ActNorm help prevent exponential growth or shrinkage of activations by sensible weight initialization and normalization.
content:
Initialization: He initialization was first introduced by He et al. (2015). It follows closely from Glorot or Xavier initialization (Glorot & Bengio, 2010), which is very similar but does not consider the effect of the ReLU layer and so differs by a factor of two. Essentially the same method was proposed much earlier by LeCun et al. (2012) but with a slightly different motivation; in this case, sigmoidal activation functions were used, which naturally normalize the range of outputs at each layer, and hence help prevent an exponential increase in the magnitudes of the hidden units. However, if the pre-activations are too large, they fall into the flat regions of the sigmoid function and result in very small gradients.

Hence, it is still important to initialize the weights sensibly. Klambauer et al. (2017) introduce the scaled exponential linear unit (SeLU) and show that, within a certain range of inputs, this activation function tends to make the activations in network layers automatically converge to mean zero and unit variance. A completely different approach is to pass data through the network and then normalize by the empirically observed variance. Layer-sequential unit variance initialization (Mishkin & Matas, 2016) is an example of this kind of method, in which the weight matrices are initialized as orthonormal. GradInit (Zhu et al., 2021) randomizes the initial weights and temporarily fixes them while it learns non-negative scaling factors for each weight matrix. These factors are selected to maximize the decrease in the loss for a fixed learning rate subject to a constraint on the maximum gradient norm. Activation normalization or ActNorm adds a learnable scaling and offset parameter after each network layer at each hidden unit. They run an initial batch through the network and then choose the offset and scale so that the mean of the activations is zero and the variance one. After this, these extra parameters are learned as part of the model.
motivation_md: Proper weight initialization prevents exponential growth or shrinkage of activations and gradients, ensuring stable training and avoiding issues like vanishing or exploding gradients.
recap_md:
- He initialization builds on Glorot/Xavier but accounts for ReLU effects.
- SeLU activation helps activations converge to zero mean and unit variance.
- Methods like Layer-sequential unit variance and ActNorm normalize activations empirically.

title: BatchNorm
one_liner: BatchNorm normalizes the variance of each batch during processing at every step to stabilize training.
content: Closely related to these methods are schemes such as BatchNorm (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015), in which the network normalizes the variance of each batch as part of its processing at every step. BatchNorm and its variants are discussed in chapter 11. Other initialization schemes have
motivation_md: BatchNorm exists to stabilize and accelerate training by normalizing batch variances during network processing.
recap_md:
- BatchNorm normalizes variance of each batch during processing.
- It is related to other initialization and normalization methods.
- Variants of BatchNorm are discussed further in chapter 11.

title: gradient checkpointing
one_liner: Gradient checkpointing stores activations only every N layers during forward pass and recomputes missing activations during backward pass to reduce memory requirements.
content: Gradient checkpointing (Chen et al., 2016a) and micro-batching (Huang et al., 2019). In gradient checkpointing, the activations are only stored every N layers during the forward pass. During the backward pass, the intermediate missing activations are recalculated from the nearest checkpoint. In this manner, we can drastically reduce the memory requirements at the computational
motivation_md: Gradient checkpointing reduces memory usage during training by storing fewer activations and recomputing them as needed during backpropagation.
recap_md:
- Stores activations only every N layers during forward pass.
- Missing activations are recomputed during backward pass.
- Reduces memory requirements significantly.

title: micro-batching
one_liner: Micro-batching subdivides a batch into smaller parts and aggregates gradient updates from each sub-batch before applying them to the network.
content: Cost of performing the forward pass twice (problem 7.11). In micro-batching, the batch is subdivided into smaller parts, and the gradient updates are aggregated from each sub-batch before being applied to the network. A completely different approach is to build a reversible network
motivation_md: Micro-batching helps manage memory and computational resources by processing smaller batch parts sequentially and aggregating their gradients for efficient training.
recap_md:
- Batch is subdivided into smaller parts called micro-batches.
- Gradient updates from each micro-batch are aggregated before application.
- Helps manage memory and computational resources during training.

title: Distributed training
one_liner: Distributed training runs training in parallel across multiple processors using data, pipeline, or tensor model parallelism to handle large models beyond single-processor capacity.
content:
For sufficiently large models, the memory requirements or total required time may be too much for a single processor. In this case, we must use distributed training, in which training takes place in parallel across multiple processors. There are several approaches to parallelism. In data parallelism, each processor or node contains a full copy of the model but runs a subset of the batch (see Xing et al., 2015; Li et al., 2020b). The gradients from each node are aggregated centrally and then redistributed back to each node to ensure that the models remain consistent. This is known as synchronous training. The synchronization required to aggregate and redistribute the gradients can be a performance bottleneck, and this leads to the idea of asynchronous training. For example, in the Hogwild! algorithm (Recht et al., 2011), the gradient from a node is used to update a central model whenever it is ready. The updated model is then redistributed to the node. This means that each node may have a slightly different version of the model at any given time, so the gradient updates may be stale; however, it works well in practice. Other decentralized schemes have also been developed. For example, in Zhang et al. (2016a), the individual nodes update one another in a ring structure.

Data parallelism methods still assume that the entire model can be held in the memory of a single node. Pipeline model parallelism stores different layers of the network on different nodes and hence does not have this requirement. In a naïve implementation, the first node runs the forward pass for the batch on the first few layers and passes the result to the next node, which runs the forward pass on the next few layers and so on. In the backward pass, the gradients are updated in the opposite order. The obvious disadvantage of this approach is that each machine lies idle for most of the cycle. Various schemes revolving around each node processing micro-batches sequentially have been proposed to reduce this inefficiency (e.g., Huang et al., 2019; Narayanan et al., 2021a). Finally, in tensor model parallelism, computation at a single network layer is distributed across nodes (e.g., Shoeybi et al., 2019). A good overview of distributed training methods can be found in Narayanan et al. (2021b), who combine tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism to train a language model with one trillion parameters on 3072 GPUs.
motivation_md: Distributed training enables handling very large models by splitting computation and memory across multiple processors, overcoming single-processor limitations.
recap_md:
- Distributed training runs training in parallel across multiple processors.
- Data parallelism replicates the model on each node and splits batches.
- Pipeline and tensor model parallelism split layers or computations across nodes.

title: effects of weight initialization variance on forward and backward pass
one_liner: If the variance σ² of initialized weights is too small or too large, pre-activations shrink or grow through the network, causing vanishing or exploding gradients during training.
content:
Gradient descent and Adam are used to train the model, but parameter initialization before training is crucial. During the forward pass, each set of pre-activations $f_k$ is computed as:

$$f_k = \beta_k + \Omega_k h_k = \beta_k + \Omega_k a[f_{k-1}],$$

where $a[\cdot]$ applies the ReLU function, and $\Omega_k$ and $\beta_k$ are the weights and biases, respectively. Assuming all biases are initialized to zero and elements of $\Omega_k$ are initialized from a normal distribution with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2$, consider two scenarios:

- If $\sigma^2$ is very small (e.g., $10^{-5}$), each element of $\beta_k + \Omega_k h_k$ is a weighted sum with very small weights, resulting in smaller magnitude than the input. The ReLU clips values less than zero, so the range of $h_k$ is half that of $f_{k-1}$. Consequently, pre-activation magnitudes shrink through the network.

- If $\sigma^2$ is very large (e.g., $10^5$), each element is a weighted sum with very large weights, likely resulting in larger magnitude than the input. Although ReLU halves the input range, magnitudes still grow through the network.

In both cases, pre-activation values can become too small or too large to represent with finite precision floating point arithmetic.

The same logic applies to the backward pass, where each gradient update involves multiplication by $\Omega^T$. Poor initialization of $\Omega$ can cause gradients to decrease or increase uncontrollably during backpropagation. These are known as the vanishing gradient problem and the exploding gradient problem, respectively. In the vanishing gradient case, model updates become vanishingly small; in the exploding gradient case, updates become unstable.
motivation_md: Proper weight initialization prevents pre-activations and gradients from shrinking or exploding during forward and backward passes, ensuring stable and effective training of deep neural networks.
recap_md:
- Small weight variance causes pre-activations to shrink through layers, leading to vanishing gradients.
- Large weight variance causes pre-activations to grow, leading to exploding gradients.
- Proper initialization balances variance to maintain stable forward and backward passes.

title: vanishing gradient problem
one_liner: The vanishing gradient problem occurs when gradient updates become vanishingly small during the backward pass.
content: These cases are known as the vanishing gradient problem and the exploding gradient problem, respectively. In the former case, updates to the model become vanishingly small. In the latter case, they become unstable.
motivation_md: Vanishing gradients hinder learning by making parameter updates too small to improve the model effectively during training.
recap_md:
- Vanishing gradient problem: gradients become very small during backpropagation.
- Causes model updates to be negligible.
- Leads to slow or stalled training.

title: exploding gradient problem
one_liner: The exploding gradient problem occurs when gradient updates become unstable and grow uncontrollably during the backward pass.
content: These cases are known as the vanishing gradient problem and the exploding gradient problem, respectively. In the former case, updates to the model become vanishingly small. In the latter case, they become unstable.
motivation_md: Exploding gradients cause unstable training by making parameter updates excessively large, which can prevent convergence.
recap_md:
- Exploding gradient problem: gradients grow uncontrollably during backpropagation.
- Causes unstable and large parameter updates.
- Can prevent model convergence.

title: parameter initialization for forward pass variance stability
one_liner: To maintain variance stability in the forward pass, weights should be initialized with variance $\sigma^2_\Omega$ satisfying $\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{2}{D_h}$, known as He initialization.
content:
Consider the computation between adjacent pre-activations $f$ and $f'$ with dimensions $D_h$ and $D_{h'}$, respectively:

$$h = a[f], \quad f' = \beta + \Omega h$$

where $h$ represents activations, $\Omega$ and $\beta$ represent weights and biases, and $a[\cdot]$ is the activation function. Assume the pre-activations $f_j$ in the input layer $f$ have variance $\sigma^2_f$. Biases $\beta_i$ are initialized to zero and weights $\Omega_{ij}$ are normally distributed with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2_\Omega$.

The expectation (mean) of $f'_i$ is:

$$E[f'_i] = E[\beta_i + \sum_{j=1}^{D_h} \Omega_{ij} h_j] = 0,$$

assuming independence between weights and activations. The variance of $f'_i$ is:

$$\sigma^2_{f'_i} = E[f'^2_i] - E[f'_i]^2 = \sigma^2_\Omega \sum_{j=1}^{D_h} E[h_j^2].$$

Assuming the distribution of $f_j$ is symmetric about zero, half of the pre-activations are clipped by ReLU, so the second moment $E[h_j^2]$ is half the variance $\sigma^2_f$ of $f_j$:

$$\sigma^2_{f'_i} = \sigma^2_\Omega D_h \frac{\sigma^2_f}{2} = \frac{1}{2} D_h \sigma^2_\Omega \sigma^2_f.$$
motivation_md: This mathematical analysis guides how to initialize weights so that the variance of pre-activations remains stable through layers during the forward pass, preventing vanishing or exploding activations.
recap_md:
- Pre-activation mean is zero if weights and biases are zero-mean and zero.
- Variance of next layer's pre-activations depends on weight variance and previous layer's activation variance.
- ReLU halves variance, leading to $\sigma^2_{f'} = \frac{1}{2} D_h \sigma^2_\Omega \sigma^2_f$.

title: He initialization
one_liner: He initialization sets weight variance to $\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{2}{D_h}$ to maintain stable variance of activations and gradients in deep ReLU networks.
content:
Consider a deep network with 50 hidden layers and $D_h = 100$ hidden units per layer. The input $x$ is initialized from a standard normal distribution, with a fixed target $y=0$ and a least squares loss function. Bias vectors $\beta_k$ are initialized to zero, and weight matrices $\Omega_k$ are initialized with a normal distribution with mean zero and variances $\sigma^2_\Omega \in \{0.001, 0.01, 0.02, 0.1, 1.0\}$. 

(a) The variance of hidden unit activations computed in the forward pass as a function of the network layer shows that for He initialization ($\sigma^2_\Omega = 2/D_h = 0.02$), the variance is stable. Larger variances cause the variance to increase rapidly, while smaller variances cause it to decrease rapidly (note log scale).

(b) The variance of the gradients in the backward pass (solid lines) follows this trend; initializing with a value larger than 0.02 causes gradient magnitudes to increase rapidly backward through the network, while smaller values cause magnitudes to decrease. These correspond to the exploding and vanishing gradient problems, respectively.

To keep the variance $\sigma^2_{f'}$ of subsequent pre-activations equal to the variance $\sigma^2_f$ of original pre-activations during the forward pass, set:

$$\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{2}{D_h},$$

where $D_h$ is the dimension of the original layer. This is known as He initialization.
motivation_md: He initialization provides a principled way to set weight variance to maintain stable activation and gradient variances, preventing vanishing or exploding gradients in deep ReLU networks.
recap_md:
- He initialization sets $\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{2}{D_h}$.
- This stabilizes variance of activations and gradients across layers.
- Prevents vanishing and exploding gradient problems.

title: parameter initialization for backward pass variance stability
one_liner: During the backward pass, weight variance should be set as $\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{2}{D_{h'}}$ to maintain stable gradient variance.
content:
A similar argument establishes how the variance of the gradients $\partial l / \partial f_k$ changes during the backward pass. During backpropagation, we multiply by the transpose $\Omega^T$ of the weight matrix (equation 7.25), so the equivalent expression becomes:

$$\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{2}{D_{h'}},$$

where $D_{h'}$ is the dimension of the subsequent layer.
motivation_md: To prevent gradients from vanishing or exploding during backpropagation, weight variance must be chosen to stabilize gradient variance in the backward pass.
recap_md:
- Backward pass involves multiplication by $\Omega^T$.
- Gradient variance stability requires $\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{2}{D_{h'}}$.
- Ensures stable gradient magnitudes during backpropagation.

title: parameter initialization compromise for non-square weight matrices
one_liner: For non-square weight matrices, a compromise variance $\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{4}{D_h + D_{h'}}$ stabilizes both forward and backward pass variances.
content:
If the weight matrix $\Omega$ is not square (i.e., the number of hidden units in adjacent layers differ, so $D_h$ and $D_{h'}$ differ), it is not possible to choose the variance to satisfy both forward and backward pass stability equations simultaneously. One possible compromise is to use the mean $(D_h + D_{h'})/2$ as a proxy for the number of terms, which gives:

$$\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{4}{D_h + D_{h'}}.$$

Figure 7.7 shows empirically that both the variance of hidden units in the forward pass and the variance of gradients in the backward pass remain stable when parameters are initialized appropriately.
motivation_md: This compromise allows stable variance of activations and gradients when weight matrices are rectangular, ensuring effective training.
recap_md:
- Non-square weight matrices have differing input and output dimensions.
- Variance compromise uses average dimension: $\sigma^2_\Omega = \frac{4}{D_h + D_{h'}}$.
- Stabilizes variance in both forward and backward passes.

title: example training code for deep learning model
one_liner: Example PyTorch code demonstrates training a two-hidden-layer network with He initialization, SGD optimizer, and learning rate scheduling.
content:
Gradients and initialization

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import StepLR

# define input size, hidden layer size, output size
D_i, D_k, D_o = 10, 40, 5

# create model with two hidden layers
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(D_i, D_k),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(D_k, D_k),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(D_k, D_o)
)

# He initialization of weights
def weights_init(layer_in):
    if isinstance(layer_in, nn.Linear):
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(layer_in.weight)
        layer_in.bias.data.fill_(0.0)

model.apply(weights_init)

# choose least squares loss function
criterion = nn.MSELoss()

# construct SGD optimizer and initialize learning rate and momentum
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9)

# object that decreases learning rate by half every 10 epochs
scheduler = StepLR(optimizer, step_size=10, gamma=0.5)

# create 100 random data points and store in data loader class
x = torch.randn(100, D_i)
y = torch.randn(100, D_o)
data_loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(x, y), batch_size=10, shuffle=True)

# loop over the dataset 100 times
for epoch in range(100):
    epoch_loss = 0.0
    # loop over batches
    for i, data in enumerate(data_loader):
        # retrieve inputs and labels for this batch
        x_batch, y_batch = data
        # zero the parameter gradients
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        # forward pass
        pred = model(x_batch)
        loss = criterion(pred, y_batch)
        # backward pass
        loss.backward()
        # SGD update
        optimizer.step()
        # update statistics
        epoch_loss += loss.item()
    # print error
    print(f'Epoch {epoch:5d}, loss {epoch_loss:.3f}')
    # tell scheduler to consider updating learning rate
    scheduler.step()
```

Figure 7.8 Sample code for training two-layer network on random data.
motivation_md: This code example illustrates how to implement a deep learning training loop with proper weight initialization, loss function, optimizer, and learning rate scheduling in PyTorch.
recap_md:
- Defines a two-hidden-layer neural network with ReLU activations.
- Applies He initialization to weights and zero initialization to biases.
- Uses SGD optimizer with momentum and learning rate scheduler for training.

title: Lipschitz constant
one_liner: Lipschitz constant of a model is the fastest the output can change for a small input change.
content: Lipschitz constant of a model measures the fastest rate at which the output can change in response to a small change in the input. A review of the theory of over-parameterized machine learning can be found in Dar et al. (2021).
motivation_md: Understanding the Lipschitz constant helps quantify how sensitive a model's output is to small input changes, which is crucial for analyzing model stability and robustness.
recap_md:
- Lipschitz constant measures the fastest output change for small input changes.
- It quantifies model sensitivity to input variations.
- Relevant in analyzing over-parameterized machine learning models.

title: Properties of high-dimensional spaces and curse of dimensionality
one_liner: As dimensionality increases, the volume of space grows so fast that the amount of data needed to densely sample it increases exponentially.
content:
As dimensionality increases, the volume of space grows so fast that the amount of data needed to densely sample it increases exponentially. This phenomenon is known as the curse of dimensionality. High-dimensional space has many unexpected properties, and caution should be used when trying to reason about it based on low-dimensional examples. This book visualizes many aspects of deep learning in one or two dimensions, but these visualizations should be treated with healthy skepticism.

Surprising properties of high-dimensional spaces include: (i) Two randomly sampled data points from a standard normal distribution are very close to orthogonal to one another (relative to the origin) with high likelihood. (ii) The distance from the origin of samples from a standard normal distribution is roughly constant. (iii) Most of a volume of a high-dimensional sphere (hypersphere) is adjacent to its surface (a common metaphor is that most of the volume of a high-dimensional orange is in the peel, not in the pulp). (iv) If we place a unit-diameter hypersphere inside a hypercube with unit-length sides, then the hypersphere takes up a decreasing proportion of the volume of the cube as the dimension increases. Since the volume of the cube is fixed at size one, this implies that the volume of a high-dimensional hypersphere becomes close to zero. (v) For random points drawn from a uniform distribution in a high-dimensional hypercube, the ratio of the Euclidean distance between the nearest and furthest points becomes close to one. For further information, consult Beyer et al. (1999) and Aggarwal et al. (2001).
motivation_md: High-dimensional spaces behave counterintuitively, making it difficult to sample data densely or reason about geometry; understanding these properties helps avoid misleading conclusions in machine learning.
recap_md:
- Volume grows exponentially with dimensionality, causing the curse of dimensionality.
- High-dimensional points tend to be nearly orthogonal and equidistant from the origin.
- Most volume of a high-dimensional sphere lies near its surface, and its volume shrinks relative to a hypercube.

title: Issues affecting real-world performance of models
one_liner: Model performance on a held-out test set may not reflect real-world performance if data statistics change over time, causing data drift.
content:
Model performance can be evaluated using a held-out test set, but this result won’t be indicative of real-world performance if the statistics of the test set don’t match those of real-world data. Moreover, the statistics of real-world data may change over time, causing the model to become increasingly stale and performance to decrease. This is known as data drift and means that deployed models must be carefully monitored.

There are three main reasons why real-world performance may be worse than the test performance implies. First, the statistics of the input data \(x\) may change; we may now be observing parts of the function that were sparsely sampled or not sampled at all during training. This is known as covariate shift. Second, the statistics of the output data \(y\) may change; if some output values are infrequent during training, then the model may learn not to predict these in ambiguous situations and will make mistakes if they are more common in the real world. This is known as prior shift. Third, the relationship between input and output may change. This is known as concept shift. These issues are discussed in Moreno-Torres et al. (2012).
motivation_md: Real-world data often differ from test data and change over time, so understanding shifts like covariate, prior, and concept shift is essential to maintain model reliability after deployment.
recap_md:
- Test set performance may not reflect real-world performance due to data drift.
- Covariate shift: input data distribution changes.
- Prior shift: output data distribution changes; concept shift: input-output relationship changes.

title: Challenges in hyperparameter search
one_liner: Finding the best hyperparameters is a challenging optimization task due to expensive evaluations, discrete variables, noise, and conditional dependencies.
content: Finding the best hyperparameters is a challenging optimization task. Testing a single configuration of hyperparameters is expensive; we must train an entire model and measure its performance. We have no easy way to access the derivatives (i.e., how performance changes when we make a small change to a hyperparameter). Moreover, many of the hyperparameters are discrete, so we cannot use gradient descent methods. There are multiple local minima and no way to tell if we are close to the global minimum. The noise level is high since each training/validation cycle uses a stochastic training algorithm; we expect different results if we train a model twice with the same hyperparameters. Finally, some variables are conditional and only exist if others are set. For example, the number of hidden units in the third hidden layer is only relevant if we have at least three hidden layers.
motivation_md: Hyperparameter tuning is difficult because it requires costly model training, lacks gradient information, involves discrete and conditional parameters, and suffers from noisy evaluations and multiple local minima.
recap_md:
- Hyperparameter search requires expensive model training for each configuration.
- Many hyperparameters are discrete and conditional, preventing gradient methods.
- Noise and multiple local minima complicate optimization.

title: Bayesian optimization
one_liner: Bayesian optimization is a framework based on Gaussian processes that exploits previous knowledge to optimize hyperparameters.
content: Bayesian optimization is a framework based on Gaussian processes that exploits previous knowledge to guide the search for optimal hyperparameters. Its application to hyperparameter search is described in Snoek et al.
motivation_md: Bayesian optimization exists to efficiently find good hyperparameters by leveraging past evaluations to reduce costly training iterations.
recap_md:
- Bayesian optimization uses Gaussian processes to model performance.
- It exploits previous knowledge to guide hyperparameter search.
- Useful for expensive optimization tasks like hyperparameter tuning.

title: Beta-Bernoulli bandit
one_liner: The Beta-Bernoulli bandit is a model related to bandit problems, as described by Lattimore & Szepesvári (2020).
content: The Beta-Bernoulli bandit (see Lattimore & Szepesvári, 2020) is a roughly equivalent model used in bandit problem settings.
motivation_md: The Beta-Bernoulli bandit models decision-making under uncertainty, useful for balancing exploration and exploitation in sequential problems.
recap_md:
- Beta-Bernoulli bandit is a model in bandit problem literature.
- Refer to Lattimore & Szepesvári (2020) for details.
- Used for sequential decision-making under uncertainty.

title: Sequential model-based configuration (SMAC)
one_liner: Sequential model-based configuration (SMAC) uses a random forest to model the objective function for hyperparameter optimization.
content: The sequential model-based configuration (SMAC) algorithm (Hutter et al., 2011) can cope with continuous, discrete, and conditional parameters. The basic approach is to use a random forest to model the objective function where the mean of the tree predictions is the best guess about the function's value.
motivation_md: SMAC exists to efficiently optimize hyperparameters by modeling the objective function with a flexible random forest, handling various parameter types and dependencies.
recap_md:
- SMAC handles continuous, discrete, and conditional parameters.
- Uses a random forest to model the objective function.
- The mean prediction of trees estimates function values for optimization.

title: Tree-Parzen Estimators
one_liner: Tree-Parzen Estimators model the probability of hyperparameters given model performance, unlike previous methods that model performance given hyperparameters.
content: Tree-Parzen Estimators (Bergstra et al., 2011) differ from previous methods by modeling the probability of the hyperparameters given the model performance, rather than modeling the probability of the model performance given the hyperparameters.
motivation_md: Tree-Parzen Estimators provide an alternative probabilistic approach to hyperparameter optimization by focusing on the inverse conditional probability, potentially improving search efficiency.
recap_md:
- Tree-Parzen Estimators model \(P(\text{hyperparameters} | \text{performance})\).
- Previous methods model \(P(\text{performance} | \text{hyperparameters})\).
- This inversion offers a different perspective for hyperparameter search.

title: non-negative homogeneity property of the ReLU function
one_liner: ReLU[α · z] = α · ReLU[z] for α ∈ R+, known as the non-negative homogeneity property of the ReLU function.
content:
Problem 3.5 Prove that the following property holds for α ∈ R+:
ReLU[α · z] = α · ReLU[z].
(3.14)
This is known as the non-negative homogeneity property of the ReLU function.
motivation_md: This property characterizes how the ReLU function scales linearly with non-negative factors, which is important for understanding its behavior in neural networks.

title: Composing neural networks
one_liner: Composing two shallow networks with ReLU activations produces a family of piecewise linear functions with potentially more linear regions than a single shallow network.
content:
Composing neural networks
To gain insight into the behavior of deep neural networks, we first consider composing two shallow networks so the output of the first becomes the input of the second. Consider two shallow networks with three hidden units each (figure 4.1a). The first network takes an input x and returns output y and is defined by:
h1 = a[θ10 + θ11x]
h2 = a[θ20 + θ21x]
h3 = a[θ30 + θ31x],
(4.1)
and
y = ϕ0 + ϕ1h1 + ϕ2h2 + ϕ3h3.
(4.2)
The second network takes y as input and returns y′ and is defined by:
h′1 = a[θ′10 + θ′11y]
h′2 = a[θ′20 + θ′21y]
h′3 = a[θ′30 + θ′31y],
(4.3)
and
y′ = ϕ′0 + ϕ′1h′1 + ϕ′2h′2 + ϕ′3h′3.
(4.4)
With ReLU activations, this model also describes a family of piecewise linear functions. However, the number of linear regions is potentially greater than for a shallow network with six hidden units. To see this, consider choosing the first network to produce three alternating regions of positive and negative slope (figure 4.1b). This means that three different ranges of x are mapped to the same output range y ∈[−1, 1], and the subsequent mapping from this range of y to y′ is applied three times. The overall effect is that the function defined by the second network is duplicated three times to create nine linear regions. The same principle applies in higher dimensions (figure 4.2).
motivation_md: Composing shallow networks helps understand how deep networks create more complex piecewise linear functions by increasing the number of linear regions through function composition.
recap_md:
- Composing two shallow networks results in a piecewise linear function with more linear regions.
- The first network maps multiple input ranges to the same output range.
- The second network's function is applied repeatedly to these outputs, increasing complexity.

title: From composing networks to deep networks

position.section_title: From composing networks to deep networks

one_liner: Composing two shallow networks with ReLU activations forms a deep network with two hidden layers representing a broader family of piecewise linear functions.
content:
4.2 From composing networks to deep networks

h′1 = a[θ′10 + θ′11y]
h′2 = a[θ′20 + θ′21y]
h′3 = a[θ′30 + θ′31y],
(4.3)
and
y′ = ϕ′0 + ϕ′1h′1 + ϕ′2h′2 + ϕ′3h′3.
(4.4)
With ReLU activations, this model also describes a family of piecewise linear functions. However, the number of linear regions is potentially greater than for a shallow network with six hidden units. To see this, consider choosing the first network to produce three alternating regions of positive and negative slope (figure 4.1b). This means that three different ranges of x are mapped to the same output range y ∈[−1, 1], and the subsequent mapping from this range of y to y′ is applied three times. The overall effect is that the function defined by the second network is duplicated three times to create nine linear regions. The same principle applies in higher dimensions (figure 4.2).

A different way to think about composing networks is that the first network “folds” the input space x back onto itself so that multiple inputs generate the same output. Then the second network applies a function, which is replicated at all points that were folded on top of one another (figure 4.3).

The previous section showed that we could create complex functions by passing the output of one shallow neural network into a second network. We now show that this is a special case of a deep network with two hidden layers.

The output of the first network (y = ϕ0 + ϕ1h1 + ϕ2h2 + ϕ3h3) is a linear combination of the activations at the hidden units. The first operations of the second network (equation 4.3 in which we calculate θ′10 + θ′11y, θ′20 + θ′21y, and θ′30 + θ′31y) are linear in the output of the first network. Applying one linear function to another yields another linear function. Substituting the expression for y into equation 4.3 gives:

h′1 = a[θ′10 + θ′11y] = a[θ′10 + θ′11ϕ0 + θ′11ϕ1h1 + θ′11ϕ2h2 + θ′11ϕ3h3]
h′2 = a[θ′20 + θ′21y] = a[θ′20 + θ′21ϕ0 + θ′21ϕ1h1 + θ′21ϕ2h2 + θ′21ϕ3h3]
h′3 = a[θ′30 + θ′31y] = a[θ′30 + θ′31ϕ0 + θ′31ϕ1h1 + θ′31ϕ2h2 + θ′31ϕ3h3], (4.5)

which we can rewrite as:

h′1 = a[ψ10 + ψ11h1 + ψ12h2 + ψ13h3]
h′2 = a[ψ20 + ψ21h1 + ψ22h2 + ψ23h3]
h′3 = a[ψ30 + ψ31h1 + ψ32h2 + ψ33h3],
(4.6)
motivation_md: This concept explains how composing shallow networks forms a deep network, enabling the representation of more complex functions through layered linear transformations and activations.
recap_md:
- Composing shallow networks is equivalent to a deep network with two hidden layers.
- The first network folds the input space, mapping multiple inputs to the same output.
- The second network applies functions replicated over folded inputs, increasing complexity.

title: Deep networks as folding input space
