so for each xn, they are positive and sum to one (figure 12.3). For obvious reasons, this is known as dot-product self-attention.

The names “queries” and “keys” were inherited from the field of information retrieval and have the following interpretation: the dot product operation returns a measure of similarity between its inputs, so the weights a[x•, xn] depend on the relative similarities between the nth query and all of the keys. The softmax function means that the key vectors “compete” with one another to contribute to the final result. The queries and keys must have the same dimensions. However, these can differ from the dimension of the values.
motivation_md: Attention weights are nonlinear functions of inputs computed via queries and keys, enabling dynamic weighting based on input similarity, which is crucial for context-sensitive processing in self-attention.
recap_md:
- Attention weights are nonlinear functions computed from queries and keys.
- Queries and keys are linear transforms of inputs.
- Weights are computed by softmax over dot products of queries and keys.

title: Self-attention summary
one_liner: The nth output is a weighted sum of the same linear transformation applied to all inputs, where attention weights depend on similarity and sum to one.
content:
The nth output is a weighted sum of the same linear transformation $v_\bullet = \beta_v + \Omega_v x_\bullet$ applied to all of the inputs, where these attention weights are positive and sum to one. The weights depend on a measure of similarity between input $x_n$ and the other inputs. There is no activation function, but the mechanism is nonlinear due to the dot-product and a softmax operation used to compute the attention weights.

Note that this mechanism fulfills the initial requirements. First, there is a single shared set of parameters $\phi = \{\beta_v, \Omega_v, \beta_q, \Omega_q, \beta_k, \Omega_k\}$. This is independent of the number of inputs $N$, so the network can be applied to different sequence lengths. Second, there are connections between the inputs (words), and the strength of these connections depends on the inputs themselves via the attention weights.
motivation_md: Self-attention summarizes inputs by weighting them based on similarity, enabling flexible, parameter-efficient modeling of sequences of varying length.
recap_md:
- Outputs are weighted sums of a shared linear transform applied to inputs.
- Attention weights depend on similarity and sum to one.
- Parameters are shared and independent of sequence length.

title: Matrix form
one_liner: Self-attention can be expressed compactly using matrix operations on input matrix X and learned parameters.
content:
The above computation can be written in a compact form if the $N$ inputs $x_n$ form the columns of the $D \times N$ matrix $X$. The values, queries, and keys can be computed as:

$$V[X] = \beta_v 1^T + \Omega_v X$$
$$Q[X] = \beta_q 1^T + \Omega_q X$$
$$K[X] = \beta_k 1^T + \Omega_k X,$$

where $1$ is an $N \times 1$ vector containing ones. The self-attention computation is then:

$$S_a[X] = V[X] \cdot \text{Softmax}\left(K[X]^T Q[X]\right),$$
motivation_md: Expressing self-attention in matrix form enables efficient computation and implementation using standard linear algebra operations.
recap_md:
- Inputs are arranged as columns in matrix $X$.
- Values, queries, keys computed via linear transforms plus biases.
- Attention computed as $S_a[X] = V[X] \cdot \text{Softmax}(K[X]^T Q[X])$.

title: Positional encoding
one_liner: Absolute positional encodings add a matrix Π to input X to encode positional information for sequence order.
content:
Observant readers will have noticed that the self-attention mechanism overlooks important information: the computation does not take into account the order of the inputs $x_n$. More precisely, it is equivariant with respect to input permutations. However, order is important when the inputs correspond to the words in a sentence. The sentence "The woman ate the raccoon" has a different meaning than "The raccoon ate the woman." There are two main approaches to incorporating position information.

Absolute positional encodings: A matrix $\Pi$ is added to the input $X$ that encodes positional information (figure 12.5). Each column of $\Pi$ is unique and hence contains information about the absolute position in the input sequence. This matrix can be chosen by hand or learned. It may be added to the network inputs or at every network layer. Sometimes it is added to $X$ in the computation of the queries and keys but not to the values.
motivation_md: Positional encoding is needed because self-attention alone ignores input order, which is crucial for meaning in sequences like sentences.
recap_md:
- Self-attention ignores input order (permutation equivariant).
- Absolute positional encoding adds matrix $\Pi$ to inputs.
- $\Pi$ encodes unique absolute positions, can be learned or fixed.

title: Relative positional encodings
one_liner: Relative positional encodings encode the relative position between words directly, modifying the attention matrix accordingly.
content: Relative positional encodings: The input to a self-attention mechanism may be an entire sentence, many sentences, or just a fragment of a sentence, and the absolute position of a word is much less important than the relative position between two words. Of course, this can be recovered if the system knows the absolute position of both, but relative positional encodings encode this information directly. Each element of the attention matrix corresponds to a particular offset between key position $a$ and query position $b$. Relative positional encodings learn a parameter $\pi_{a,b}$ for each offset and use this to modify the attention matrix by adding these values, multiplying by them, or using them to alter the attention matrix in some other way.
motivation_md: Relative positional encodings capture the relative positions between words, which is often more important than absolute positions for understanding context in sequences.
recap_md:
- Relative positional encodings focus on offsets between word positions.
- Each attention matrix element corresponds to a position offset.
- Parameters $\pi_{a,b}$ modify the attention matrix based on relative position.

title: scaled dot-product self-attention
one_liner: Dot products in attention are scaled by the square root of query/key dimension to prevent dominance and improve training.
content:
The dot products in the attention computation can have large magnitudes and move the arguments to the softmax function into a region where the largest value completely dominates. Small changes to the inputs to the softmax function now have little effect on the output (i.e., the gradients are very small), making the model difficult to train. To prevent this, the dot products are scaled by the square root of the dimension $D_q$ of the queries and keys (i.e., the number of rows in $\Omega_q$ and $\Omega_k$, which must be the same):

$$S_a[X] = V \cdot \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{K^T Q}{\sqrt{D_q}}\right).$$

This is known as scaled dot-product self-attention.
motivation_md: Scaling dot products prevents softmax saturation, ensuring meaningful gradients and stable training of self-attention models.
recap_md:
- Dot products can have large magnitudes causing softmax saturation.
- Scaling by $\sqrt{D_q}$ prevents dominance in softmax.
- This technique improves gradient flow and training stability.

title: Scaled dot-product self-attention
one_liner: The dot products in the attention computation are scaled by the square root of the dimension of queries and keys to improve training.
content:
The dot products in the attention computation can have large magnitudes and move the arguments to the softmax function into a region where the largest value completely dominates. Small changes to the inputs to the softmax function now have little effect on the output (i.e., the gradients are very small), making the model difficult to train. To prevent this, the dot products are scaled by the square root of the dimension $D_q$ of the queries and keys (i.e., the number of rows in $\Omega_q$ and $\Omega_k$, which must be the same):

$$S_a[X] = V \cdot \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{K^T Q}{\sqrt{D_q}}\right).$$

This is known as scaled dot-product self-attention.
motivation_md: Scaling dot products by $\sqrt{D_q}$ prevents softmax saturation and improves gradient flow, making training more effective.
recap_md:
- Large dot products cause softmax to be dominated by largest value.
- Scaling by $\sqrt{D_q}$ prevents this dominance.
- This scaling facilitates better training of self-attention.

title: Multiple heads
one_liner: Multiple self-attention mechanisms are usually applied in parallel, and this is known as multi-head self-attention.
content:
Multiple self-attention mechanisms are usually applied in parallel, and this is known as multi-head self-attention. Now H different sets of values, keys, and queries are computed:

$$V_h = \beta_{vh} 1^T + \Omega_{vh} X$$
$$Q_h = \beta_{qh} 1^T + \Omega_{qh} X$$
$$K_h = \beta_{kh} 1^T + \Omega_{kh} X.$$ (12.10)

The hth self-attention mechanism or head can be written as:

$$S_{ah}[X] = V_h \cdot \text{Softmax}\left( \frac{K_h^T Q_h}{\sqrt{D_q}} \right),$$ (12.11)

where we have different parameters $\{\beta_{vh}, \Omega_{vh}\}$, $\{\beta_{qh}, \Omega_{qh}\}$, and $\{\beta_{kh}, \Omega_{kh}\}$ for each head. Typically, if the dimension of the inputs $x_m$ is $D$ and there are $H$ heads, the values, queries, and keys will all be of size $D/H$, as this allows for an efficient implementation.
motivation_md: Multi-head self-attention allows the model to attend to different parts of the input in parallel, capturing diverse information efficiently.
recap_md:
- Multi-head self-attention applies multiple self-attention mechanisms in parallel.
- Each head computes its own values, keys, and queries with separate parameters.
- Values, queries, and keys typically have dimension $D/H$ for input dimension $D$ and $H$ heads.

title: multi-head self-attention
one_liner: Multiple self-attention mechanisms are usually applied in parallel, and this is known as multi-head self-attention.
content:
Multiple self-attention mechanisms are usually applied in parallel, and this is known as multi-head self-attention. Now H different sets of values, keys, and queries are computed:

$$V_h = \beta_{vh} 1^T + \Omega_{vh} X$$
$$Q_h = \beta_{qh} 1^T + \Omega_{qh} X$$
$$K_h = \beta_{kh} 1^T + \Omega_{kh} X.$$ (12.10)

The hth self-attention mechanism or head can be written as:

$$S_{ah}[X] = V_h \cdot \text{Softmax}\left( \frac{K_h^T Q_h}{\sqrt{D_q}} \right),$$ (12.11)

where we have different parameters $\{\beta_{vh}, \Omega_{vh}\}$, $\{\beta_{qh}, \Omega_{qh}\}$, and $\{\beta_{kh}, \Omega_{kh}\}$ for each head. Typically, if the dimension of the inputs $x_m$ is $D$ and there are $H$ heads, the values, queries, and keys will all be of size $D/H$, as this allows for an efficient implementation.

The outputs of these self-attention mechanisms are vertically concatenated, and another linear transform $\Omega_c$ is applied to combine them (figure 12.6):
motivation_md: Multi-head self-attention enables the model to capture multiple aspects of the input simultaneously by computing several sets of queries, keys, and values in parallel.
recap_md:
- Multi-head self-attention computes $H$ sets of values, keys, and queries.
- Each head has its own parameters $\{\beta, \Omega\}$.
- Outputs of all heads are concatenated and combined with a linear transform $\Omega_c$.

title: Transformer layers
one_liner: Self-attention is just one part of a larger transformer layer.
content:
Self-attention is just one part of a larger transformer layer. This consists of a multi-head self-attention unit (which allows the word representations to interact with each other) followed by a fully connected network $\text{mlp}[x_\cdot]$ that operates separately on each word. Both units are residual networks, meaning their outputs are added back to the original inputs.

In addition, it is typical to add a LayerNorm operation after both the self-attention and fully connected networks. LayerNorm normalizes each embedding in each batch element separately using statistics calculated across its $D$ embedding dimensions (section 11.4 and figure 11.14).
motivation_md: Transformer layers combine self-attention and feed-forward networks with normalization and residual connections to effectively model complex dependencies in sequences.
recap_md:
- Transformer layers include multi-head self-attention and a fully connected network.
- Both units use residual connections.
- LayerNorm is applied after self-attention and feed-forward networks.

title: Transformer layer
one_liner: The transformer layer consists of a multi-head attention block, residual connections, LayerNorm, and a fully connected network applied to each word embedding.
content:
The input to a transformer layer is a $D \times N$ matrix containing the $D$-dimensional word embeddings for each of the $N$ input tokens. The output is a matrix of the same size. The transformer layer consists of a series of operations.

First, there is a multi-head attention block, allowing the word embeddings to interact with one another. This forms the processing of a residual block, so the inputs are added back to the output. Second, a LayerNorm operation is applied separately to each embedding. Third, there is a second residual layer where the same fully connected neural network is applied separately to each of the $N$ word representations (columns). Finally, LayerNorm is applied again.

The complete layer can be described by the following series of operations (figure 12.7):

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &\leftarrow X + M_h S_a[X] \\
X &\leftarrow \text{LayerNorm}[X] \\
x_n &\leftarrow x_n + \text{mlp}[x_n], \quad \forall n \in \{1, \ldots, N\} \\
X &\leftarrow \text{LayerNorm}[X],
\end{aligned}
$$

where $M_h$ is a parameter matrix and $S_a[X]$ is the multi-head self-attention output.
motivation_md: The transformer layer integrates multi-head attention, residual connections, normalization, and feed-forward networks to process word embeddings effectively.
recap_md:
- Input is a $D \times N$ matrix of word embeddings.
- Multi-head attention block with residual connection is applied.
- LayerNorm and a fully connected network with residual connection follow, ending with another LayerNorm.

title: Tokenization
one_liner: A text processing pipeline begins with a tokenizer that splits text into smaller constituent units (tokens) from a vocabulary.
content:
A text processing pipeline begins with a tokenizer. This splits the text into smaller constituent units (tokens) from a vocabulary of possible tokens. In the discussion above, we have implied that these tokens represent words, but there are several difficulties:

- Inevitably, some words (e.g., names) will not be in the vocabulary.
- It’s unclear how to handle punctuation, but this is important. If a sentence ends in a question mark, we must encode this information.
- The vocabulary would need different tokens for versions of the same word with different suffixes (e.g., walk, walks, walked, walking), and there is no way to clarify that these variations are related.

One approach would be to use letters and punctuation marks as the vocabulary, but this would mean splitting text into very small parts and requiring the subsequent network to re-learn the relations between them.

In practice, a compromise between letters and full words is used, and the final vocabulary includes both common words and word fragments from which larger and less frequent words can be composed. The vocabulary is computed using a sub-word tokenizer such as byte pair encoding (figure 12.8) that greedily merges commonly occurring sub-strings based on their frequency.
motivation_md: Tokenization breaks text into manageable units for processing, balancing vocabulary size and the ability to represent words and their variations effectively.
recap_md:
- Tokenizers split text into smaller units called tokens.
- Handling punctuation and word variations is challenging.
- Sub-word tokenizers like byte pair encoding merge common substrings to build the vocabulary.

title: Embeddings
one_liner: Each token in the vocabulary is mapped to a unique word embedding stored in a matrix $\Omega_e \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times |V|}$.
content: Each token in the vocabulary $V$ is mapped to a unique word embedding, and the embeddings for the whole vocabulary are stored in a matrix $\Omega_e \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times |V|}$. To accomplish this, the $N$ input tokens are first encoded in the matrix $T \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times N}$, where the $n$th column corresponds to the $n$th token and is a $|V| \times 1$ one-hot vector (i.e., a vector where every entry is zero except for the entry corresponding to the token, which is set to one). The input embeddings are computed as $X = \Omega_e T$, and $\Omega_e$ is learned like any other network parameter (figure 12.9). A typical embedding size $D$ is 1024, and a typical total vocabulary size $|V|$ is 30,000, so even before the main network, there are many parameters in $\Omega_e$ to learn.
motivation_md: Embeddings convert discrete tokens into continuous vector representations that can be processed by neural networks.
recap_md:
- Each token maps to a unique embedding vector.
- Embeddings are stored in a matrix $\Omega_e \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times |V|}$.
- Input tokens are one-hot encoded and multiplied by $\Omega_e$ to get embeddings.

title: Transformer model
one_liner: The embedding matrix representing the text is passed through a series of $K$ transformer layers, called a transformer model.
content:
Finally, the embedding matrix $X$ representing the text is passed through a series of $K$ transformer layers, called a transformer model. There are three types of transformer models.

An encoder transforms the text embeddings into a representation that can support a variety of tasks.

A decoder predicts the next token to continue the input text. Encoder-decoders are used in sequence-to-sequence tasks, where one text string is converted into another (e.g., machine translation). These variations are described in sections 12.6–12.8, respectively.
motivation_md: Transformer models process text embeddings through multiple layers to perform various NLP tasks like encoding, decoding, and sequence-to-sequence transformations.
recap_md:
- Transformer models apply $K$ transformer layers to embeddings.
- Encoders transform embeddings for diverse tasks.
- Decoders predict next tokens; encoder-decoders handle sequence-to-sequence tasks.

title: BERT
one_liner: BERT is an encoder model using 30,000 tokens, 1024-dimensional embeddings, 24 transformer layers, and 16 attention heads per layer.
content:
BERT is an encoder model that uses a vocabulary of 30,000 tokens. Input tokens are converted to 1024-dimensional word embeddings and passed through 24 transformer layers. Each contains a self-attention mechanism with 16 heads. The queries, keys, and values for each head are of dimension 64 (i.e., the matrices $\Omega_{vh}$, $\Omega_{qh}$, $\Omega_{kh}$ are $64 \times 1024$). The dimension of the single hidden layer in the fully connected networks is 4096. The total number of parameters is approximately 340 million. When BERT was introduced, this was considered large, but it is now much smaller than state-of-the-art models.

Encoder models like BERT exploit transfer learning (section 9.3.6). During pre-training, the parameters of the transformer architecture are learned using self-supervision from a large corpus of text. The goal here is for the model to learn general information about the statistics of language. In the fine-tuning stage, the resulting network is adapted to solve a particular task using a smaller body of labelled training data.
motivation_md: BERT demonstrates how large transformer encoder models can be pretrained on large corpora and fine-tuned for specific tasks, leveraging transfer learning.
recap_md:
- BERT uses 30,000 token vocabulary and 1024-dimensional embeddings.
- It has 24 transformer layers with 16 attention heads each.
- Pretrained with self-supervision and fine-tuned for tasks.

title: Regularization methods for residual networks
aliases: block dropout methods for residual networks
one_liner: Several regularization methods have been developed that are targeted specifically at residual architectures.
content: Several regularization methods have been developed that are targeted specifically at residual architectures. ResDrop (Yamada et al., 2016), stochastic depth (Huang et al., 2016), and RandomDrop (Yamada et al., 2019) all regularize residual networks by randomly dropping residual blocks during the training process. In the latter case, the propensity for dropping a block is determined by a Bernoulli variable, whose parameter is linearly decreased during training. At test time, the residual blocks are added back in with their expected probability. These methods are effectively versions of dropout, in which all the hidden units in a block are simultaneously dropped.
motivation_md: Regularization methods like ResDrop, stochastic depth, and RandomDrop help prevent overfitting in residual networks by randomly dropping residual blocks during training, improving generalization.
recap_md:
- ResDrop, stochastic depth, and RandomDrop regularize residual networks by randomly dropping residual blocks during training.
- The dropping probability is controlled by a Bernoulli variable that decreases linearly during training.
- At test time, residual blocks are included with their expected probability, acting like block-wise dropout.

title: Variations of batch normalization
one_liner: Several variants of BatchNorm have been proposed (figure 11.14).
content:
Variations of batch normalization include several proposed variants (figure 11.14). BatchNorm normalizes each channel separately based on statistics gathered across the batch. Ghost batch normalization or GhostNorm (Hoffer et al., 2017) uses only part of the batch to compute the normalization statistics, making them noisier and increasing regularization when the batch size is very large (figure 11.14b).

When the batch size is very small or fluctuations within a batch are large (common in natural language processing), BatchNorm statistics may become unreliable. Ioffe (2017) proposed batch renormalization, which keeps a running average of batch statistics and modifies normalization to be more representative.

Batch normalization is unsuitable for recurrent neural networks because statistics must be stored at each sequence step, and it's unclear how to handle test sequences longer than training sequences.

BatchNorm also requires access to the whole batch, which may be difficult when training is distributed across machines.

Layer normalization or LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016) avoids batch statistics by normalizing each data example separately, using statistics across channels and spatial positions (figure 11.14c). It retains separate learned scale γ and offset δ per channel.

Group normalization or GroupNorm (Wu & He, 2018) divides channels into groups and computes statistics for each group separately across within-group channels and spatial positions (figure 11.14d), also retaining separate scale and offset per channel.

Instance normalization or InstanceNorm (Ulyanov et al., 2016) normalizes each channel separately, using statistics gathered only across spatial position (figure 11.14e).
motivation_md: BatchNorm variants address limitations like unreliable statistics with small batches, unsuitability for recurrent networks, and distributed training challenges by modifying how normalization statistics are computed and applied.
recap_md:
- GhostNorm computes normalization statistics from part of the batch to increase regularization for large batch sizes.
- Batch renormalization keeps running averages to improve reliability with small or variable batches.
- LayerNorm, GroupNorm, and InstanceNorm normalize differently to avoid batch dependence and suit different architectures.

title: Why BatchNorm helps
one_liner: BatchNorm helps control the initial gradients in a residual network (figure 11.6c).
content:
BatchNorm helps control the initial gradients in a residual network (figure 11.6c). However, the mechanism by which BatchNorm improves performance is not well understood. The stated goal of Ioffe & Szegedy (2015) was to reduce problems caused by internal covariate shift, the change in the distribution of inputs to a layer caused by updating preceding layers during backpropagation. Santurkar et al. (2018) provided evidence against this view by artificially inducing covariate shift and showing that networks with and without BatchNorm performed equally well.

Motivated by this, they searched for another explanation and showed empirically for the VGG network that adding batch normalization decreases variation in both the loss and its gradient as we move in the gradient direction. In other words, the loss surface is smoother and changes more slowly, allowing larger learning rates.

They also provide theoretical proofs for these phenomena and show that for any parameter initialization, the distance to the nearest optimum is less for networks with batch normalization. Bjorck et al. (2018) also argue that BatchNorm improves loss landscape properties and allows larger learning rates.

Other explanations include decreasing the importance of tuning the learning rate (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015; Arora et al., 2018). Li & Arora (2019) show that using an exponentially increasing learning rate schedule is possible with batch normalization. This is because batch normalization makes the network invariant to the scales of the weight matrices (see Huszár, 2019, for an intuitive visualization).

Hoffer et al. (2017) identified that BatchNorm has a regularizing effect due to statistical fluctuations.
motivation_md: BatchNorm improves training by smoothing the loss surface and stabilizing gradients, enabling larger learning rates and better optimization, beyond just reducing internal covariate shift.
recap_md:
- BatchNorm controls initial gradients and smooths the loss surface, allowing larger learning rates.
- It reduces variation in loss and gradients, improving optimization stability.
- BatchNorm makes networks invariant to weight scale and has a regularizing effect.

title: Alternatives to batch normalization
one_liner: Although BatchNorm is widely used, it is not strictly necessary to train deep residual nets; there are other ways of making the loss surface tractable.
content:
Although BatchNorm is widely used, it is not strictly necessary to train deep residual nets; there are other ways of making the loss surface tractable. Balduzzi et al. (2017) proposed rescaling by \(\sqrt{1/2} \) in figure 11.6b; they argued that it prevents gradient explosion but does not resolve shattered gradients.

Other work has investigated rescaling the function’s output in the residual block before adding it back to the input. For example, De & Smith (2020) introduce SkipInit, placing a learnable scalar multiplier at the end of each residual branch, helping if initialized to less than \(\sqrt{1/K} \), where \(K\) is the number of residual blocks; they suggest initializing this to zero.

Similarly, Hayou et al. (2021) introduce Stable ResNet, which rescales the output of the function in the \(k\)th residual block by a constant \(\lambda_k\). They prove that in the infinite width limit, the expected gradient norm of the first layer weights is lower bounded by the sum of squares of the scalings \(\lambda_k\). Setting these to a constant \(\sqrt{1/K} \) allows training networks with up to 1000 blocks.

Zhang et al. (2019a) introduce FixUp, initializing every layer using He normalization but setting the last linear/convolutional layer of every residual block to zero. This stabilizes the initial forward pass and prevents gradient explosion. They also rescale branches so that the expected parameter change magnitude is constant regardless of residual block count.

These methods allow training deep residual networks but usually don’t achieve the same test performance as BatchNorm, likely because they lack regularization from noisy batch statistics. De & Smith (2020) modify their method to induce regularization via dropout, helping close this gap.
motivation_md: Alternatives to BatchNorm exist to stabilize training of deep residual networks without batch statistics, enabling training of very deep nets but often with less regularization benefit.
recap_md:
- Rescaling outputs in residual blocks can prevent gradient explosion but may not solve shattered gradients.
- Methods like SkipInit, Stable ResNet, and FixUp rescale or initialize residual branches to stabilize training.
- These alternatives often lack BatchNorm's regularization but can be combined with dropout to improve performance.

title: DenseNet and U-Net
one_liner: DenseNet was first introduced by Huang et al. (2017b), U-Net was developed by Ronneberger et al. (2015), and stacked hourglass networks by Newell et al. (2016).
content:
DenseNet was first introduced by Huang et al. (2017b), U-Net was developed by Ronneberger et al. (2015), and stacked hourglass networks by Newell et al. (2016). Of these architectures, U-Net has been the most extensively adapted. Çiçek et al. (2016) introduced 3D U-Net, and Milletari et al. (2016) introduced V-Net, both extending U-Net to process 3D data.

Zhou et al. (2018) combine ideas of DenseNet and U-Net in an architecture that downsamples and re-upsamples the image but also repeatedly uses intermediate representations. U-Nets are commonly used in medical image segmentation (see Siddique et al., 2021, for a review). They have also been applied to depth estimation (Garg et al., 2016), semantic segmentation (Iglovikov & Shvets, 2018), inpainting (Zeng et al., 2019), pansharpening (Yao et al., 2018), and image-to-image translation (Isola et al., 2017).
motivation_md: DenseNet and U-Net architectures facilitate effective feature reuse and multi-scale processing, enabling advances in medical imaging and other computer vision tasks.
recap_md:
- DenseNet, U-Net, and stacked hourglass networks are influential architectures for image processing.
- U-Net has many adaptations, including 3D U-Net and V-Net for 3D data.
- U-Nets are widely used in medical image segmentation and other vision tasks.

title: Transformers
one_liner: Transformers were initially targeted at natural language processing (NLP) problems, where the network input is a series of high-dimensional embeddings representing words or word fragments.
content:
Chapter 10 introduced convolutional networks, specialized for processing data on regular grids, particularly images with many input variables, where fully connected networks are impractical. Each convolutional layer uses parameter sharing so local image patches are processed similarly at every position.

This chapter introduces transformers, initially targeted at natural language processing (NLP) problems, where the input is a series of high-dimensional embeddings representing words or word fragments. Language datasets share characteristics with image data: large numbers of input variables and similar statistics at every position, making it inefficient to relearn word meanings at every position. However, language data sequences vary in length, and unlike images, there is no easy way to resize them.
motivation_md: Transformers address challenges in processing variable-length sequences in NLP by enabling parameter sharing and context-dependent connections, unlike convolutional networks designed for fixed grid data.
recap_md:
- Convolutional networks process regular grid data like images using parameter sharing.
- Transformers handle variable-length sequences in NLP with high-dimensional embeddings.
- Transformers enable context-dependent connections and parameter sharing across sequence positions.

title: Dot-product self-attention
one_liner: The transformer acquires parameter sharing and input-dependent connections by using dot-product self-attention.
content:
The previous section argued that a model for processing text will (i) use parameter sharing to cope with long input passages of differing lengths and (ii) contain connections between word representations that depend on the words themselves. The transformer acquires both properties by using dot-product self-attention.

A standard neural network layer \(f[x]\) takes a \(D \times 1\) input \(x\) and applies a linear transformation followed by an activation function like a ReLU, so:
\[ f[x] = \text{ReLU}[\beta + \Omega x], \]
where \(\beta\) contains biases and \(\Omega\) contains weights.

A self-attention block \(sa[\cdot]\) takes \(N\) inputs \(x_1, \ldots, x_N\), each of dimension \(D \times 1\), and returns \(N\) outputs, each also size \(D \times 1\). In NLP, each input represents a word or word fragment. First, a set of values are computed for each input:
\[ v_m = \beta_v + \Omega_v x_m, \]
where \(\beta_v \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times 1}\) and \(\Omega_v \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\) are biases and weights.

Then the \(n\)th output \(sa_n[x_1, \ldots, x_N]\) is a weighted sum of all values \(v_1, \ldots, v_N\):
\[ sa_n[x_1, \ldots, x_N] = \sum_{m=1}^N a[x_m, x_n] v_m. \]
The scalar weight \(a[x_m, x_n]\) is the attention the \(n\)th output pays to input \(x_m\). The \(N\) weights \(a[\cdot, x_n]\) are non-negative and sum to one, so self-attention routes values in different proportions to create each output (figure 12.1).

The following sections examine dot-product self-attention in more detail, including how values and weights are computed.
motivation_md: Dot-product self-attention enables transformers to share parameters across sequence positions and create input-dependent connections, essential for modeling context in language.
recap_md:
- Dot-product self-attention computes outputs as weighted sums of value vectors derived from inputs.
- Attention weights are non-negative and sum to one, acting as routing coefficients.
- This mechanism enables parameter sharing and context-dependent connections in transformers.

title: Self-attention as routing
one_liner: Self-attention can be thought of as routing the values in different proportions to create each output.
content:
The self-attention mechanism takes \(N\) inputs \(x_1, \ldots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^D\) (here \(N=3\) and \(D=4\)) and processes each separately to compute \(N\) value vectors. The \(n\)th output \(sa_n[x_1, \ldots, x_N]\) (written as \(sa_n[x_\cdot]\) for short) is computed as a weighted sum of the \(N\) value vectors, where the weights are positive and sum to one.

For example:
- Output \(sa_1[x_\cdot]\) is computed as \(a[x_1,x_1] = 0.1\) times the first value vector, \(a[x_2,x_1] = 0.3\) times the second, and \(a[x_3,x_1] = 0.6\) times the third.
- Output \(sa_2[x_\cdot]\) uses weights 0.5, 0.2, and 0.3 respectively.
- Output \(sa_3[x_\cdot]\) uses a different weighting again.

Each output can hence be thought of as a different routing of the \(N\) values.
motivation_md: Viewing self-attention as routing clarifies how outputs selectively combine input values based on learned attention weights, enabling flexible context modeling.
recap_md:
- Self-attention outputs are weighted sums of input value vectors.
- Weights are positive and sum to one, acting as routing coefficients.
- Different outputs use different weightings, routing values differently.

title: Encoder-decoder model example: machine translation
one_liner: Translation between languages is an example of a sequence-to-sequence task using an encoder-decoder model.
content:
Translation between languages is an example of a sequence-to-sequence task. One common approach uses both an encoder (to compute a good representation of the source sentence) and a decoder (to generate the sentence in the target language). This is aptly called an encoder-decoder model.

Consider translating from English to French. The encoder receives the sentence in English and processes it through a series of transformer layers to create an output representation for each token. During training, the decoder receives the ground truth translation in French and passes it through a series of transformer layers that use masked self-attention and predict the following word at each position. However, the decoder layers also attend to the output of the encoder. Consequently, each French output word is conditioned on the previous output words and the source English sentence (figure 12.13).

This is achieved by modifying the transformer layers in the decoder. Originally, these consisted of a masked self-attention layer followed by a neural network applied individually to each embedding (figure 12.12). A new self-attention layer is added between these two components, in which the decoder embeddings attend to the encoder embeddings. This uses a version of self-attention known as encoder-decoder attention or cross-attention, where the queries are computed from the decoder embeddings and the keys and values from the encoder embeddings (figure 12.14).
motivation_md: Machine translation requires converting a source language sentence into a target language sentence, which is a sequence-to-sequence task. The encoder-decoder model efficiently represents the source and generates the target sentence by combining encoder and decoder transformer layers.
recap_md:
- Translation is a sequence-to-sequence task handled by encoder-decoder models.
- The encoder processes the source sentence into token representations.
- The decoder uses masked self-attention and cross-attention to generate the target sentence.

title: Transformers for long sequences
one_liner: The computational complexity of transformers scales quadratically with sequence length, limiting sequence length and motivating methods to extend transformers for longer sequences.
content:
Since each token in a transformer encoder model interacts with every other token, the computational complexity scales quadratically with the length of the sequence. For a decoder model, each token only interacts with previous tokens, so there are roughly half the number of interactions, but the complexity still scales quadratically. These relationships can be visualized as interaction matrices (figure 12.15a–b).

This quadratic increase in the amount of computation ultimately limits the length of sequences that can be used. Many methods have been developed to extend the transformer to cope with longer sequences. One approach is to prune the self-attention interactions or, equivalently, to sparsify the interaction matrix (figures 12.15c-h).

For example, this can be restricted to a convolutional structure so that each token only interacts with a few neighboring tokens. Across multiple layers, tokens still interact at larger distances as the receptive field expands. As for convolution in images, the kernel can vary in size and dilation rate.

A pure convolutional approach requires many layers to integrate information over large distances. One way to speed up this process is to allow certain tokens (perhaps at the start of every sentence) to attend to all other tokens (encoder model) or all previous tokens (decoder model). A similar idea is to have a small number of global tokens that connect to all the other tokens and themselves. Like the <cls> token, these do not represent any word but serve to provide long-distance connections.
motivation_md: Transformers' quadratic complexity limits the maximum sequence length they can handle; sparsifying self-attention or using convolutional structures helps manage longer sequences efficiently.
recap_md:
- Transformer encoder complexity scales quadratically with sequence length.
- Sparsifying self-attention or using convolutional structures reduces complexity.
- Global tokens or selective attention enable long-distance interactions efficiently.

title: sparsifying self-attention interactions to reduce complexity
one_liner: Sparsifying self-attention interactions reduces quadratic complexity by limiting token interactions to neighbors or selected global tokens.
content:
Figure 12.15 Interaction matrices for self-attention. a) In an encoder, every token interacts with every other token, and computation expands quadratically with the number of tokens. b) In a decoder, each token only interacts with the previous tokens, but complexity is still quadratic. c) Complexity can be reduced by using a convolutional structure (encoder case). d) Convolutional structure for decoder case. e–f) Convolutional structure with dilation rate of two and three (decoder case). g) Another strategy is to allow selected tokens to interact with all the other tokens (encoder case) or all the previous tokens (decoder case pictured). h) Alternatively, global tokens can be introduced (left two columns and top two rows). These interact with all of the tokens as well as with each other.

One approach is to prune the self-attention interactions or, equivalently, to sparsify the interaction matrix (figures 12.15c-h). For example, this can be restricted to a convolutional structure so that each token only interacts with a few neighboring tokens. Across multiple layers, tokens still interact at larger distances as the receptive field expands. As for convolution in images, the kernel can vary in size and dilation rate.

A pure convolutional approach requires many layers to integrate information over large distances. One way to speed up this process is to allow certain tokens (perhaps at the start of every sentence) to attend to all other tokens (encoder model) or all previous tokens (decoder model). A similar idea is to have a small number of global tokens that connect to all the other tokens and themselves. Like the <cls> token, these do not represent any word but serve to provide long-distance connections.
motivation_md: Reducing the quadratic complexity of self-attention by sparsifying interactions enables transformers to handle longer sequences more efficiently.
recap_md:
- Full self-attention has quadratic complexity due to all-token interactions.
- Sparsifying with convolutional structures limits interactions to neighbors.
- Global tokens or selective attention provide long-distance connections.

title: Transformers for images
one_liner: Transformer networks for images have eclipsed convolutional networks despite challenges like quadratic complexity and lack of spatial inductive bias.
content:
There are several reasons why transformers for images face challenges. First, there are many more pixels in an image than words in a sentence, so the quadratic complexity of self-attention poses a practical bottleneck. Second, convolutional nets have a good inductive bias because each layer is equivariant to spatial translation and takes into account the 2D structure of the image. However, this must be learned in a transformer network.

Regardless of these apparent disadvantages, transformer networks for images have now eclipsed the performance of convolutional networks for image classification and other tasks. This is partly because of the enormous scale at which they can be constructed and the large amounts of data that can be used to pre-train the networks. This section describes transformer models for images.
motivation_md: Transformers face challenges with images due to pixel count and lack of spatial bias, but large-scale training and model size enable them to outperform convolutional networks.
recap_md:
- Images have many pixels, making self-attention costly.
- Convolutional nets have spatial inductive bias; transformers must learn it.
- Transformers now outperform convolutional nets with large-scale training.

title: transformers for images outperform convolutional networks with large-scale training data
one_liner: Transformer networks for images have eclipsed convolutional networks due to their large scale and extensive pre-training data.
content: Regardless of these apparent disadvantages, transformer networks for images have now eclipsed the performance of convolutional networks for image classification and other tasks. This is partly because of the enormous scale at which they can be constructed and the large amounts of data that can be used to pre-train the networks. This section describes transformer models for images.
motivation_md: Despite challenges, transformers outperform convolutional networks in image tasks due to scale and pre-training data availability.
recap_md:
- Transformers for images outperform convolutional networks.
- Large model scale and extensive pre-training are key factors.
- This advancement enables improved image classification and tasks.

title: ImageGPT
one_liner: ImageGPT is a transformer decoder that autoregressively models image pixels to predict subsequent pixel values.
content:
ImageGPT is a transformer decoder; it builds an autoregressive model of image pixels that ingests a partial image and predicts the subsequent pixel value. The quadratic complexity of the transformer network means that the largest model (which contained 6.8 billion parameters) could still only operate on 64×64 images. Moreover, to make this tractable, the original 24-bit RGB color space had to be quantized into a nine-bit color space, so the system ingests (and predicts) one of 512 possible tokens at each position.

Images are naturally 2D objects, but ImageGPT simply learns a different positional encoding at each pixel. Hence it must learn that each pixel has a close relationship with its preceding neighbors and also with nearby pixels in the row above. Figure 12.16 shows example generation results.

The internal representation of this decoder was used as a basis for image classification. Each pixel’s final embedding is averaged, and a linear layer maps these values to activations which are passed through a softmax layer to predict class probabilities. The system is pre-trained on a large corpus of web images and then fine-tuned on the ImageNet database resized to 48 × 48 pixels using a loss function that contains both a cross-entropy term for image classification and a generative loss term for predicting the pixels. Despite using a large amount of external training data, the system achieved only a 27.4% top-1 error rate on ImageNet (figure 10.15). This was worse than convolutional architectures of the time (see figure 10.21) but is still impressive given the small input image size; unsurprisingly, it fails where the target object is small or thin.
motivation_md: ImageGPT models images autoregressively with transformers, enabling pixel prediction and classification despite computational and input size constraints.
recap_md:
- ImageGPT is a transformer decoder modeling images autoregressively.
- Operates on 64×64 images with quantized color tokens.
- Used for image classification with pre-training and fine-tuning on ImageNet.

title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
one_liner: The Vision Transformer divides images into 16×16 patches, embeds them, and uses a transformer encoder with a <cls> token for classification.
content:
The Vision Transformer tackled the problem of image resolution by dividing the image into 16×16 patches (figure 12.17). Each patch is mapped to an input embedding via a learned linear transformation, and these representations are fed into the transformer network. Once again, standard 1D positional encodings are learned.

This is an encoder model with a <cls> token (see figures 12.10–12.11). However, unlike BERT, it uses supervised pre-training on a large database of 303 million labeled images from 18,000 classes. The <cls> token is mapped via a final network layer to create activations that are fed into a softmax function to generate class probabilities. After pre-training, the system is applied to the final classification task by replacing this
motivation_md: The Vision Transformer addresses image resolution by patch embedding and uses supervised pre-training with a <cls> token for effective image classification.
recap_md:
- Images are divided into 16×16 patches and embedded.
- Uses a transformer encoder with a <cls> token for classification.
- Pre-trained on a large labeled image dataset with supervised learning.

title: Vision Transformer patch embedding and positional encoding
one_liner: The Vision Transformer divides images into patches, embeds them, and uses learned 1D positional encodings with a <cls> token for classification.
content:
The Vision Transformer tackled the problem of image resolution by dividing the image into 16×16 patches (figure 12.17). Each patch is mapped to an input embedding via a learned linear transformation, and these representations are fed into the transformer network. Once again, standard 1D positional encodings are learned.

This is an encoder model with a <cls> token (see figures 12.10–12.11). However, unlike BERT, it uses supervised pre-training on a large database of 303 million labeled images from 18,000 classes. The <cls> token is mapped via a final network layer to create activations that are fed into a softmax function to generate class probabilities. After pre-training, the system is applied to the final classification task by replacing this
motivation_md: Vision Transformer uses patch embeddings and positional encodings to handle image resolution and applies supervised pre-training for classification.
recap_md:
- Images are divided into 16×16 patches and embedded.
- Learned 1D positional encodings are used.
- Uses a <cls> token and supervised pre-training on large labeled datasets.

title: graph expansion problem
one_liner: This is known as the graph expansion problem.
content: Input node may be in the receptive field of every output, and this may not reduce the graph size at all. This is known as the graph expansion problem. Two approaches that
motivation_md: Graph expansion problem arises because an input node can influence many outputs, causing the graph size to remain large and inefficient to process.
recap_md:
- The graph expansion problem occurs when an input node is in the receptive field of every output.
- This can prevent any reduction in graph size.
- It presents a challenge in scaling graph-based computations.

title: Neighborhood sampling
one_liner: Neighborhood sampling: The full graph that feeds into the batch of nodes is sampled, thereby reducing the connections at each network layer (figure 13.10).
content: Neighborhood sampling: The full graph that feeds into the batch of nodes is sampled, thereby reducing the connections at each network layer (figure 13.10). For example, we might start with the batch nodes and randomly sample a fixed number of their neighbors in the previous layer. Then, we randomly sample a fixed number of their neighbors in the layer before, and so on. The graph still increases in size with each layer but in a much more controlled way. This is done anew for each batch, so the contributing neighbors differ even if the same batch is drawn twice. This is also reminiscent of
motivation_md: Neighborhood sampling controls graph size growth by sampling a fixed number of neighbors at each layer, making graph neural network computations more efficient.
recap_md:
- Neighborhood sampling reduces connections by sampling neighbors at each layer.
- Sampling is done anew for each batch, so neighbors differ even for the same batch.
- This approach controls graph size growth across layers.

title: Graph partitioning
one_liner: Graph partitioning: A second approach is to cluster the original graph into disjoint subsets of nodes (i.e., smaller graphs that are not connected to one another) before processing (figure 13.11).
content: Graph partitioning: A second approach is to cluster the original graph into disjoint subsets of nodes (i.e., smaller graphs that are not connected to one another) before processing (figure 13.11). There are standard algorithms to choose these subsets to maximize the number of internal links. These smaller graphs can each be treated as batches, or a random subset of them can be combined to form a batch (reinstating any edges between them from the original graph). This work is subject to a Creative Commons CC-BY-NC-ND license. (C) MIT Press.
motivation_md: Graph partitioning reduces computational complexity by dividing a large graph into smaller, disconnected subsets that can be processed independently or combined efficiently.
recap_md:
- Graph partitioning clusters the graph into disjoint subsets before processing.
- Algorithms maximize internal links within subsets.
- Smaller graphs can be processed as batches or combined with original edges reinstated.

title: Layers for graph convolutional networks
one_liner: We now consider different approaches to both (i) the combination of the current embedding with the aggregated neighbors and (ii) the aggregation process itself.
content: Layers for graph convolutional networks: In the previous examples, we combined messages from adjacent nodes by summing them together with the transformed current node. This was accomplished by post-multiplying the node embedding matrix H by the adjacency matrix plus the identity A + I. We now consider different approaches to both (i) the combination of the current embedding with the aggregated neighbors and (ii) the aggregation process itself.
motivation_md: Exploring different methods to combine current node embeddings with aggregated neighbor information and how to aggregate neighbors helps improve graph convolutional network performance.
recap_md:
- Previous GCN layers combined adjacent node messages by summing with the current node.
- This used multiplication of H by A + I.
- New approaches explore different combination and aggregation methods.

title: Combining current node and aggregated neighbors
one_liner: In the example GCN layer above, we combined the aggregated neighbors HA with the current nodes H by just summing them.
content:
Combining current node and aggregated neighbors: In the example GCN layer above, we combined the aggregated neighbors HA with the current nodes H by just summing them:

H_{k+1} = a\left( \beta_k 1^T + \Omega_k H_k (A + I) \right).

(13.13)
motivation_md: Combining the current node embedding with aggregated neighbor embeddings by summation provides a simple way to integrate local graph information in GCN layers.
recap_md:
- Aggregated neighbors HA and current nodes H are combined by summation.
- The formula is given by equation (13.13).
- This method integrates neighbor information into node embeddings.

title: diagonal enhancement
one_liner: In another variation, the current node is multiplied by a factor of (1 + ϵk) before contributing to the sum, where ϵk is a learned scalar that is different for each layer.
content:
In another variation, the current node is multiplied by a factor of (1 + \epsilon_k) before contributing to the sum, where \epsilon_k is a learned scalar that is different for each layer:

H_{k+1} = a\left( \beta_k 1^T + \Omega_k H_k (A + (1 + \epsilon_k) I) \right).

(13.14)
motivation_md: Diagonal enhancement adjusts the contribution of the current node by a learned scalar, allowing the model to weigh self-information differently at each layer.
recap_md:
- The current node is scaled by (1 + ϵ_k) before summation.
- ϵ_k is a learned scalar unique to each layer.
- This variation is expressed in equation (13.14).

title: Mean aggregation
one_liner: Sometimes it’s better to take the average of the neighbors rather than the sum; this can be superior if the embedding information is more important and the structural information less so.
content:
Mean aggregation: The above methods aggregate the neighbors by summing the node embeddings. However, it’s possible to combine the embeddings in different ways. Sometimes it’s better to take the average of the neighbors rather than the sum; this can be superior if the embedding information is more important and the structural information less so since the magnitude of the neighborhood contributions will not depend on the number of neighbors:

\[
\text{agg}[n] = \frac{1}{|\text{ne}[n]|} \sum_{m \in \text{ne}[n]} h_m,
\]

where as before, \text{ne}[n] denotes a set containing the indices of the neighbors of the nth node. Equation 13.17 can be computed neatly in matrix form by introducing the diagonal N \times N degree matrix D. Each non-zero element of this matrix contains the number of neighbors for the associated node. It follows that each diagonal element in the inverse matrix D^{-1} contains the denominator that we need to compute the average. The new GCN layer can be written as:

\[
H_{k+1} = a\left( \beta_k 1^T + \Omega_k H_k (A D^{-1} + I) \right).
\]

(13.18)
motivation_md: Mean aggregation normalizes neighbor contributions by their count, emphasizing embedding information over structural size, which can improve graph neural network performance.
recap_md:
- Mean aggregation averages neighbor embeddings instead of summing.
- Uses degree matrix D to normalize contributions.
- The GCN layer formula is given by equation (13.18).

title: Kipf normalization
one_liner: In Kipf normalization, the sum of the node representations is normalized to down-weight information from nodes with many neighbors.
content:
Kipf normalization: There are many variations of graph neural networks based on mean aggregation. Sometimes the current node is included with its neighbors in the mean computation rather than treated separately. In Kipf normalization, the sum of the node representations is normalized as:

\[
\text{agg}[n] = \sum_{m \in \text{ne}[n]} h_m \frac{1}{\sqrt{|\text{ne}[n]| |\text{ne}[m]|}},
\]

with the logic that information coming from nodes with a very large number of neighbors should be down-weighted since there are many connections and they provide less unique information. This can also be expressed in matrix form using the degree matrix:

\[
H_{k+1} = a\left( \beta_k 1^T + \Omega_k H_k (D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2} + I) \right).
\]

(13.20)
motivation_md: Kipf normalization adjusts neighbor contributions by their degrees to reduce the influence of highly connected nodes, improving representation quality in graph neural networks.
recap_md:
- Kipf normalization includes the current node with neighbors in mean computation.
- Normalizes sums by the square root of neighbor degrees.
- Expressed in matrix form as equation (13.20).

title: Multi-scale vision transformers
one_liner: Several transformer models that process the image at multiple scales have been proposed.
content:
The Vision Transformer differs from convolutional architectures in that it operates on a single scale and has a receptive field that covers the whole image. Several transformer models that process the image at multiple scales have been proposed. Similarly to convolutional networks, these generally start with small high resolution patches and few channels and gradually enlarge the receptive field, decrease the spatial resolution and increase the number of channels (embedding dimension).

A representative example of a multi-scale transformer is the shifted-window or SWin transformer. This is an encoder transformer that divides the image into patches and groups these patches into a grid of windows within which self-attention is applied independently (figure 12.18). These windows are shifted in adjacent transformers, so the effective receptive field at a given patch can expand beyond the window border. The scale is reduced periodically by concatenating features from non-overlapping 2×2 patches and applying a linear transformation that maps these concatenated features to twice the original number of channels. This architecture does not have a <cls> token but instead averages the output features at the last layer. These are then mapped via a linear layer to the desired number of classes and passed through a softmax function to output class probabilities. At the time of writing, the most sophisticated version of this architecture achieves a 9.89% top-1 error rate on the ImageNet database.

A related idea is periodically to integrate information from across the whole image. Dual attention vision transformers (DaViT) alternate two types of transformers. In the first, image patches attend to one another, and the self-attention computation uses all the channels. In the second, the channels attend to one another, and the self-attention computation uses all the image patches. This architecture reaches a 9.60% top-1 error rate on ImageNet and is close to the state-of-the-art at the time of writing.
motivation_md: Multi-scale vision transformers address the limitation of single-scale Vision Transformers by processing images at multiple scales, enabling larger receptive fields and better spatial feature integration for improved image classification accuracy.
recap_md:
- Multi-scale vision transformers process images at multiple scales, starting with small patches and increasing receptive field while reducing spatial resolution.
- The shifted-window (SWin) transformer applies self-attention within windows that shift to expand receptive field.
- Dual attention vision transformers alternate spatial and channel attention to integrate information effectively.

title: multiscale transformers expand receptive field and reduce spatial resolution
one_liner: Several transformer models that process the image at multiple scales have been proposed.
content:
The Vision Transformer differs from convolutional architectures in that it operates on a single scale and has a receptive field that covers the whole image. Several transformer models that process the image at multiple scales have been proposed. The scale is reduced periodically by concatenating features from non-overlapping 2×2 patches and applying a linear transformation that maps these concatenated features to twice the original number of channels. A related idea is periodically to integrate information from across the whole image. Dual attention vision transformers (DaViT) alternate two types of transformers.
