recap_md:
- Multi-scale transformers start with small high-resolution patches and few channels.
- They gradually enlarge the receptive field and decrease spatial resolution while increasing channels.
- This approach improves image classification accuracy, e.g., SWin transformer achieves 9.89% top-1 error on ImageNet.

title: shifted window (SWin) transformer architecture
one_liner: The SWin transformer breaks the image into a grid of windows and each of these windows into a sub-grid of patches, applying self-attention within each window independently.
content: Figure 12.18 Shifted window (SWin) transformer (Liu et al., 2021c). a) Original image. b) The SWin transformer breaks the image into a grid of windows and each of these windows into a sub-grid of patches. The transformer network applies self-attention to the patches within each window independently (i.e., patches only attend to other patches in the same window). c) Each alternate layer shifts the windows so that the subsets of patches that interact with one another change, and information can propagate across the whole image. d) After several layers, the 2×2 blocks of patch representations are concatenated to increase the effective patch (and window) size. e) Alternate layers use shifted windows at this new lower resolution. f) Eventually, the resolution is such that there is just a single window, and the patches span the entire image.
motivation_md: The shifted window (SWin) transformer architecture enables efficient self-attention by restricting it to local windows that shift across layers, allowing information to propagate globally while keeping computation manageable.
recap_md:
- The SWin transformer divides the image into windows and sub-grids of patches.
- Self-attention is applied independently within each window.
- Windows are shifted in alternate layers to enable global information flow.

title: dual attention vision transformers (DaViT) alternating spatial and channel attention
one_liner: Dual attention vision transformers (DaViT) alternate two types of transformers: one attending over image patches and the other attending over channels.
content: Dual attention vision transformers (DaViT) alternate two types of transformers. In the first, image patches attend to one another, and the self-attention computation uses all the channels. In the second, the channels attend to one another, and the self-attention computation uses all the image patches. This architecture reaches a 9.60% top-1 error rate on ImageNet and is close to the state-of-the-art at the time of writing.
motivation_md: DaViT integrates spatial and channel attention alternately to improve feature representation and classification accuracy in vision transformers.
recap_md:
- DaViT alternates between spatial self-attention over image patches and channel self-attention.
- This dual attention mechanism enhances feature integration.
- Achieves 9.60% top-1 error rate on ImageNet, near state-of-the-art.

title: training transformers requires learning rate warm-up and Adam optimizer
one_liner: Training transformers is challenging and requires both learning rate warm-up and Adam optimizer.
content: Training transformers is challenging and requires both learning rate warm-up (Goyal et al., 2018) and Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015). Indeed Xiong et al. (2020a) and Huang et al. (2020a) show that the gradients vanish, and the Adam updates decrease in magnitude without learning rate warm-up. Several interacting factors cause this problem. Residual connections cause the exploding gradients (figure 11.6), but normalization layers prevent this. Vaswani et al. (2017) used LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm because NLP statistics are highly variable between batches, although subsequent work has modified BatchNorm for transformers (Shen et al., 2020a). The positioning of the LayerNorm outside of the residual block causes gradients to shrink as they pass back through the network (Xiong et al., 2020a). In addition, the relative weight of the residual connections and main self-attention mechanism varies as we move through the network upon initialization (see figure 11.6c). There is the additional complication that the gradients for the query and key parameters are smaller than for the value parameters (Liu et al., 2020), which necessitates the use of Adam. These factors interact in a complex way, making training unstable and necessitating learning rate warm-up.
motivation_md: Training transformers is unstable due to gradient vanishing and exploding issues; learning rate warm-up and Adam optimizer help stabilize training by addressing these gradient problems.
recap_md:
- Training transformers requires learning rate warm-up to prevent gradient vanishing.
- Adam optimizer is necessary due to smaller gradients for query and key parameters.
- Residual connections and LayerNorm placement affect gradient stability.

title: transformers combined with convolutional networks for vision tasks
one_liner: Transformers have been combined with convolutional neural networks for many vision tasks, often requiring large datasets for superior performance.
content: Transformers and convolutional networks: Transformers have been combined with convolutional neural networks for many tasks, including image classification (Wu et al., 2020a), object detection (Hu et al., 2018a; Carion et al., 2020), video processing (Wang et al., 2018c; Sun et al., 2019), unsupervised object discovery (Locatello et al., 2020) and various text/vision tasks (Chen et al., 2020d; Lu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019). Transformers can outperform convolutional networks for vision tasks but usually require large quantities of data to achieve superior performance. Often, they are pre-trained on enormous datasets like JRT (Sun et al., 2017) and LAION (Schuhmann et al., 2021). The transformer doesn’t have the inductive bias of convolutional networks, but by using huge amounts of data, it can surmount this disadvantage.
motivation_md: Combining transformers with convolutional networks leverages strengths of both architectures for vision tasks, but transformers need large data to overcome lack of convolutional inductive bias.
recap_md:
- Transformers combined with convolutional networks are used for diverse vision tasks.
- Transformers can outperform CNNs but require large datasets.
- Pre-training on massive datasets helps transformers overcome lack of convolutional inductive bias.

title: transformers adapted for video processing
one_liner: Transformers were subsequently adapted to video processing.
content: Transformers were subsequently adapted to video processing (Arnab et al., 2021; Bertasius et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021c; Neimark et al., 2021; Patrick et al., 2021). A survey of transformers applied to video can be found in Selva et al. (2022).
motivation_md: Adapting transformers for video processing enables modeling of temporal and spatial information in videos, expanding their application beyond images.
recap_md:
- Transformers have been adapted for video processing tasks.
- Multiple studies have explored transformer architectures for video.
- A comprehensive survey is available in Selva et al. (2022).

title: CLIP joint encoder for images and text captions
one_liner: CLIP learns a joint encoder for images and their captions using a contrastive pre-training task.
content: Combining images and text: CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) learns a joint encoder for images and their captions using a contrastive pre-training task. The system ingests N images and their captions and produces a matrix of compatibility between images and captions. The loss function encourages the correct pairs to have a high score and the incorrect pairs to have a low score. Ramesh et al. (2021) and Ramesh et al. (2022) train a diffusion decoder to invert the CLIP image encoder for text-conditional image generation (see chapter 18).
motivation_md: CLIP enables learning a shared representation space for images and text, facilitating tasks like image-caption matching and text-conditional image generation.
recap_md:
- CLIP jointly encodes images and their captions using contrastive learning.
- It produces compatibility scores between image-caption pairs.
- Diffusion decoders can invert CLIP encodings for text-conditional image generation.

title: Max pooling aggregation
one_liner: The max pooling aggregation operator computes the element-wise maximum of the vectors from neighbors of a node, providing a permutation-invariant operation.
content:
Max pooling aggregation is an alternative operation that is invariant to permutation and computes the maximum of a set of objects. The max pooling aggregation operator is defined as:

agg[n] = max_{m \in ne[n]} (h_m),

where the operator max[•] returns the element-wise maximum of the vectors h_m that are neighbors to the current node n.
motivation_md: Max pooling aggregation provides a permutation-invariant way to combine neighbor information by selecting the maximum values element-wise, which is useful for graph neural network layers.
recap_md:
- Max pooling aggregation computes the element-wise maximum of neighbor vectors.
- It is invariant to permutation of neighbors.
- Provides an alternative to averaging or summing neighbor embeddings.

title: Aggregation by attention
one_liner: In graph attention layers, weights depend on the data at the nodes and are computed via a learned similarity function and masked softmax over neighbors.
content:
Aggregation by attention differs from previous methods by weighting neighbor contributions based on the data at the nodes rather than equally or solely on graph topology. A linear transform is applied to the current node embeddings:

H'_k = \beta_k 1^T + \Omega_k H_k.

The similarity s_{mn} between transformed node embeddings h'_m and h'_n is computed by concatenating the pairs, taking a dot product with a learned parameter vector \phi_k, and applying an activation function:

s_{mn} = a(\phi_k^T [h'_m \| h'_n]).

These similarities form an N × N matrix S representing pairwise node similarities. Attention weights are normalized using a softmax, but only for the current node and its neighbors, by applying a masking function Softmask[S, A + I] that sets non-neighbor entries to negative infinity. The updated embeddings are then:

H_{k+1} = a(H'_k \cdot \text{Softmask}[S, A + I]),

where a[•] is an activation function. This mechanism resembles dot-product self-attention in transformers but differs in similarity measure and masking to restrict attention to neighbors. Multiple attention heads can be used in parallel and recombined.
motivation_md: Graph attention layers allow the model to learn data-dependent weights for neighbor contributions, improving expressiveness beyond fixed or topology-based weighting.
recap_md:
- Attention weights depend on node data via learned similarity.
- Similarities are masked to include only neighbors and self.
- The mechanism resembles transformer self-attention but is adapted for graphs.

title: Edge graphs
one_liner: Edge graphs transform edges of the original graph into nodes, connecting new nodes if their original edges share a node, enabling processing of edge embeddings.
content: Edge graphs, also known as adjoint or line graphs, transform the original graph by making each edge into a node. Two new nodes are connected if their corresponding edges in the original graph share a common node (figure 13.13). This complementary graph representation allows the same techniques used for node embeddings to be applied to edge embeddings by translating the graph to its edge graph. When both node and edge embeddings exist, translation back and forth between the two graphs is possible, enabling four types of updates: nodes updating nodes, nodes updating edges, edges updating nodes, and edges updating edges. These updates can be alternated or combined, and nodes can be updated simultaneously from both nodes and edges with minor modifications.
motivation_md: Edge graphs enable graph neural networks to process edge embeddings by converting edges into nodes, allowing flexible updates involving both nodes and edges.
recap_md:
- Edge graphs convert edges into nodes connected if original edges share a node.
- This allows applying node-based techniques to edge embeddings.
- Enables updates between nodes and edges in various combinations.

title: Summary
one_liner: Graph neural networks process graphs with node and edge embeddings, ensuring permutation equivariance and enabling updates via spatial-based convolutional layers and edge graph representations.
content: Graphs consist of nodes connected by edges, with data attached as node embeddings and edge embeddings. Many real-world problems can be framed as graphs, aiming to determine properties of the entire graph, individual nodes or edges, or detect additional edges. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are deep learning models applied to graphs. Because node order is arbitrary, GNN layers must be equivariant to permutations of node indices. Spatial-based convolutional networks aggregate information from neighbors to update node embeddings. Processing graphs is challenging because they often appear in a transductive setting with only one large partially labeled graph, requiring sampling and partitioning algorithms. The edge graph representation, where each edge becomes a node, allows GNNs to update edge embeddings.
motivation_md: Graph neural networks provide a principled way to learn from graph-structured data, handling permutation invariance and enabling updates to both node and edge embeddings.
recap_md:
- Graphs have nodes and edges with embeddings.
- GNN layers must be permutation equivariant.
- Edge graphs enable updates to edge embeddings.

title: Spectral methods
one_liner: Spectral methods apply convolution in the Fourier domain using the eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian but face challenges of non-local filters and high computational cost.
content: Spectral methods apply convolution operations in the Fourier domain of graphs. The Fourier basis vectors are obtained by eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian matrix L = D - A, where D is the degree matrix and A is the adjacency matrix. These methods have disadvantages: the filters are not localized, and the eigendecomposition is computationally expensive for large graphs. Henaff et al. (2015) addressed the localization issue by enforcing smoothness in the Fourier representation, which corresponds to spatial localization. Defferrard et al. (2016) introduced ChebNet, which efficiently approximates filters using the recursive properties of Chebyshev polynomials, providing spatially localized filters and reducing computation. Kipf & Welling (2017) further simplified this approach to filters using only a 1-hop neighborhood, bridging spectral and spatial methods.
motivation_md: Spectral methods enable graph convolution via Fourier analysis but require improvements to handle localization and scalability for large graphs.
recap_md:
- Spectral methods use graph Laplacian eigendecomposition for convolution.
- Filters are initially non-local and computationally expensive.
- ChebNet and Kipf & Welling methods improve localization and efficiency.

title: Spatial methods
one_liner: Spatial methods define graph convolutions directly in the spatial domain, addressing limitations of spectral methods when graphs change.
content: Spatial methods were developed to overcome limitations of spectral methods, which rely on the graph Laplacian and require retraining if the graph changes. Duvenaud et al. (2015) defined convolutions in the spatial domain by using different weight matrices to combine adjacent embeddings based on node degree. However, this approach becomes impractical for nodes with very large numbers of connections. Diffusion convolutional neural networks (Atwood & Towsley, 2016) use powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to blend features across different scales and sum these, then pointwise multiply by...
motivation_md: Spatial methods allow graph convolutions to adapt dynamically to changing graphs without retraining, improving flexibility over spectral methods.
recap_md:
- Spatial methods define convolutions directly on graph neighborhoods.
- They avoid retraining when the graph changes.
- Some methods use degree-based weighting or diffusion processes.

title: Aggregate and combine
one_liner: Graph convolutional networks aggregate neighbor embeddings with weighted averages or neural networks, then combine them with linear mappings and nonlinearities.
content: Graph convolutional networks (Kipf & Welling, 2017) aggregate information by taking a weighted average of neighbors and the current node, then applying a linear mapping followed by a ReLU activation. GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017a) applies a neural network layer to each neighbor and aggregates by taking the elementwise maximum. Chiang et al. (2019) propose diagonal enhancement, weighting the previous embedding more than neighbors. Kipf & Welling introduced Kipf normalization, which normalizes the sum of neighboring embeddings based on node degrees. The mixture model network (MoNet) (Monti et al., 2017) learns weightings based on degrees by associating a pseudo-coordinate system with each node and sampling a continuous function defined by a mixture of Gaussians at the neighbors' pseudo-coordinates. Pham et al. (2017) use a gating mechanism that linearly interpolates between the node embedding and neighbors with different weights per dimension, where the gating weights depend on the data.
motivation_md: Aggregating and combining neighbor information with learned weightings and nonlinearities enables flexible and expressive graph convolutional layers.
recap_md:
- Aggregation can be weighted averages, max pooling, or learned functions.
- Normalization based on node degrees improves stability.
- MoNet learns continuous weighting functions based on pseudo-coordinates.

title: Higher-order convolutional layers
one_liner: Higher-order convolutional layers aggregate information from neighbors at multiple walk lengths or motifs, capturing broader graph structure.
content: Higher-order convolutional layers extend neighborhood aggregation beyond immediate neighbors. Zhou & Li (2017) replace the adjacency matrix A with \tilde{A} = \min[A^L + I, 1], where L is the maximum walk-length, 1 is a matrix of ones, and \min[•] is the pointwise minimum, so updates sum contributions from nodes reachable by walks of length up to L. Abu-El-Haija et al. (2019) proposed MixHop, which computes node updates from neighbors (using A), neighbors of neighbors (A^2), and so on, concatenating these updates at each layer. Lee et al. (2018) incorporate information from nodes beyond immediate neighbors using geometric motifs, which are small local geometric patterns in the graph such as fully connected cliques of five nodes.
motivation_md: Higher-order convolutional layers capture broader graph context by aggregating information from multi-hop neighborhoods and motifs.
recap_md:
- Replace adjacency matrix with powers to include multi-hop neighbors.
- MixHop concatenates updates from multiple neighborhood ranges.
- Geometric motifs capture local graph patterns beyond edges.

title: Residual connections
one_liner: Residual connections add or concatenate previous embeddings to updated ones in various ways to improve graph neural network performance.
content: Residual connections: Kipf & Welling (2017) proposed a residual connection in which the original embeddings are added to the updated ones. Hamilton et al. (2017b) concatenate the previous embedding to the output of the next layer (see equation 13.16). Rossi et al. (2020) present an inception-style network where the node embedding is concatenated to not only the aggregation of its neighbors but also the aggregation of all neighbors within a walk of two (via computing powers of the adjacency matrix). Xu et al. (2018) introduced jump knowledge connections in which the final output at each node consists of the concatenated node embeddings throughout the network. Zhang & Meng (2019) present a general formulation of residual embeddings called GResNet and investigate several variations in which the embeddings from the previous layer are added, the input embeddings are added, or versions of these that aggregate information from their neighbors (without further transformation) are added.
motivation_md: Residual connections help improve graph neural networks by combining previous and updated embeddings, enabling better information flow and richer representations across layers. This addresses challenges in training deep networks and capturing multi-hop neighborhood information.
recap_md:
- Residual connections add or concatenate previous embeddings to updated ones.
- Variations include adding input embeddings, previous layer embeddings, or neighbor-aggregated embeddings.
- Jump knowledge connections concatenate embeddings from all layers for final output.

title: Attention in graph neural networks
one_liner: Graph attention networks use multiple attention heads combined symmetrically to capture graph structure, with variations including gated attention and positional embeddings.
content: Attention in graph neural networks: Veličković et al. (2019) developed the graph attention network (figure 13.12c). Their formulation uses multiple heads whose outputs are combined symmetrically. Gated Attention Networks (Zhang et al., 2018a) weight the output of the different heads in a way that depends on the data itself. Graph-BERT (Zhang et al., 2020) performs node classification using self-attention alone; the graph’s structure is captured by adding position embeddings to the data, similarly to how the absolute or relative position of words is captured in the transformer (chapter 12). For example, they add positional information that depends on the number of hops between nodes in the graph.
motivation_md: Attention mechanisms allow graph neural networks to weigh neighbor contributions adaptively, improving representation learning by focusing on important nodes and capturing graph structure effectively.
recap_md:
- Graph attention networks use multiple attention heads combined symmetrically.
- Gated Attention Networks weight heads based on data.
- Graph-BERT uses self-attention with positional embeddings encoding hop distances.

title: Permutation invariance
one_liner: Permutation invariance ensures functions on sets produce the same output regardless of input order, as in DeepSets and Janossy pooling.
content: Permutation invariance: In DeepSets, Zaheer et al. (2017) presented a general permutation invariant operator for processing sets. Janossy pooling (Murphy et al., 2018) accepts that many functions are not permutation equivariant and instead uses a permutation-sensitive function and averages the results across many permutations.
motivation_md: Permutation invariance is crucial for processing sets where the order of elements should not affect the output, ensuring consistent and meaningful representations.
recap_md:
- DeepSets introduced a general permutation invariant operator for sets.
- Janossy pooling averages permutation-sensitive function outputs over many permutations.
- Permutation invariance ensures output is independent of input order.

title: Permutation invariance
one_liner: Permutation invariance ensures functions on sets produce the same output regardless of input order, as in DeepSets and Janossy pooling.
content: Permutation invariance: In DeepSets, Zaheer et al. (2017) presented a general permutation invariant operator for processing sets. Janossy pooling (Murphy et al., 2018) accepts that many functions are not permutation equivariant and instead uses a permutation-sensitive function and averages the results across many permutations.
motivation_md: Permutation invariance is crucial for processing sets where the order of elements should not affect the output, ensuring consistent and meaningful representations.
recap_md:
- DeepSets introduced a general permutation invariant operator for sets.
- Janossy pooling averages permutation-sensitive function outputs over many permutations.
- Permutation invariance ensures output is independent of input order.

title: Edge graphs
one_liner: Edge graphs, also called line or adjoint graphs, involve updating node and edge embeddings through interleaved layers.
content: Edge graphs: The notation of the edge graph, line graph, or adjoint graph dates to Whitney (1932). The idea of “weaving” layers that update node embeddings from node embeddings, node embeddings from edge embeddings, edge embeddings from edge embeddings, and edge embeddings from node embeddings was proposed by Kearnes et al. (2016). However, here the node-node and edge-edge updates do not involve the neighbors. Monti et al. (2018) introduced the dual-primal graph CNN, a modern formulation in a CNN framework that alternates between updates in the original and edge graphs.
motivation_md: Edge graphs enable richer graph representations by updating embeddings of nodes and edges in an interleaved manner, capturing complex relational information.
recap_md:
- Edge graphs are also called line or adjoint graphs.
- "Weaving" layers update node and edge embeddings from each other.
- Dual-primal graph CNN alternates updates between original and edge graphs.

title: Edge graphs
one_liner: Edge graphs, also called line or adjoint graphs, involve updating node and edge embeddings through interleaved layers.
content: Edge graphs: The notation of the edge graph, line graph, or adjoint graph dates to Whitney (1932). The idea of “weaving” layers that update node embeddings from node embeddings, node embeddings from edge embeddings, edge embeddings from edge embeddings, and edge embeddings from node embeddings was proposed by Kearnes et al. (2016). However, here the node-node and edge-edge updates do not involve the neighbors. Monti et al. (2018) introduced the dual-primal graph CNN, a modern formulation in a CNN framework that alternates between updates in the original and edge graphs.
motivation_md: Edge graphs enable richer graph representations by updating embeddings of nodes and edges in an interleaved manner, capturing complex relational information.
recap_md:
- Edge graphs are also called line or adjoint graphs.
- "Weaving" layers update node and edge embeddings from each other.
- Dual-primal graph CNN alternates updates between original and edge graphs.

title: Power of graph neural networks
one_liner: Graph isomorphism networks match the discriminative power of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test to distinguish graph structures.
content:
Power of graph neural networks: Xu et al. (2019) argue that a neural network should be able to distinguish different graph structures; it is undesirable to map two graphs to the same output if they have the same initial node embeddings but different adjacency matrices. They identified graph structures that could not be distinguished by previous approaches such as GCNs (Kipf & Welling, 2017) and GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017a). They developed a more powerful architecture with the same discriminative power as the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test (Weisfeiler & Leman, 1968), which is known to discriminate a broad class of graphs. This resulting graph isomorphism network was based on the aggregation operation:
h(n)_{k+1} = mlp\left[ (1 + \epsilon_k) h(n)_k + \sum_{m \in ne[n]} h(m)_k \right]. (13.26)
motivation_md: Graph neural networks need sufficient power to distinguish different graph structures; the graph isomorphism network achieves this by matching the Weisfeiler-Lehman test's discriminative ability.
recap_md:
- Previous GNNs like GCNs and GraphSAGE cannot distinguish some graph structures.
- Graph isomorphism networks match the Weisfeiler-Lehman test's discriminative power.
- Aggregation operation includes node's own embedding plus neighbors' embeddings.

title: Power of graph neural networks
one_liner: Graph isomorphism networks match the discriminative power of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test to distinguish graph structures.
content:

(2019) argue that a neural network should be able to distinguish different graph structures; it is undesirable to map two graphs to the same output if they have the same initial node embeddings but different adjacency matrices. They identified graph structures that could not be distinguished by previous approaches such as GCNs (Kipf & Welling, 2017) and GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017a).
