one_liner: GAN training alternates updating the discriminator and generator so generated samples become indistinguishable from real examples.
content:
Figure 15.1 illustrates this scheme. We start with a training set {x_i} of real 1D examples. A different batch of ten of these examples {x_i}_{i=1}^{10} is shown in each panel (cyan arrows). To create a batch of samples {x^*_j}, we use the simple generator: x^*_j = g[z_j, θ] = z_j + θ, where latent variables {z_j} are drawn from a standard normal distribution, and the parameter θ translates the generated samples along the x-axis (figure 15.1).

At initialization, θ = 3.0, and the generated samples (orange arrows) lie to the left of the real examples (cyan arrows). The discriminator is trained to distinguish the generated samples from the real examples (the sigmoid curve indicates the probability that a data point is real). During training, the generator parameters θ are manipulated to increase the probability that its samples are classified as real. Here, this means increasing θ so that the samples move rightwards where the sigmoid curve is higher.

We alternate between updating the discriminator and the generator. Figures 15.1b–c show two iterations of this process. It gradually becomes harder to classify the data, so the impetus to change θ becomes weaker (i.e., the sigmoid becomes flatter). At the end of the process, there is no way to distinguish the two sets of data; the discriminator, which now has chance performance, is discarded, and we are left with a generator that makes plausible samples.
motivation_md: Alternating updates to the discriminator and generator enable the generator to produce samples indistinguishable from real data, solving the problem of generating realistic data.
recap_md:
- GAN training alternates updating discriminator and generator parameters.
- The generator shifts samples to increase their likelihood of being classified as real.
- Training ends when the discriminator can no longer distinguish real from generated samples.

title: GAN loss function
one_liner: The GAN loss function uses binary cross-entropy to train the discriminator to distinguish real from generated samples and the generator to fool the discriminator.
content:
GAN loss function
We now define the loss function for training GANs more precisely. The discriminator f[x, ϕ] takes input x, has parameters ϕ, and returns a scalar that is higher when it believes the input is a real example. This is a binary classification task, so we adapt the binary cross-entropy loss function (section 5.4), which originally had the form:

ˆϕ = argmin_ϕ \sum_i \big[-(1 - y_i) \log(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x_i, ϕ]]) - y_i \log(\mathrm{sig}[f[x_i, ϕ]])\big],

where y_i ∈ {0, 1} is the label, and sig[•] is the logistic sigmoid function (figure 5.7). In this case, we assume that the real examples x have label y = 1 and the generated samples x^* have label y = 0 so that:

ˆϕ = argmin_ϕ \left[ \sum_j -\log(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x^*_j, ϕ]]) - \sum_i \log(\mathrm{sig}[f[x_i, ϕ]]) \right],

where i and j index the real examples and generated samples, respectively.

Now we substitute the definition for the generator x^*_j = g[z_j, θ] and note that we must maximize with respect to θ since we want the generated samples to be misclassified (i.e., have low likelihood of being synthetic or high negative log-likelihood):

ˆθ = argmax_θ \left[ \min_ϕ \left[ \sum_j -\log(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[g[z_j, θ], ϕ]]) - \sum_i \log(\mathrm{sig}[f[x_i, ϕ]]) \right] \right].
motivation_md: The loss function formalizes training so the discriminator learns to classify real vs. generated samples, while the generator learns to fool the discriminator by maximizing misclassification.
recap_md:
- The discriminator uses binary cross-entropy loss to classify real (y=1) and generated (y=0) samples.
- The generator maximizes the loss to produce samples that fool the discriminator.
- Training involves a min-max optimization over discriminator parameters ϕ and generator parameters θ.

title: GAN training characterized as a minimax game and Nash equilibrium
one_liner: GAN training is a minimax game where the generator tries to fool the discriminator, and the solution is a Nash equilibrium.
content:
Training GANs
Equation 15.4 is a more complex loss function than we have seen before; the discriminator parameters ϕ are manipulated to minimize the loss function, and the generative parameters θ are manipulated to maximize the loss function. GAN training is characterized as a minimax game; the generator tries to find new ways to fool the discriminator, which in turn searches for new ways to distinguish generated samples from real examples. Technically, the solution is a Nash equilibrium — the optimization algorithm searches for a position that is simultaneously a minimum of one function and a maximum of the other. If training proceeds as planned, then upon convergence, g[z, θ] will be drawn from the same distribution as the data, and sig[f[•, ϕ]] will be at chance (i.e., 0.5).
motivation_md: Viewing GAN training as a minimax game clarifies the adversarial nature of the process and the goal of reaching a Nash equilibrium where generated samples match the real data distribution.
recap_md:
- GAN training involves minimizing the discriminator loss and maximizing the generator loss.
- The process is a minimax game between generator and discriminator.
- The solution corresponds to a Nash equilibrium where generated and real distributions match.

title: deep convolutional GAN or DCGAN
one_liner: The deep convolutional GAN (DCGAN) is an architecture specialized for generating images using convolutional layers and a 100D latent input.
content:
The deep convolutional GAN or DCGAN was an early GAN architecture specialized for generating images (figure 15.3). The input to the generator g[z, θ] is a 100D latent variable z sampled from a uniform distribution. This is then mapped to a 4×4 spatial representation with 1024 channels using a linear transformation.

Four convolutional layers follow, each of which uses a fractionally-strided convolution that doubles the resolution (i.e., a convolution with a stride of 0.5). At the final layer, the 64×64×3 signal is passed through a tanh function to generate an image x^* in the range [−1, 1]. The discriminator f[•, ϕ] is a standard convolutional network where the final convolutional layer reduces the size to 1×1 with one channel. This single number is passed through a sigmoid function sig[•] to create the output probability.

After training, the discriminator is discarded. To create new samples, latent variables z are drawn from the base distribution and passed through the generator. Example results are shown in figure 15.4.
motivation_md: DCGAN architecture uses convolutional layers to effectively generate images from latent variables, enabling high-quality image synthesis.
recap_md:
- DCGAN uses a 100D latent variable mapped to a 4×4×1024 representation.
- Fractionally-strided convolutions upsample to 64×64×3 images passed through tanh.
- The discriminator is a convolutional net producing a real/fake probability via sigmoid.

title: Difficulties in training GANs and techniques for DCGAN training
one_liner: GANs are notoriously difficult to train, requiring specific architectural and optimization techniques for reliable DCGAN training.
content: Theoretically, the GAN is fairly straightforward. However, GANs are notoriously difficult to train. For example, to get the DCGAN to train reliably, it was necessary to (i) use strided convolutions for upsampling and downsampling; (ii) use BatchNorm in both generator and discriminator except in the last and first layers, respectively; (iii) use the leaky ReLU activation function (figure 3.13) in the discriminator; and (iv) use the Adam optimizer but with a lower momentum coefficient than usual. This is unusual. Most deep learning models are relatively robust to such choices.
motivation_md: Training GANs is challenging due to instability; specific architectural and optimization choices help stabilize DCGAN training.
recap_md:
- GANs are difficult to train reliably.
- DCGAN training requires strided convolutions, BatchNorm, leaky ReLU, and tuned Adam optimizer.
- These choices improve training stability, unlike most deep learning models.

title: Mode collapse and mode dropping in GANs
one_liner: Mode collapse occurs when the generator produces limited or identical samples, ignoring the latent variables.
content: A common failure mode is that the generator makes plausible samples, but these only represent a subset of the data (e.g., for faces, it might never generate faces with beards). This is known as mode dropping. An extreme version of this phenomenon can occur where the generator entirely or mostly ignores the latent variables z and collapses all samples to one or a few points; this is known as mode collapse (figure 15.5).
motivation_md: Mode collapse limits GAN diversity by causing the generator to produce only a few types of samples, reducing the model's usefulness.
recap_md:
- Mode dropping is when the generator produces samples from only a subset of the data.
- Mode collapse is an extreme case where the generator ignores latent variables and outputs few points.
- Both phenomena reduce the diversity of generated samples.

title: Analysis of GAN loss function as Jensen-Shannon divergence
one_liner: The GAN loss function corresponds to minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the generated and real data distributions.
content:
Analysis of GAN loss function
If we divide the two sums in the first line of equation 15.5 by the numbers I, J of real and generated samples, then the loss function can be written in terms of expectations:

L[ϕ] = -\frac{1}{J} \sum_{j=1}^J \log(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x^*_j, ϕ]]) - \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I \log(\mathrm{sig}[f[x_i, ϕ]])

\approx -\mathbb{E}_{x^*}[\log(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x^*, ϕ]])] - \mathbb{E}_x[\log(\mathrm{sig}[f[x, ϕ]])]

= - \int Pr(x^*) \log(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x^*, ϕ]]) dx^* - \int Pr(x) \log(\mathrm{sig}[f[x, ϕ]]) dx,

where Pr(x^*) is the probability distribution over the generated samples, and Pr(x) is the true probability distribution over the real examples.

When I = J, the optimal discriminator for an example \tilde{x} of unknown origin is:

Pr(real|\tilde{x}) = \mathrm{sig}[f[\tilde{x}, ϕ]] = \frac{Pr(\tilde{x}|real)}{Pr(\tilde{x}|generated) + Pr(\tilde{x}|real)} = \frac{Pr(x)}{Pr(x^*) + Pr(x)},

where on the right hand side, we evaluate \tilde{x} against the generated distribution Pr(x^*) and the real distribution Pr(x). Substituting into equation 15.6, we get:

L[ϕ] = - \int Pr(x^*) \log \left(1 - \mathrm{sig}[f[x^*, ϕ]]\right) dx^* - \int Pr(x) \log \left(\mathrm{sig}[f[x, ϕ]]\right) dx

= - \int Pr(x^*) \log \left( \frac{Pr(x^*)}{Pr(x^*) + Pr(x)} \right) dx^* - \int Pr(x) \log \left( \frac{Pr(x)}{Pr(x^*) + Pr(x)} \right) dx.

Disregarding additive and multiplicative constants, this is the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the synthesized distribution Pr(x^*) and the true distribution Pr(x):

D_{JS}[Pr(x^*) || Pr(x)] = \frac{1}{2} D_{KL}\left(Pr(x^*) \| \frac{Pr(x^*) + Pr(x)}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{2} D_{KL}\left(Pr(x) \| \frac{Pr(x^*) + Pr(x)}{2}\right),

where D_{KL}[•||•] is the Kullback-Leibler divergence.
motivation_md: Analyzing the GAN loss reveals it minimizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence between generated and real data distributions, explaining the adversarial training objective.
recap_md:
- The GAN loss can be expressed as expectations over real and generated samples.
- The optimal discriminator estimates the probability an input is real based on data distributions.
- Minimizing the GAN loss corresponds to minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between distributions.

title: What makes a good generative model?

position.section_title: What makes a good generative model?

one_liner: Generative models based on latent variables should have properties like efficient sampling, high-quality sampling, coverage, well-behaved and disentangled latent spaces, and efficient likelihood computation.
content:
Generative models based on latent variables should have the following properties:
• Efficient sampling: Generating samples from the model should be computationally inexpensive and take advantage of the parallelism of modern hardware.
• High-quality sampling: The samples should be indistinguishable from the real data with which the model was trained.
• Coverage: Samples should represent the entire training distribution. It is insufficient to generate samples that all look like a subset of the training examples.
• Well-behaved latent space: Every latent variable z corresponds to a plausible data example x. Smooth changes in z correspond to smooth changes in x.
• Disentangled latent space: Manipulating each dimension of z should correspond to changing an interpretable property of the data. For example, in a model of language, it might change the topic, tense, or verbosity.
• Efficient likelihood computation: If the model is probabilistic, we would like to be able to calculate the probability of new examples efficiently and accurately.
This naturally leads to the question of whether the generative models that we consider satisfy these properties. The answer is subjective, but figure 14.3 provides guidance. The precise assignments are disputable, but most practitioners would agree that there is no single model that satisfies all of these characteristics.
motivation_md: Generative models need to efficiently produce high-quality, diverse samples that cover the entire data distribution, with interpretable latent variables and the ability to compute likelihoods, to be useful and reliable in practice.
recap_md:
- Generative models should enable efficient and high-quality sampling.
- Samples must cover the entire training data distribution.
- Latent spaces should be well-behaved and disentangled for interpretability.

title: Quantifying performance
one_liner: Quantitative measures of success for generative models include test likelihood, inception score, Fréchet inception distance, and manifold precision/recall.
content:
The previous section discussed the desirable properties of generative models. We now consider quantitative measures of success for generative models. Much experimentation with generative models has used images due to the widespread availability of that data and the ease of qualitatively judging the samples. Consequently, some of these metrics only apply to images.

Test likelihood:
One way to compare probabilistic models is to measure their likelihood for a test dataset. It is ineffective to measure the training data likelihood because a model could assign a very high probability to each training point and very low probabilities in between. This model would have a very high training likelihood but could only reproduce the training data. The test likelihood captures how well the model generalizes from the training data and also the coverage; if the model assigns a high probability to just a subset of the training data, it must assign lower probabilities elsewhere, so a portion of the test examples will have low probability.

Test likelihood is a sensible way to quantify probabilistic models, but unfortunately, it is not relevant for generative adversarial models (which do not assign a probability) and is expensive to estimate for variational autoencoders and diffusion models (although it is possible to compute a lower bound on the log-likelihood). Normalizing flows are the only type of model for which the likelihood can be computed exactly and efficiently.

Inception score:
The inception score (IS) is specialized for images and ideally for generative models trained on the ImageNet database. The score is calculated using a pretrained classification model – usually the “Inception” model, from which the name is derived. It is based on two criteria. First, each generated image x* should look like one and only one of the 1000 possible classes y in the ImageNet database. Hence, the probability distribution Pr(y|x*_i) should be highly peaked at the correct class. Second, the entire set of generated images should be assigned to the classes with equal probability, so Pr(y) should be flat when averaged over all generated examples.

The inception score measures the average distance between these two distributions over the generated set. This distance will be large if one is peaked and the other flat (figure 14.4). More precisely, it returns the exponential of the expected KL-divergence between Pr(y|x*_i) and Pr(y):

\[
IS = \exp \left[ \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I D_{KL} \bigl( Pr(y|x*_i) \| Pr(y) \bigr) \right],
\]

where I is the number of generated examples and:

\[
Pr(y) = \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I Pr(y|x*_i).
\]

This metric is only sensible for generative models of the ImageNet database and is sensitive to the particular classification model; retraining this model can give quite different numerical results. Moreover, it does not reward diversity within an object class; it returns a high value if the model only generates one realistic example of each class.

Fréchet inception distance:
This measure is also intended for images and computes a symmetric distance between the distributions of generated samples and real examples. This must be approximate since it is hard to characterize either distribution (indeed, characterizing the distribution of real examples is the job of generative models in the first place). Hence, the Fréchet inception distance approximates both distributions by multivariate Gaussians and (as the name suggests) estimates the distance between them using the Fréchet distance.

However, it does not model the distance with respect to the original data but rather the activations in the deepest layer of the inception classification network. These hidden units are the ones most associated with object classes, so the comparison occurs at a semantic level, ignoring the more fine-grained details of the images. This metric does take account of diversity within classes but relies heavily on the information retained by the features in the inception network; any information discarded by the network does not contribute to the result. Some of this discarded information may still be important to generate realistic samples.

Manifold precision/recall:
Fréchet inception distance is sensitive both to the realism of the samples and their diversity but does not distinguish between these factors. To disentangle these qualities, we consider the overlap between the data manifold (i.e., the subset of the data space where the real examples lie) and the model manifold (i.e., where the generated samples lie). The precision is the fraction of model samples that fall into the data manifold. This measures the proportion of generated samples that are realistic. The recall is the fraction of data examples that fall within the model manifold. This measures the proportion of the real data the model can generate (figure 14.5).

To estimate the manifold, we place a hypersphere around each data example, whose radius is the distance to the kth nearest neighbor. The union of these spheres is an approximation of the manifold, and it’s easy to determine if a new point lies within it. This manifold is also typically computed in the feature space of a classifier with the advantages and disadvantages that entails.
motivation_md: Quantitative metrics are needed to objectively evaluate how well generative models produce realistic, diverse samples and generalize beyond training data, especially for image data where qualitative judgment is easier.
recap_md:
- Test likelihood measures how well probabilistic models generalize to new data.
- Inception score evaluates image quality and class diversity using a pretrained classifier.
- Fréchet inception distance and manifold precision/recall assess similarity and diversity between generated and real data distributions.

title: Inception score
one_liner: The inception score uses a pretrained classifier to measure if generated images are realistic and diverse across classes.
content:
The inception score (IS) is specialized for images and ideally for generative models trained on the ImageNet database. The score is calculated using a pretrained classification model – usually the “Inception” model, from which the name is derived. It is based on two criteria. First, each generated image x* should look like one and only one of the 1000 possible classes y in the ImageNet database. Hence, the probability distribution Pr(y|x*_i) should be highly peaked at the correct class. Second, the entire set of generated images should be assigned to the classes with equal probability, so Pr(y) should be flat when averaged over all generated examples.

The inception score measures the average distance between these two distributions over the generated set. This distance will be large if one is peaked and the other flat (figure 14.4). More precisely, it returns the exponential of the expected KL-divergence between Pr(y|x*_i) and Pr(y):

\[
IS = \exp \left[ \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I D_{KL} \bigl( Pr(y|x*_i) \| Pr(y) \bigr) \right],
\]

where I is the number of generated examples and:

\[
Pr(y) = \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I Pr(y|x*_i).
\]

This metric is only sensible for generative models of the ImageNet database and is sensitive to the particular classification model; retraining this model can give quite different numerical results. Moreover, it does not reward diversity within an object class; it returns a high value if the model only generates one realistic example of each class.
motivation_md: The inception score quantifies how realistic and class-diverse generated images are, using a pretrained classifier to evaluate sample quality and distribution coverage.
recap_md:
- Inception score uses a pretrained classifier (Inception model) for evaluation.
- It measures if generated images are confidently classified into one class.
- It rewards diversity by expecting uniform class distribution across samples.

title: Fréchet inception distance
one_liner: Fréchet inception distance measures the distance between generated and real image distributions using activations from a pretrained classifier.
content:
Fréchet inception distance:
This measure is also intended for images and computes a symmetric distance between the distributions of generated samples and real examples. This must be approximate since it is hard to characterize either distribution (indeed, characterizing the distribution of real examples is the job of generative models in the first place). Hence, the Fréchet inception distance approximates both distributions by multivariate Gaussians and (as the name suggests) estimates the distance between them using the Fréchet distance.

However, it does not model the distance with respect to the original data but rather the activations in the deepest layer of the inception classification network. These hidden units are the ones most associated with object classes, so the comparison occurs at a semantic level, ignoring the more fine-grained details of the images. This metric does take account of diversity within classes but relies heavily on the information retained by the features in the inception network; any information discarded by the network does not contribute to the result. Some of this discarded information may still be important to generate realistic samples.
motivation_md: Fréchet inception distance provides a semantic-level measure of similarity between generated and real images, capturing both sample quality and diversity.
recap_md:
- Approximates distributions of generated and real images as multivariate Gaussians.
- Measures distance using the Fréchet distance on classifier activations.
- Focuses on semantic features, ignoring fine-grained image details.

title: Manifold precision/recall
one_liner: Manifold precision and recall measure how well generated samples overlap with real data distribution in terms of realism and diversity.
content:
Fréchet inception distance is sensitive both to the realism of the samples and their diversity but does not distinguish between these factors. To disentangle these qualities, we consider the overlap between the data manifold (i.e., the subset of the data space where the real examples lie) and the model manifold (i.e., where the generated samples lie). The precision is the fraction of model samples that fall into the data manifold. This measures the proportion of generated samples that are realistic. The recall is the fraction of data examples that fall within the model manifold. This measures the proportion of the real data the model can generate (figure 14.5).

To estimate the manifold, we place a hypersphere around each data example, whose radius is the distance to the kth nearest neighbor. The union of these spheres is an approximation of the manifold, and it’s easy to determine if a new point lies within it. This manifold is also typically computed in the feature space of a classifier with the advantages and disadvantages that entails.
motivation_md: Manifold precision and recall help separately evaluate how realistic generated samples are and how well they cover the real data distribution, clarifying model strengths and weaknesses.
recap_md:
- Precision measures the fraction of generated samples that lie within the real data manifold.
- Recall measures the fraction of real data covered by the generated samples manifold.
- Manifolds are approximated by unions of hyperspheres around data points.

title: Generative adversarial network or GAN
one_liner: A generative adversarial network (GAN) generates new samples indistinguishable from training data but does not model data probability distributions.
content:
A generative adversarial network or GAN is an unsupervised model that aims to generate new samples that are indistinguishable from a set of training examples. GANs are just mechanisms to create new samples; they do not build a probability distribution over the modeled data and hence cannot evaluate the probability that a new data point belongs to the same distribution.

In a GAN, the main generator network creates samples by mapping random noise to the output data space. If a second discriminator network cannot distinguish between the generated samples and the real examples, the samples must be plausible. If this network can tell the difference, this provides a training signal that can be fed back to improve the quality of the samples. This idea is simple, but training GANs is difficult: the learning algorithm can be unstable, and although GANs may learn to generate realistic samples, this does not imply that they learn to generate all possible samples.

GANs have been applied to many types of data, including audio, 3D models, text, video, and graphs. However, they have found the most success in the image domain, where they can produce samples that are almost indistinguishable from real pictures.
motivation_md: GANs provide a framework to generate realistic new samples by training a generator and discriminator in opposition, enabling sample creation without explicit probability modeling.
recap_md:
- GANs generate samples indistinguishable from training data without modeling probabilities.
- A generator creates samples from noise; a discriminator tries to distinguish real from fake.
- Training alternates between improving generator and discriminator for realistic samples.

title: Discrimination as a signal
one_liner: A discriminator network provides a training signal by distinguishing real from generated samples, guiding the generator to produce realistic data.
content:
We aim to generate new samples {x*_j} that are drawn from the same distribution as a set of real training data {x_i}. A single new sample x*_j is generated by (i) choosing a latent variable z_j from a simple base distribution (e.g., a standard normal) and then (ii) passing this data through a network x*_j = g[z_j, \theta] with parameters \theta. This network is known as the generator. During the learning process, the goal is to find parameters \theta so that the samples {x*_j} look “similar” to the real data {x_i} (see figure 14.2a).

Similarity can be defined in many ways, but the GAN uses the principle that the samples should be statistically indistinguishable from the true data.

To this end, a second network f[•, \phi] with parameters \phi called the discriminator is introduced. This network aims to classify its input as being a real example or a generated sample. If this proves impossible, the generated samples are indistinguishable from the real examples, and we have succeeded. If it is possible, the discriminator provides a signal that can be used to improve the generation process.

Figure 15.1 illustrates this scheme.

We start with a training set {x_i} of real 1D examples. A different batch of ten of these examples {x_i}_{i=1}^{10} is shown in each panel (cyan arrows). To create a batch of samples {x*_j}, we use the simple generator:

\[
x*_j = g[z_j, \theta] = z_j + \theta,
\]

where latent variables {z_j} are drawn from a standard normal distribution, and the parameter \theta translates the generated samples along the x-axis (figure 15.1).

At initialization, \theta = 3.0, and the generated samples (orange arrows) lie to the left of the real examples (cyan arrows). The discriminator is trained to distinguish the generated samples from the real examples (the sigmoid curve indicates the probability that a data point is real). During training, the generator parameters \theta are manipulated to increase the probability that its samples are classified as real. Here, this means increasing \theta so that the samples move rightwards where the sigmoid curve is higher.

We alternate between updating the discriminator and the generator. Figures 15.1b–c show two iterations of this process. It gradually becomes harder to classify the data, so the impetus to change \theta becomes weaker (i.e., the sigmoid becomes flatter). At the end of the process, there is no way to distinguish the two sets of data; the discriminator, which now has chance performance, is discarded, and we are left with a generator that makes plausible samples.
motivation_md: Using a discriminator to distinguish real from generated samples provides a feedback signal that guides the generator to produce more realistic data.
recap_md:
- The generator maps latent variables to samples aiming to mimic real data.
- The discriminator classifies inputs as real or generated, providing a training signal.
- Alternating updates lead to generated samples indistinguishable from real data.

title: generator
one_liner: A generator is a network that maps latent variables to data samples, aiming to produce outputs similar to real data.
content: A latent variable z_j is drawn from a simple base distribution (e.g., a standard normal) and then passed through a network x*_j = g[z_j, \theta] with parameters \theta. This network is known as the generator. During the learning process, the goal is to find parameters \theta so that the samples {x*_j} look “similar” to the real data {x_i} (see figure 14.2a).
motivation_md: The generator transforms latent variables into data samples, enabling the creation of new examples resembling the training data.
recap_md:
- The generator maps latent variables z_j to data samples x*_j.
- It is parameterized by \theta, which is learned during training.
- The goal is to produce samples similar to the real data.

title: auxiliary classifier GAN or ACGAN
one_liner: The auxiliary classifier GAN (ACGAN) simplifies conditional generation by requiring the discriminator to correctly predict the attribute.
content: The auxiliary classifier GAN or ACGAN simplifies conditional generation by requiring that the discriminator correctly predicts the attribute (figure 15.13b). For a discrete attribute with C categories, the discriminator takes the real or synthesized image as input and has C + 1 outputs. The first output is passed through a sigmoid function to predict if the sample is generated or real. The remaining outputs are passed through a softmax function to predict the probability that the data belongs to each of the C classes. Networks trained with this method can synthesize multiple classes from ImageNet (figure 15.14). The generator of the auxiliary classifier GAN (ACGAN) takes a discrete attribute variable. The discriminator must both (i) determine if its input is real or synthetic and (ii) identify the class correctly.
motivation_md: ACGAN enables conditional image generation by training the discriminator to predict both authenticity and class attributes, improving control over generated samples.
recap_md:
- ACGAN requires the discriminator to predict both real/fake and class labels.
- The discriminator outputs C + 1 values: one for real/fake, others for class probabilities.
- Enables synthesis of multiple classes from datasets like ImageNet.

title: InfoGAN
one_liner: InfoGAN attempts to identify important attributes automatically by splitting the latent vector into noise and attribute variables.
content: InfoGAN differs from conditional GAN and ACGAN by attempting to identify important attributes automatically. The generator takes a vector consisting of random noise variables z and random attribute variables c. The discriminator both predicts whether the image is real or synthesized and estimates the attribute variables. The insight is that interpretable real-world characteristics should be easiest to predict and hence will be represented in the attribute variables c. The attributes in c may be discrete (using a binary or multiclass cross-entropy loss) or continuous (using a least squares loss). The discrete variables identify categories in the data, and the continuous ones identify gradual modes of variation (figure 15.15).
motivation_md: InfoGAN aims to discover meaningful, interpretable attributes automatically without manual labeling, enabling disentangled latent representations.
recap_md:
- InfoGAN splits latent variables into noise z and attributes c.
- Discriminator predicts real/fake and estimates attribute variables.
- Attributes c can be discrete or continuous, capturing categories and gradual variations.

title: image translation
one_liner: Adversarial discriminators can be used as priors favoring realism in tasks that translate one image to another, such as colorization or denoising.
content: Although the adversarial discriminator was first used in the context of GANs for generating random samples, it can also be used as a prior that favors realism in tasks that translate one data example into another. This is most commonly done with images, where we might want to translate a grayscale image to color, a noisy image to a clean one, a blurry image to a sharp one, or a sketch to a photo-realistic image. This section discusses three image translation models that use different amounts of manual labeling. The Pix2Pix model uses before/after pairs for training. Models with adversarial losses use before/after pairs for the main model but also exploit unpaired “after” images in the discriminator. The CycleGAN model uses unpaired images.
motivation_md: Image translation models use adversarial discriminators to produce realistic transformations between image styles or conditions, improving output quality.
recap_md:
- Adversarial discriminators help produce realistic image translations.
- Tasks include grayscale to color, denoising, sharpening, or sketch to photo.
- Models vary in supervision: Pix2Pix uses paired data; CycleGAN uses unpaired data.

title: Pix2Pix model
one_liner: The Pix2Pix model maps one image to another style using a U-Net and combines content loss with adversarial loss for realistic outputs.
content: The Pix2Pix model (figure 15.16) is a network \( \hat{x} = g[c, \theta] \) that maps one image \( c \) to a different style image \( x \) using a U-Net (figure 11.10) with parameters \( \theta \). A typical use case would be colorization, where the input \( c \) is grayscale, and the output \( g[c, \theta] \) is color. The output should be similar to the input, and this is encouraged using a content loss that penalizes the \( \ell_1 \) norm \( ||x - g[c, \theta]||_1 \) between the input \( c \) and ground truth output \( x \). However, the output image should also look like a realistic conversion of the input. This is encouraged by using an adversarial discriminator \( f[c, x, \phi] \), which ingests the before and after images \( c \) and \( x \). At each step, the discriminator tries to distinguish between a real before/after pair and a before/synthesized pair.
motivation_md: Pix2Pix addresses image-to-image translation by combining pixel-level similarity with adversarial training to produce realistic and accurate style conversions.
recap_md:
- Pix2Pix uses a U-Net to map input image \( c \) to output image \( x \).
- Content loss penalizes \( \ell_1 \) difference between output and ground truth.
- Adversarial discriminator encourages realistic before/after image pairs.

title: PatchGAN loss
one_liner: The PatchGAN loss uses a convolutional classifier where each hidden unit indicates if its receptive field region is real or synthesized.
content: The PatchGAN loss is based on a purely convolutional classifier. At the last layer, each hidden unit indicates whether the region within its receptive field is real or synthesized. These responses are averaged to provide the final output.
motivation_md: PatchGAN loss enables local-level realism assessment by classifying image patches, improving detail quality in generated images.
recap_md:
- PatchGAN loss uses a convolutional classifier.
- Each hidden unit judges if its receptive field region is real or fake.
- Outputs are averaged to produce the final realism score.

title: Adversarial loss
one_liner: Adversarial loss penalizes a model if a discriminator can distinguish its output from real examples, improving realism in supervised learning.
content: The discriminator of the Pix2Pix model attempted to distinguish whether before/after pairs in an image translation task were plausible. This has the disadvantage that we need ground truth before/after pairs to exploit the discriminator loss. Fortunately, there is a simpler way to exploit the power of adversarial discriminators in the context of supervised learning without the need for additional labeled training data. An adversarial loss adds a penalty if a discriminator can distinguish the output of a supervised network from a real example from its output domain. Accordingly, the supervised model changes its predictions to decrease this penalty. This may be done at the scale of the entire output or at the level of patches, as in the Pix2Pix algorithm. This helps improve the realism of complex structured outputs. However, it doesn’t necessarily lead to a better solution in terms of the original loss function. The super-resolution GAN or SRGAN uses this approach (figure 15.17). The main model consists of a convolutional network with residual connections that ingests a low-resolution image and converts this via upsampling layers to a high-resolution image. The network is trained with three losses. The content loss measures the squared difference between the output and the true high-resolution image. The VGG loss or perceptual loss passes the synthesized and ground truth outputs through the VGG network and measures the squared difference between their activations. This encourages the image to be semantically similar to the target. Finally, the adversarial loss uses a discriminator that attempts to distinguish whether this is a real high-resolution image or an upsampled one. This encourages the output to be indistinguishable from real examples.
motivation_md: Adversarial loss improves output realism by penalizing distinguishable outputs, enabling better quality in supervised tasks without extra labeled data.
recap_md:
- Adversarial loss penalizes outputs distinguishable from real examples.
- Can be applied at whole output or patch level.
- SRGAN uses adversarial loss with content and perceptual losses for super-resolution.

title: adversarial loss for supervised learning
one_liner: An adversarial loss adds a penalty if a discriminator can distinguish supervised network outputs from real examples, improving realism without extra labeled data.
content: The discriminator of the Pix2Pix model attempted to distinguish whether before/after pairs in an image translation task were plausible. This has the disadvantage that we need ground truth before/after pairs to exploit the discriminator loss. Fortunately, there is a simpler way to exploit the power of adversarial discriminators in the context of supervised learning without the need for additional labeled training data. An adversarial loss adds a penalty if a discriminator can distinguish the output of a supervised network from a real example from its output domain. Accordingly, the supervised model changes its predictions to decrease this penalty. This may be done at the scale of the entire output or at the level of patches, as in the Pix2Pix algorithm. This helps improve the realism of complex structured outputs. However, it doesn’t necessarily lead to a better solution in terms of the original loss function. The super-resolution GAN or SRGAN uses this approach (figure 15.17). The main model consists of a convolutional network with residual connections that ingests a low-resolution image and converts this via upsampling layers to a high-resolution image. The network is trained with three losses. The content loss measures the squared difference between the output and the true high-resolution image. The VGG loss or perceptual loss passes the synthesized and ground truth outputs through the VGG network and measures the squared difference between their activations. This encourages the image to be semantically similar to the target. Finally, the adversarial loss uses a discriminator that attempts to distinguish whether this is a real high-resolution image or an upsampled one. This encourages the output to be indistinguishable from real examples.
motivation_md: Adversarial loss for supervised learning enhances output realism without requiring additional labeled data, enabling better structured predictions.
recap_md:
- Adversarial loss penalizes outputs distinguishable from real data.
- Can be applied at full output or patch level.
- SRGAN combines content, perceptual, and adversarial losses for super-resolution.

title: CycleGAN
one_liner: CycleGAN trains two models to translate images between domains without paired data by enforcing cycle-consistency and adversarial losses.
content: The adversarial loss assumes that we have labeled before/after images for the main supervised network. The CycleGAN addresses the situation where we have two sets of data with distinct styles but no matching pairs. An example is converting a photo to the artistic style of Monet. There exist many photos and many Monet paintings, but no correspondence between them. CycleGAN exploits the idea that converting an image in one direction (e.g., photo→Monet) and then back again should recover the original. The CycleGAN loss function is a weighted sum of three losses (figure 15.18). The content loss encourages the before and after images to be similar and is based on the \( \ell_1 \) norm. The adversarial loss uses a discriminator to encourage the output to be indistinguishable from real examples of the target domain. Finally, the cycle-consistency loss encourages the mapping to be reversible. Here, two models are trained together. One maps from the first domain to the second, and the other in the opposite direction. The cycle-consistency loss will be low if the translated image can be itself translated successfully back to the image in the original domain. The model combines these three losses to train networks to translate images from one style to another and back again.
motivation_md: CycleGAN enables image translation between domains without paired data by enforcing reversibility and realism, expanding applicability to unpaired datasets.
recap_md:
- CycleGAN translates images between domains without paired data.
- Uses content, adversarial, and cycle-consistency losses.
- Cycle-consistency loss ensures mapping reversibility between domains.

title: GLOW model for image synthesis
one_liner: Generative flows, or GLOW, is a normalizing flow model that can create high-fidelity images and uses many of the ideas from this chapter.
content: Generative flows, or GLOW, is a normalizing flow model that can create high-fidelity images (figure 16.12) and uses many of the ideas from this chapter. It is easiest understood in the normalizing direction. GLOW starts with a 256 × 256 × 3 tensor containing an RGB image. It uses coupling layers, in which the channels are partitioned into two halves. The second half is subject to a different affine transform at each spatial position, where the parameters of the affine transformation are computed by a 2D convolutional neural network run on the other half of the channels. The coupling layers are alternated with 1 × 1 convolutions, parameterized as LU decompositions which mix the channels. Periodically, the resolution is halved by combining each 2 × 2 patch into one position with four times as many channels. GLOW is a multi-scale flow, and some of the channels are periodically removed to become part of the latent vector z. Images are discrete (due to the quantization of RGB values), so noise is added to the inputs to prevent the training likelihood increasing without bound. This is known as dequantization. To sample more realistic images, the GLOW model samples from the base density raised to a positive power. This chooses examples that are closer to the center of the density rather than from the tails. This is similar to the truncation trick in GANs
motivation_md: GLOW is designed to generate high-quality images by modeling complex image distributions using normalizing flows, coupling layers, and multi-scale architectures, addressing challenges in image synthesis and sampling.
recap_md:
- GLOW uses coupling layers partitioning channels into halves with affine transforms.
- It alternates coupling layers with 1×1 convolutions parameterized by LU decompositions.
- Sampling involves raising the base density to a positive power, similar to GAN truncation tricks.

title: dequantization
one_liner: Images are discrete (due to the quantization of RGB values), so noise is added to the inputs to prevent the training likelihood increasing without bound; this is known as dequantization.
content: Images are discrete due to the quantization of RGB values, so noise is added to the inputs to prevent the training likelihood from increasing without bound. This process is known as dequantization.
motivation_md: Dequantization addresses the problem that discrete image data can cause unbounded likelihood during training by adding noise to make the data effectively continuous.
recap_md:
- Images have discrete RGB values causing challenges in likelihood training.
- Noise addition to inputs prevents likelihood from increasing without bound.
- This noise addition process is called dequantization.

title: truncation trick in GANs
one_liner: To sample more realistic images, the GLOW model samples from the base density raised to a positive power, choosing examples closer to the center of the density rather than from the tails; this is similar to the truncation trick in GANs.
content: To sample more realistic images, the GLOW model samples from the base density raised to a positive power. This chooses examples that are closer to the center of the density rather than from the tails. This is similar to the truncation trick in GANs.
motivation_md: Sampling from a modified density focuses on more typical examples, improving image realism by avoiding unlikely tail samples, analogous to GAN truncation tricks.
recap_md:
- GLOW samples from the base density raised to a positive power.
- This favors examples near the center of the density.
- This approach is similar to the truncation trick used in GANs.

title: Truncation trick in GLOW model sampling
one_liner: Sampling from the base density raised to a positive power chooses examples closer to the center of the density rather than from the tails; this is similar to the truncation trick in GANs.
content: Sampling from the base density raised to a positive power chooses examples that are closer to the center of the density rather than from the tails. This is similar to the truncation trick in GANs.
motivation_md: This sampling method improves image quality by focusing on typical samples, avoiding unlikely extremes, paralleling GAN truncation tricks.
recap_md:
- Sampling uses base density raised to a positive power.
- This selects examples near the density center.
- It resembles the truncation trick in GANs.

title: interpolation using GLOW
one_liner: Interpolation using GLOW involves projecting real images to latent space, interpolating there, and projecting back to image space.
content: Figure 16.13 Interpolation using GLOW model. The left and right images are real people. The intermediate images were computed by projecting the real images to the latent space, interpolating, and then projecting the interpolated points back to image space. Adapted from Kingma & Dhariwal (2018).
motivation_md: Interpolation in latent space allows smooth transitions between images, demonstrating the model's ability to capture meaningful representations.
recap_md:
- Real images are projected to latent space.
- Interpolation is performed in latent space.
- Interpolated points are projected back to image space.

title: approximating other density models
one_liner: Normalizing flows can learn to generate samples approximating an existing density which is easy to evaluate but difficult to sample from.
content: Normalizing flows can also learn to generate samples that approximate an existing density which is easy to evaluate but difficult to sample from. In this context, we denote the normalizing flow Pr(x|ϕ) as the student and the target density q(x) as the teacher. To make progress, we generate samples xi = f[zi, ϕ] from the student. Since we generated these samples ourselves, we know their corresponding latent variables zi, and we can calculate their likelihood in the student model without inversion. Thus, we can use a model like a masked-autoregressive flow where inversion is slow. We define a loss function based on the reverse KL divergence that encourages the student and teacher likelihood to be identical and use this to train the student model (figure 16.14):
motivation_md: This approach enables efficient sampling from complex densities by training a normalizing flow to mimic a target distribution that is easy to evaluate but hard to sample.
recap_md:
- Normalizing flows approximate densities easy to evaluate but hard to sample.
- The flow model is the student; the target density is the teacher.
- Training uses reverse KL divergence to align student and teacher likelihoods.

title: Latent variable models
one_liner: Latent variable models describe a probability distribution Pr(x) indirectly by modeling a joint distribution Pr(x, z) with an unobserved latent variable z and marginalizing over z.
content:
Latent variable models take an indirect approach to describing a probability distribution Pr(x) over a multi-dimensional variable x. Instead of directly writing the expression for Pr(x), they model a joint distribution Pr(x, z) of the data x and an unobserved hidden or latent variable z. They then describe the probability Pr(x) as a marginalization of this joint probability so that:

$$
Pr(x) = \int Pr(x, z) dz.
$$
motivation_md: Latent variable models simplify complex distributions by introducing hidden variables, enabling modeling of complicated data distributions through marginalization.
recap_md:
- Latent variable models define a joint distribution Pr(x, z).
- The latent variable z is unobserved or hidden.
- The data distribution Pr(x) is obtained by marginalizing over z.

title: mixture of Gaussians
one_liner: A 1D mixture of Gaussians models data with a discrete latent variable z having categorical prior and Gaussian likelihoods for each component.
content:
In a 1D mixture of Gaussians (figure 17.1a), the latent variable z is discrete, and the prior Pr(z) is a categorical distribution (figure 5.9) with one probability \(\lambda_n\) for each possible value of z. The likelihood Pr(x|z = n) of the data x given that the latent variable z takes value n is normally distributed with mean \(\mu_n\) and variance \(\sigma_n^2\):

\[
Pr(z = n) = \lambda_n
\]

\[
Pr(x|z = n) = \text{Norm}_x(\mu_n, \sigma_n^2).
\]

As in equation 17.2, the probability Pr(x) is given by the marginalization over the latent variable z (figure 17.1b). Here, the latent variable is discrete, so we sum over its possible values to marginalize:

\[
Pr(x) = \sum_{n=1}^N Pr(x, z = n) = \sum_{n=1}^N Pr(x|z = n) \cdot Pr(z = n) = \sum_{n=1}^N \lambda_n \cdot \text{Norm}_x(\mu_n, \sigma_n^2).
\]
motivation_md: Mixture of Gaussians models complex distributions by combining multiple Gaussian components weighted by categorical latent variables, enabling flexible density modeling.
recap_md:
- The latent variable z is discrete with categorical prior \(\lambda_n\).
- Data likelihood given z is Gaussian with mean \(\mu_n\) and variance \(\sigma_n^2\).
- The overall data probability is a sum over weighted Gaussian components.

title: ELBO properties
one_liner: For any fixed θ, the ELBO is a function of the parameters that must lie below the original likelihood function.
content: When first encountered, the ELBO is a somewhat mysterious object, so we now provide some intuition about its properties. Consider that the original log-likelihood of the data is a function of the parameters ϕ and that we want to find its maximum. For any fixed θ, the ELBO is still a function of the parameters but one that must lie below the original likelihood function. When we change θ, we modify this function, and depending on our choice, the lower bound may move closer or further from the log-likelihood. When we change ϕ, we move along the lower bound function (figure 17.6).
motivation_md: Understanding ELBO's properties helps us see how it bounds the log-likelihood and how parameter choices affect this bound, guiding optimization in variational inference.
recap_md:
- ELBO is a function lying below the original log-likelihood for fixed θ.
- Changing θ modifies the ELBO function, moving the lower bound closer or further from the log-likelihood.
- Changing ϕ moves along the ELBO lower bound function.

title: KL divergence
one_liner: We have just used the definition of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence.
content:
KL divergence
last line, we have just used the definition of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence.
motivation_md: KL divergence measures how one probability distribution diverges from a second, expected distribution, crucial for variational inference.
recap_md:
- KL divergence quantifies difference between two probability distributions.
- It is used to measure how well an approximate distribution matches the true posterior.
- Minimizing KL divergence improves variational approximations.

title: ELBO as reconstruction loss minus KL distance to prior
one_liner: A third way to express the ELBO is as reconstruction error minus the distance to the prior.
content:
Equations 17.16 and 17.17 are two different ways to express the ELBO. A third way is to consider the bound as reconstruction error minus the distance to the prior:
ELBO[θ, ϕ] = \int q(z|θ) \log \left(\frac{\Pr(x, z|ϕ)}{q(z|θ)}\right) dz = \int q(z|θ) \log \left(\frac{\Pr(x|z, ϕ)\Pr(z)}{q(z|θ)}\right) dz = \int q(z|θ) \log [\Pr(x|z, ϕ)] dz + \int q(z|θ) \log \left( \frac{\Pr(z)}{q(z|θ)} \right) dz = \int q(z|θ) \log \left( \Pr(x|z, ϕ) \right) dz - D_{KL} \left[ q(z|θ) \| \Pr(z) \right], (17.18)
motivation_md: Expressing ELBO as reconstruction loss minus KL divergence clarifies its role in balancing data fit and regularization to the prior.
recap_md:
- ELBO can be written as expected log-likelihood minus KL divergence to prior.
- This form shows ELBO balances reconstruction accuracy and regularization.
- It provides intuition for optimizing variational models.

title: decoder
one_liner: q(z|θ) log \left( \Pr(x|z, ϕ) \right) dz − D_{KL}
content: q(z|θ) log \left( \Pr(x|z, ϕ) \right) dz − D_{KL}
motivation_md: This fragment appears incomplete; presumably it relates to the decoder's role in modeling data likelihood given latent variables.
recap_md:
- The decoder models Pr(x|z, ϕ).
- It appears in the ELBO expression as expected log-likelihood.
- The KL term regularizes the latent distribution.

title: Variational approximation
one_liner: We choose a simple parametric form for q(z|θ) to approximate the true posterior, called a variational approximation.
content:
Variational approximation
We saw in equation 17.17 that the ELBO is tight when q(z|θ) is the posterior Pr(z|x, ϕ). In principle, we can compute the posterior using Bayes’ rule:
\Pr(z|x, ϕ) = \frac{\Pr(x|z, ϕ)\Pr(z)}{\Pr(x|ϕ)}, (17.19)
but in practice, this is intractable because we can’t evaluate the evidence term Pr(x|ϕ) in the denominator (see section 17.3).
One solution is to make a variational approximation: we choose a simple parametric form for q(z|θ) and use this to approximate the true posterior.
Here, we choose a multivariate normal distribution with mean µ and diagonal covariance Σ. This will not always match the posterior well but will be better for some values of µ and Σ than others. During training, we will find the normal distribution that is “closest” to the true posterior Pr(z|x) (figure 17.8). This corresponds to minimizing the KL divergence in equation 17.17 and moving the colored curves in figure 17.6 upwards.
Since the optimal choice for q(z|θ) was the posterior Pr(z|x), and this depends on the data example x, the variational approximation should do the same, so we choose:
q(z|x, θ) = \mathrm{Norm}_z \left[ g_\mu[x, θ], g_\Sigma[x, θ] \right], (17.20)
motivation_md: Variational approximation allows practical inference by approximating an intractable posterior with a simpler parametric distribution, enabling optimization.
recap_md:
- The true posterior Pr(z|x, ϕ) is often intractable.
- Variational approximation uses a simpler parametric q(z|θ) to approximate it.
- Typically, a multivariate normal with diagonal covariance is chosen and optimized to minimize KL divergence.

title: encoder
one_liner: The variational approximation depends on the data example x, so we choose q(z|x, θ) = Norm_z [g_μ[x, θ], g_Σ[x, θ]].
content:
the data example x, the variational approximation should do the same, so we choose:
q(z|x, θ) = \mathrm{Norm}_z \left[ g_\mu[x, θ], g_\Sigma[x, θ] \right],
motivation_md: The encoder maps data examples to parameters of the variational distribution, enabling data-dependent latent variable inference.
recap_md:
- The variational approximation q(z|x, θ) depends on data x.
- It is modeled as a normal distribution with parameters given by functions g_μ and g_Σ.
- This forms the encoder in variational autoencoders.

title: The variational autoencoder
one_liner: The variational autoencoder builds a network that computes the ELBO using q(z|x, θ) as the approximate posterior.
content:
The variational autoencoder
Finally, we can describe the VAE. We build a network that computes the ELBO:
ELBO[θ, ϕ] = \int q(z|x, θ) \log \left( \Pr(x|z, ϕ) \right) dz - D_{KL} \left[ q(z|x, θ) \| \Pr(z) \right], (17.21)
where the distribution q(z|x, θ) is the approximation from equation 17.20.
motivation_md: The variational autoencoder provides a practical framework to optimize the ELBO by learning both encoder and decoder networks.
recap_md:
- VAE computes ELBO using an approximate posterior q(z|x, θ).
- The ELBO balances reconstruction and KL divergence to the prior.
- The approximate posterior q(z|x, θ) is learned as part of the model.

title: Monte Carlo estimate
one_liner: The expectation Ez[a[z]] can be approximated by a Monte Carlo estimate using samples from q(z|x, θ).
content: E_z \left[ a[z] \right] = \int a[z] q(z|x, θ) dz \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N a[z^*_n], (17.22)
motivation_md: Monte Carlo estimates enable approximating expectations under complex distributions when analytical solutions are infeasible.
recap_md:
- Expectations under q(z|x, θ) can be approximated by sampling.
- Monte Carlo estimate averages function values over samples.
- This approach supports optimization in variational inference.

title: KL divergence between normal distributions
one_liner: The KL divergence between two normal distributions can be calculated in closed form; for one with parameters µ, Σ and the other a standard normal, it is given by: DKL[q(z|x, θ) || Pr(z)] = 1/2 [Tr[Σ] + µᵀµ − Dz − log det[Σ]].
content:
The second term is the KL divergence between the variational distribution q(z|x, θ) = Normz[µ, Σ] and the prior Pr(z) = Normz[0, I]. The KL divergence between two normal distributions can be calculated in closed form. For the special case where one distribution has parameters µ, Σ and the other is a standard normal, it is given by:
$$
D_{KL}\left[q(z|x, \theta) \| Pr(z)\right] = \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathrm{Tr}[\Sigma] + \mu^T \mu - D_z - \log \det[\Sigma] \right).
$$
motivation_md: KL divergence quantifies how different the variational distribution is from the prior, allowing us to measure and minimize this difference during training for better latent variable modeling.
recap_md:
- KL divergence between normals has a closed-form formula.
- For q(z|x, θ) = Norm[µ, Σ] and prior Pr(z) = Norm[0, I], the formula is: $\frac{1}{2}[\mathrm{Tr}[\Sigma] + \mu^T\mu - D_z - \log \det[\Sigma]]$.
- This term appears in the ELBO as a regularizer.

title: VAE algorithm
one_liner: To compute the ELBO for a data point x, we compute the mean µ and variance Σ of q(z|θ, x), sample z*, and then compute the ELBO using equation 17.23.
content:
To summarize, we aim to build a model that computes the evidence lower bound (ELBO) for a point x. Then we use an optimization algorithm to maximize this lower bound over the dataset and hence improve the log-likelihood. To compute the ELBO we:
- compute the mean µ and variance Σ of the variational posterior distribution q(z|θ, x) for this data point x using the network g[x, θ],
- draw a sample z* from this distribution, and
- compute the ELBO using equation 17.23.
motivation_md: We need an algorithm to efficiently compute and maximize the ELBO for each data point to train the VAE model.
recap_md:
- Compute mean µ and variance Σ of q(z|θ, x) via encoder network.
- Sample z* from this variational posterior.
- Compute ELBO using the sampled z* and optimize it.

title: The reparameterization trick
one_liner: The reparameterization trick moves the stochastic sampling step outside the main pipeline by expressing z* = µ + Σ^{1/2}ϵ*, allowing backpropagation through the network.
content:
There is one complication: the network involves a sampling step, which is difficult to differentiate through. Differentiating past this step is necessary to update the parameters θ that precede it in the network. Fortunately, there is a simple solution; we can move the stochastic part into a branch of the network that draws a sample ϵ* from Normϵ[0, I] and then use the relation:
$$
z^* = \mu + \Sigma^{1/2} \epsilon^*,
$$
to draw from the intended Gaussian. Now we can compute the derivatives as usual because the backpropagation algorithm does not need to pass down the stochastic branch. This is known as the reparameterization trick (figure 17.11).
motivation_md: The reparameterization trick enables gradient-based optimization by allowing differentiation through stochastic sampling steps in the network.
recap_md:
- Sampling step in network is non-differentiable.
- Reparameterize as $z^* = \mu + \Sigma^{1/2} \epsilon^*$ with $\epsilon^* \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$.
- This allows backpropagation through the stochastic layer.

title: Importance sampling
one_liner: Importance sampling focuses sampling on relevant areas by using an auxiliary distribution q(z), often the variational posterior q(z|x), to estimate Pr(x) more efficiently.
content: The product Pr(x|z)Pr(z) that we are trying to integrate is proportional to the posterior distribution Pr(z|x) (by Bayes’ rule). Hence, a sensible choice of auxiliary distribution q(z) is the variational posterior q(z|x) computed by the encoder. If Pr(x|z) has high likelihood, then we will focus the sampling on the relevant area of space and estimate Pr(x) much more efficiently.
motivation_md: Importance sampling improves efficiency by focusing sampling on regions where the posterior is large, reducing variance in estimates.
recap_md:
- Importance sampling uses an auxiliary distribution q(z) to focus sampling.
- Choosing q(z) close to the posterior Pr(z|x) improves efficiency.
- Variational posterior q(z|x) is a natural choice for q(z).

title: Generation quality in VAE
one_liner: Sampling from the aggregated posterior rather than the prior improves VAE generation quality, and modern VAEs use hierarchical priors and specialized architectures for high-quality samples.
content:
Vanilla VAEs are generally low-quality (figure 17.12a–c). This is partly because of the naïve spherical Gaussian noise model and partly because of the Gaussian models used for the prior and variational posterior. One trick to improve generation quality is to sample from the aggregated posterior
$$
q(z|\theta) = \frac{1}{I} \sum_i q(z|x_i, \theta),
$$
rather than the prior; this is the average posterior over all samples and is a mixture of Gaussians that is more representative of the true distribution in latent space.
Modern VAEs can produce high-quality samples (figure 17.12d), but only by using hierarchical priors and specialized network architecture and regularization techniques. Diffusion models (chapter 18) can be viewed as VAEs with hierarchical priors. These also create very high-quality samples.
motivation_md: Improving generation quality in VAEs requires better latent space modeling and sampling strategies beyond simple Gaussian assumptions.
recap_md:
- Vanilla VAEs produce low-quality samples due to simple noise and Gaussian assumptions.
- Sampling from the aggregated posterior improves representativeness.
- Hierarchical priors and advanced architectures enable high-quality generation.

title: Resynthesis
one_liner: Resynthesis is encoding input data and then decoding it again, which can be done with VAEs, GANs, or normalizing flows.
content: The process of encoding (and possibly modifying) input data before decoding again is known as resynthesis. This can also be done with GANs and normalizing flows. However, in GANs, there is no encoder, so a separate procedure must be used to find the latent variable that corresponds to the observed data.
motivation_md: Resynthesis enables data reconstruction and manipulation by encoding and decoding, facilitating tasks like data compression and transformation.
recap_md:
- Resynthesis involves encoding and then decoding input data.
- It can be performed with VAEs, GANs, or normalizing flows.
- GANs lack an encoder, requiring separate latent variable inference.

title: Disentanglement
one_liner: Disentanglement means the latent space coordinates correspond to independent real-world factors, often encouraged by adding regularization terms to the loss function.
content:
In the resynthesis example above, the directions in space representing interpretable properties had to be estimated using labeled training data. Other work attempts to improve the characteristics of the latent space so that its coordinate directions correspond to real-world properties. When each dimension represents an independent real-world factor, the latent space is described as disentangled. For example, when modeling face images, we might hope to uncover head pose or hair color as independent factors.
Methods to encourage disentanglement typically add regularization terms to the loss function based on either (i) the posterior q(z|x, θ) over the latent variables z, or (ii) the aggregated posterior
$$
q(z|\theta) = \frac{1}{I} \sum_i q(z|x_i, \theta):
$$
$$
L_{new} = -ELBO[\theta, \phi] + \lambda_1 \mathbb{E}_{Pr(x)} \left[r_1\left(q(z|x, \theta)\right)\right] + \lambda_2 r_2\left(q(z|\theta)\right).
$$
motivation_md: Disentanglement aims to make latent variables correspond to meaningful independent factors, improving interpretability and control over generated data.
recap_md:
- Disentangled latent space has coordinates representing independent real-world factors.
- Achieved by adding regularization terms to the loss function.
- Regularization can depend on posterior or aggregated posterior distributions.

title: Beta VAE regularization
one_liner: The beta VAE upweights the KL divergence term in the ELBO to encourage disentanglement.
content:
For example, the beta VAE upweights the second term in the ELBO (equation 17.18):
$$
ELBO[\theta, \phi] \approx \log \left( Pr(x|z^*, \phi) \right) - \beta \cdot D_{KL} \left[ q(z|x, \theta) \| Pr(z) \right],
$$
motivation_md: Increasing the weight on the KL divergence term encourages the model to learn more disentangled latent representations.
recap_md:
- Beta VAE modifies ELBO by scaling the KL divergence term by β.
- This encourages disentangled latent variables.
- The ELBO becomes: $\log Pr(x|z^*, \phi) - \beta \cdot D_{KL}[q(z|x, \theta) \| Pr(z)]$.

title: Total correlation VAE
one_liner: The VAE model is modified so that the loss function encourages the total correlation of the latent variables to be minimized and hence encourages disentanglement.
content: Figure 17.14 Disentanglement in the total correlation VAE. The VAE model is modified so that the loss function encourages the total correlation of the latent variables to be minimized and hence encourages disentanglement. When trained on a dataset of images of chairs, several of the latent dimensions have clear real-world interpretations, including a) rotation, b) overall size, and c) legs (swivel chair versus normal). In each case, the central column depicts samples from the model, and as we move left to right, we are subtracting or adding a coordinate vector in latent space. Adapted from Chen et al. (2018d).
motivation_md: Minimizing total correlation in the latent variables encourages disentanglement, allowing the model to learn interpretable features such as rotation and size in images.
recap_md:
- Total correlation VAE modifies the loss to minimize total correlation of latent variables.
- This encourages disentanglement in the latent space.
- Latent dimensions correspond to real-world interpretable features like rotation and size.

title: Posterior collapse
one_liner: One potential problem in training is posterior collapse, in which the encoder always predicts the prior distribution.
content: One potential problem in training is posterior collapse, in which the encoder always predicts the prior distribution. This was identified by Bowman et al. (2015) and can be mitigated by gradually increasing the term that encourages the KL distance between the posterior and the prior to be small during training. Several other methods have been proposed to prevent posterior collapse (Razavi et al., 2019a; Lucas et al., 2019b,a), and this is also part of the motivation for using a discrete latent space (Van Den Oord et al., 2017).
motivation_md: Posterior collapse causes the encoder to ignore the input by always predicting the prior, which undermines learning meaningful latent representations.
recap_md:
- Posterior collapse occurs when the encoder predicts the prior distribution regardless of input.
- It was identified by Bowman et al. (2015).
- Mitigation includes gradually increasing the KL divergence term during training and using discrete latent spaces.

title: Posterior collapse
one_liner: One potential problem in training is posterior collapse, in which the encoder always predicts the prior distribution.
content: One potential problem in training is posterior collapse, in which the encoder always predicts the prior distribution. This was identified by Bowman et al. (2015) and can be mitigated by gradually increasing the term that encourages the KL distance between the posterior and the prior to be small during training. Several other methods have been proposed to prevent posterior collapse (Razavi et al., 2019a; Lucas et al., 2019b,a), and this is also part of the motivation for using a discrete latent space (Van Den Oord et al., 2017).
motivation_md: Posterior collapse causes the encoder to ignore the input by always predicting the prior, which undermines learning meaningful latent representations.
recap_md:
- Posterior collapse occurs when the encoder predicts the prior distribution regardless of input.
- It was identified by Bowman et al. (2015).
- Mitigation includes gradually increasing the KL divergence term during training and using discrete latent spaces.

title: Blurry reconstructions
one_liner: Zhao et al. (2017c) provide evidence that the blurry reconstructions are partly due to Gaussian noise and also because of the sub-optimal posterior distributions induced by the variational approximation.
content: Zhao et al. (2017c) provide evidence that the blurry reconstructions are partly due to Gaussian noise and also because of the sub-optimal posterior distributions induced by the variational approximation. It is perhaps not coincidental that some of the best synthesis results have come from using a discrete latent space modeled by a sophisticated autoregressive model (Razavi et al., 2019b) or from using hierarchical latent spaces (Vahdat & Kautz, 2020; see figure 17.12d). Figure 17.12a-c used a VAE that was trained on the CELEBA
motivation_md: Blurry reconstructions in VAEs arise from Gaussian noise and sub-optimal posterior approximations, motivating improved latent space modeling techniques.
recap_md:
- Blurry reconstructions partly result from Gaussian noise and sub-optimal posterior distributions.
- Discrete latent spaces with autoregressive models improve synthesis quality.
- Hierarchical latent spaces also enhance results.

title: Blurry reconstructions
one_liner: Zhao et al. (2017c) provide evidence that the blurry reconstructions are partly due to Gaussian noise and also because of the sub-optimal posterior distributions induced by the variational approximation.
content: Zhao et al. (2017c) provide evidence that the blurry reconstructions are partly due to Gaussian noise and also because of the sub-optimal posterior distributions induced by the variational approximation. It is perhaps not coincidental that some of the best synthesis results have come from using a discrete latent space modeled by a sophisticated autoregressive model (Razavi et al., 2019b) or from using hierarchical latent spaces (Vahdat & Kautz, 2020; see figure 17.12d). Figure 17.12a-c used a VAE that was trained on the CELEBA database (Liu et al., 2015). Figure 17.12d uses a hierarchical VAE that was trained on the CELEBA HQ dataset (Karras et al., 2018).
motivation_md: Blurry reconstructions occur due to Gaussian noise and sub-optimal posterior approximations, motivating the use of discrete or hierarchical latent spaces for better synthesis.
recap_md:
- Blurry reconstructions arise from Gaussian noise and sub-optimal posterior distributions.
- Using discrete latent spaces with autoregressive models improves results.
- Hierarchical VAEs trained on CELEBA HQ yield better synthesis (Figure 17.12d).

title: Information preference problem
one_liner: Chen et al. (2017) noted that when more complex likelihood terms are used, such as the PixelCNN, the output can cease to depend on the latent variables at all.
content: Chen et al. (2017) noted that when more complex likelihood terms are used, such as the PixelCNN (Van den Oord et al., 2016c), the output can cease to depend on the latent variables at all. They term this the information preference problem. This was addressed by Zhao et al. (2017b) in the InfoVAE, which added an extra term that maximized the mutual information between the latent and observed distributions.
motivation_md: The information preference problem arises when complex likelihoods cause the model to ignore latent variables, motivating methods that maximize mutual information to retain latent dependence.
recap_md:
- Complex likelihoods like PixelCNN can cause outputs to ignore latent variables.
- This is called the information preference problem.
- InfoVAE addresses this by maximizing mutual information between latent and observed distributions.

title: Information preference problem
one_liner: Chen et al. (2017) noted that when more complex likelihood terms are used, such as the PixelCNN, the output can cease to depend on the latent variables at all.
content: Chen et al. (2017) noted that when more complex likelihood terms are used, such as the PixelCNN (Van den Oord et al., 2016c), the output can cease to depend on the latent variables at all. They term this the information preference problem. This was addressed by Zhao et al. (2017b) in the InfoVAE, which added an extra term that maximized the mutual information between the latent and observed distributions.
motivation_md: The information preference problem occurs when complex likelihoods cause the model to ignore latent variables, motivating methods that maximize mutual information to retain latent dependence.
recap_md:
- Complex likelihoods like PixelCNN can cause outputs to ignore latent variables.
- This is called the information preference problem.
- InfoVAE addresses this by maximizing mutual information between latent and observed distributions.

title: Holes in latent space
one_liner: Another problem with the VAE is that there can be “holes” in the latent space that do not correspond to any realistic sample.
content: Another problem with the VAE is that there can be “holes” in the latent space that do not correspond to any realistic sample. Xu et al. (2020) introduce the constrained posterior VAE, which helps prevent these vacant regions in latent space by adding a regularization term. This allows for better interpolation from real samples.
motivation_md: Holes in latent space cause unrealistic samples and poor interpolation, motivating regularization methods to fill these gaps for better sample quality.
recap_md:
- VAEs can have "holes" in latent space with no realistic samples.
- The constrained posterior VAE adds regularization to prevent these holes.
- This improves interpolation between real samples.

title: Nonlinear latent variable model
one_liner: In the nonlinear latent variable model, both the data x and the latent variable z are continuous and multivariate, with a standard multivariate normal prior and a normally distributed likelihood whose mean is a nonlinear function of z.
content:
In the nonlinear latent variable model, both the data x and the latent variable z are continuous and multivariate. The prior Pr(z) is a standard multivariate normal distribution: Pr(z) = Normz[0, I]. The likelihood Pr(x|z, ϕ) is also normally distributed; its mean is a nonlinear function f[z, ϕ] of the latent variable, and its covariance σ2I is spherical:
Pr(x|z, ϕ) = Normx[f[z, ϕ], σ2I].
motivation_md: This model allows representing complex data distributions by mapping latent variables through nonlinear functions, enabling flexible generative modeling of continuous multivariate data.
recap_md:
- The prior Pr(z) is a standard multivariate normal: Normz[0, I].
