- Misuse can occur even if AI systems function correctly.

title: Dirac delta function
one_liner: The Dirac delta function δ[z] has a total area of one, all of which is at position z = 0.
content:
The Dirac delta function \(\delta[z]\) has a total area of one, all of which is concentrated at position \(z = 0\). A dataset with \(N\) elements can be thought of as a probability distribution consisting of a sum of \(N\) delta functions centered at each data point \(x_i\) and scaled by \(1/N\). The delta function is usually drawn as an arrow (e.g., figure 5.12). The delta function has the key property that:

$$
\int f[x]\delta[x - x_0] \, dx = f[x_0].
\tag{B.3}
$$
motivation_md: The Dirac delta function models an idealized point mass or impulse, allowing representation of discrete data points as continuous probability distributions and enabling evaluation of functions at specific points.
recap_md:
- The Dirac delta function \(\delta[z]\) has total area one at \(z=0\).
- A dataset can be represented as a sum of scaled delta functions at data points.
- Key property: \(\int f[x]\delta[x - x_0] dx = f[x_0]\).

title: Stirling’s formula
one_liner: Stirling’s formula approximates the factorial function (and hence the Gamma function) using the formula: $x! \approx \sqrt{2\pi x} \left(\frac{x}{e}\right)^x$.
content:
Stirling’s formula (figure B.2) approximates the factorial function (and hence the Gamma function) using the formula:

$$
x! \approx \sqrt{2\pi x} \left(\frac{x}{e}\right)^x.
$$
motivation_md: Stirling’s formula provides a practical approximation for factorials, which grow very quickly and are computationally expensive to calculate exactly for large \(x\).
recap_md:
- Stirling’s formula approximates factorials as \(x! \approx \sqrt{2\pi x} (x/e)^x\).
- It also approximates the Gamma function.
- Useful for large values of \(x\) where exact factorials are costly.

title: Binomial coeﬀicients
one_liner: Binomial coefficients are positive integers representing the number of ways of choosing an unordered subset of k items from a set of n items without replacement.
content:
Binomial coefficients are written as \(\binom{n}{k}\) and pronounced as “n choose k.” They are positive integers that represent the number of ways of choosing an unordered subset of \(k\) items from a set of \(n\) items without replacement. Binomial coefficients can be computed using the simple formula:

$$
\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}.
\tag{B.5}
$$
motivation_md: Binomial coefficients count combinations, fundamental in probability, combinatorics, and algebra for selecting subsets without regard to order.
recap_md:
- Binomial coefficients \(\binom{n}{k}\) count ways to choose \(k\) items from \(n\).
- They are positive integers.
- Computed by \(\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\).

title: Autocorrelation
one_liner: The autocorrelation r[τ] of a continuous function f[z] is defined as $r[\tau] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f[t + \tau] f[t] dt$.
content:
The autocorrelation \(r[\tau]\) of a continuous function \(f[z]\) is defined as:

$$
r[\tau] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f[t + \tau] f[t] \, dt,
\tag{B.6}
$$
motivation_md: Autocorrelation measures how a function correlates with a shifted version of itself, useful in signal processing and time series analysis.
recap_md:
- Autocorrelation \(r[\tau]\) measures similarity of \(f\) with a shifted version.
- Defined by \(r[\tau] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f[t+\tau] f[t] dt\).
- Useful in analyzing repeating patterns or signals.

title: Transpose
one_liner: The transpose $A^T$ of a matrix $A$ is formed by reflecting it around the principal diagonal so that the kth column becomes the kth row and vice-versa.
content:
The transpose \(A^T \in \mathbb{R}^{D_2 \times D_1}\) of a matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1 \times D_2}\) is formed by reflecting it around the principal diagonal so that the \(k\)th column becomes the \(k\)th row and vice-versa. If we take the transpose of a matrix product \(AB\), then we take the transpose of the original matrices but reverse the order so that

$$(AB)^T = B^T A^T.$$
motivation_md: The transpose operation rearranges matrix elements to switch rows and columns, which is fundamental in linear algebra and matrix computations.
recap_md:
- The transpose \(A^T\) reflects matrix \(A\) around its principal diagonal.
- The \(k\)th column becomes the \(k\)th row.
- Transpose of a product reverses order: \((AB)^T = B^T A^T\).

title: **Transpose**
one_liner: The transpose $A^T$ of a matrix $A$ is formed by reflecting it around the principal diagonal so that the kth column becomes the kth row and vice-versa.
content:
The transpose \(A^T \in \mathbb{R}^{D_2 \times D_1}\) of a matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1 \times D_2}\) is formed by reflecting it around the principal diagonal so that the \(k\)th column becomes the \(k\)th row and vice-versa. If we take the transpose of a matrix product \(AB\), then we take the transpose of the original matrices but reverse the order so that

$$(AB)^T = B^T A^T.
\tag{B.7}
$$
The transpose of a column vector \(a\) is a row vector \(a^T\) and vice-versa.
motivation_md: Transposing matrices and vectors rearranges their elements, which is essential for many algebraic manipulations and proofs.
recap_md:
- The transpose \(A^T\) reflects a matrix around its principal diagonal.
- Transpose of product reverses order: \((AB)^T = B^T A^T\).
- The transpose of a column vector is a row vector and vice-versa.

title: Vector and matrix norms
one_liner: For a vector $z$, the \(\ell_p\) norm is defined as $\|z\|_p = \left(\sum_{d=1}^D |z_d|^p \right)^{1/p}$ for real-valued $p > 1$.
content:
For a vector \(z\), the \(\ell_p\) norm is defined as:

$$
\|z\|_p = \left( \sum_{d=1}^D |z_d|^p \right)^{1/p},
\tag{B.8}
$$
for real-valued \(p > 1\). When \(p = 2\), this returns the length of the vector, and this is known as the Euclidean norm. It is this case that is most commonly used in deep learning, and often the exponent \(p\) is omitted, and the Euclidean norm is just written as \(\|z\|\). When \(p = \infty\), the operator returns the maximum absolute value in the vector.

motivation_md: Vector and matrix norms measure size or length, which is crucial for optimization, error measurement, and regularization in machine learning and mathematics.
recap_md:
- The \(\ell_p\) norm of vector \(z\) is \(\|z\|_p = (\sum |z_d|^p)^{1/p}\).
- \(p=2\) gives the Euclidean norm (vector length).
- \(p=\infty\) returns the maximum absolute value in the vector.

title: **Vector and matrix norms**
one_liner: For a vector $z$, the \(\ell_p\) norm is defined as $\|z\|_p = \left(\sum_{d=1}^D |z_d|^p \right)^{1/p}$ for real-valued $p > 1$.
content:
For a vector \(z\), the \(\ell_p\) norm is defined as:

$$
\|z\|_p = \left( \sum_{d=1}^D |z_d|^p \right)^{1/p},

motivation_md: Vector norms quantify the size of vectors, essential for measuring distances and magnitudes in mathematics and machine learning.

title: **Determinant and trace**
one_liner: Every square matrix A has a scalar called the determinant, which is the product of the eigenvalues, and the trace, which is the sum of the diagonal values or eigenvalues.
content:
Every square matrix A has a scalar associated with it called the determinant and denoted by |A| or det[A], which is the product of the eigenvalues. It is hence related to the average scaling applied by the matrix for different inputs. Matrices with small absolute determinants tend to decrease the norm of vectors upon multiplication, while matrices with large absolute determinants tend to increase the norm. If a matrix is singular, the determinant will be zero, indicating at least one direction in space is mapped to the origin when the matrix is applied. Determinants of matrix expressions obey the following rules:
|A^T| = |A|
|AB| = |A||B|
|A^{-1}| = 1/|A|.

The trace of a square matrix is the sum of the diagonal values (the matrix itself need not be diagonal) or the sum of the eigenvalues. Traces obey these rules:
trace[A^T] = trace[A]
trace[AB] = trace[BA]
trace[A + B] = trace[A] + trace[B]
trace[ABC] = trace[BCA] = trace[CAB],
where in the last relation, the trace is invariant for cyclic permutations only, so in general, trace[ABC] ≠ trace[BAC].
motivation_md: Determinants and traces summarize key properties of matrices: determinants measure volume scaling and singularity, while traces relate to eigenvalues and cyclic invariance, aiding in understanding matrix behavior and transformations.
recap_md:
- The determinant of a square matrix is the product of its eigenvalues and indicates scaling and singularity.
- The trace is the sum of the diagonal entries or eigenvalues.
- Determinants and traces obey specific algebraic rules, including cyclic invariance for traces.

title: **Diagonal matrices**
one_liner: A diagonal matrix has zeros everywhere except on the principal diagonal, and its determinant is the product of the diagonal values.
content: A diagonal matrix has zeros everywhere except on the principal diagonal. If these diagonal entries are all non-zero, the inverse is also a diagonal matrix, with each diagonal entry d_{ii} replaced by 1/d_{ii}. The determinant is the product of the values on the diagonal. A special case of this is the identity matrix, which has ones on the diagonal. Consequently, its inverse is also the identity matrix, and its determinant is one.
motivation_md: Diagonal matrices simplify computations since their inverse and determinant are straightforward to find, making them fundamental in linear algebra.
recap_md:
- Diagonal matrices have zeros off the principal diagonal.
- Their inverse is diagonal if all diagonal entries are non-zero, with entries inverted.
- The determinant is the product of diagonal entries; the identity matrix is a special case.

title: **Triangular matrices**
one_liner: A lower triangular matrix has non-zero values on and below the principal diagonal; an upper triangular matrix has non-zero values on and above it.
content: A lower triangular matrix has all of its non-zero values on the principal diagonal and/or the positions below this. An upper triangular matrix has all of its non-zero values on the principal diagonal and/or the positions above this. In both cases, the matrix can be inverted in O[D^2] time (see problem 16.4), and the determinant is just the product of the diagonal entries.
motivation_md: Triangular matrices allow efficient inversion and determinant calculation, which is useful in solving linear systems and matrix factorizations.
recap_md:
- Lower triangular matrices have non-zero entries on and below the diagonal.
- Upper triangular matrices have non-zero entries on and above the diagonal.
- Both types can be inverted efficiently, and their determinant is the product of diagonal entries.

title: **Orthogonal matrices**
one_liner: Orthogonal matrices represent rotations and reflections, have eigenvalues of magnitude one, and satisfy A^{-1} = A^T.
content: Orthogonal matrices represent rotations and reflections around the origin, so the circle would be mapped to another circle of unit radius but rotated and possibly reflected. Accordingly, the eigenvalues must all have magnitude one, and the determinant must be either one or minus one. The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is its transpose, so A^{-1} = A^T.
motivation_md: Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and angles, making them important for representing rotations and reflections in linear algebra.
recap_md:
- Orthogonal matrices represent rotations and reflections.
- Their eigenvalues have magnitude one, and determinant is ±1.
- The inverse equals the transpose: A^{-1} = A^T.

title: **Permutation matrices**
one_liner: Permutation matrices have exactly one 1 in each row and column, permute vector entries, and are orthogonal with determinant ±1.
content:
A permutation matrix has exactly one non-zero entry in each row and column, and all of these entries take the value one. It is a special case of an orthogonal matrix, so its inverse is its own transpose, and its determinant is always ±1. As the name suggests, it has the effect of permuting the entries of a vector. For example:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
a \\
b \\
c
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
b \\
c \\
a
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
(B.16)
motivation_md: Permutation matrices reorder vector components and are useful for rearranging data or variables in linear algebra.
recap_md:
- Permutation matrices have one 1 per row and column, zeros elsewhere.
- They are orthogonal with inverse equal to transpose.
- Their determinant is always ±1 and they permute vector entries.

title: **Linear algebra**
one_liner: Linear algebra studies linear functions of the form f[z] = ϕ₁z₁ + ϕ₂z₂ + ... + ϕ_D z_D, often including a constant term.
content:
Linear algebra is the mathematics of linear functions, which have the form:
f[z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_D] = \phi_1 z_1 + \phi_2 z_2 + \ldots + \phi_D z_D,
where \phi_1, \ldots, \phi_D are parameters that define the function.
We often add a constant term \phi_0 to the right-hand side. This is technically an affine function but is commonly referred to as linear in machine learning. We adopt this convention throughout.
motivation_md: Linear algebra provides the framework to study and manipulate linear functions, fundamental in many areas including machine learning.
recap_md:
- Linear functions are sums of parameters times variables.
- Often a constant term is added, making the function affine.
- In machine learning, affine functions are commonly called linear.

title: **Linear equations in matrix form**
one_liner: A system of linear functions can be expressed compactly in matrix form as y = ϕ₀ + Φz.
content:
Consider a collection of linear functions:
\[
y_1 = \phi_{10} + \phi_{11} z_1 + \phi_{12} z_2 + \phi_{13} z_3
\]
\[
y_2 = \phi_{20} + \phi_{21} z_1 + \phi_{22} z_2 + \phi_{23} z_3
\]
\[
y_3 = \phi_{30} + \phi_{31} z_1 + \phi_{32} z_2 + \phi_{33} z_3.
\]
These can be written in matrix form as:
\[
\begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ y_3 \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} \phi_{10} \\ \phi_{20} \\ \phi_{30} \end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix} \phi_{11} & \phi_{12} & \phi_{13} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22} & \phi_{23} \\ \phi_{31} & \phi_{32} & \phi_{33} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} z_1 \\ z_2 \\ z_3 \end{bmatrix},
\]
or as y = \phi_0 + \Phi z for short, where y_i = \phi_{i0} + \sum_{j=1}^3 \phi_{ij} z_j.
motivation_md: Expressing linear functions in matrix form simplifies computation and analysis, especially for systems with multiple outputs.
recap_md:
- Multiple linear functions can be combined into matrix form.
- The form is y = ϕ_0 + Φ z, compactly representing constants and coefficients.
- This facilitates efficient computation and notation.

title: **Matrix calculus**
one_liner: Matrix calculus extends derivatives to functions mapping vectors and matrices, with derivatives taking vector, matrix, or tensor forms.
content:
Most readers of this book will be accustomed to the idea that if we have a function y = f[x], we can compute the derivative \partial y / \partial x, representing how y changes when we make a small change in x. This idea extends to functions y = f[x] mapping a vector x to a scalar y, functions y = f[x] mapping a vector x to a vector y, functions y = f[X] mapping a matrix X to a vector y, and so on. The rules of matrix calculus help us compute derivatives of these quantities. The derivatives take the following forms:

• For a function y = f[x] where y \in \mathbb{R} and x \in \mathbb{R}^D, the derivative \partial y / \partial x is also a D-dimensional vector, where the ith element is computed as \partial y / \partial x_i.

• For a function y = f[x] where y \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y} and x \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}, the derivative \partial y / \partial x is a D_x \times D_y matrix where element (i, j) contains the derivative \partial y_j / \partial x_i. This is known as a Jacobian and is sometimes written as \nabla_{xy} in other documents.

• For a function y = f[X] where y \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y} and X \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1 \times D_2}, the derivative \partial y / \partial X is a 3D tensor containing the derivatives \partial y_i / \partial x_{jk}.

Often these matrix and vector derivatives have superficially similar forms to the scalar case. For example, we have:

\[
y = a x \quad \rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = a,
\]

and

\[
y = A x \quad \rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = A^T.
\]
motivation_md: Matrix calculus generalizes derivatives to vector and matrix functions, enabling efficient computation of gradients in multivariate and matrix-valued functions.
recap_md:
- Derivatives extend from scalars to vectors, matrices, and tensors in matrix calculus.
- The Jacobian matrix contains partial derivatives for vector-to-vector functions.
- Matrix calculus rules simplify computing derivatives of functions like y = Ax.

title: Frobenius norm
one_liner: The ℓ2 norm of a matrix Z (known as the Frobenius norm) is calculated as: ||Z||_F = (∑_{i=1}^I ∑_{j=1}^J |z_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}.
content:
Norms can be computed in a similar way for matrices. For example, the ℓ2 norm of a matrix Z (known as the Frobenius norm) is calculated as:

||Z||_F = \left( \sum_{i=1}^I \sum_{j=1}^J |z_{ij}|^2 \right)^{1/2}.
(B.9)
motivation_md: The Frobenius norm extends the concept of vector norms to matrices, providing a way to measure the size or magnitude of a matrix in a consistent manner.
recap_md:
- The Frobenius norm is the ℓ2 norm of a matrix.
- It is computed as the square root of the sum of the squares of all entries.
- Denoted as ||Z||_F = (∑_{i,j} |z_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}.

title: **Product of matrices**
one_liner: The product C = AB of two matrices A ∈ ℝ^{D1×D2} and B ∈ ℝ^{D2×D3} is a third matrix C ∈ ℝ^{D1×D3} where C_{ij} = ∑_{d=1}^{D2} A_{id} B_{dj}.
content:
Product of matrices
The product C = AB of two matrices A \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1 \times D_2} and B \in \mathbb{R}^{D_2 \times D_3} is a third matrix C \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1 \times D_3} where:

C_{ij} = \sum_{d=1}^{D_2} A_{id} B_{dj}.
(B.10)
motivation_md: Matrix multiplication combines two matrices into a new matrix, enabling transformations and linear mappings in higher dimensions.
recap_md:
- Matrix product C = AB combines A ∈ ℝ^{D1×D2} and B ∈ ℝ^{D2×D3}.
- Resulting matrix C ∈ ℝ^{D1×D3}.
- Each element C_{ij} = ∑_{d=1}^{D2} A_{id} B_{dj}.

title: Product of matrices
one_liner: The product C = AB of two matrices A ∈ ℝ^{D1×D2} and B ∈ ℝ^{D2×D3} is a third matrix C ∈ ℝ^{D1×D3} where C_{ij} = ∑_{d=1}^{D2} A_{id} B_{dj}.
content:
Product of matrices
The product C = AB of two matrices A \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1 \times D_2} and B \in \mathbb{R}^{D_2 \times D_3} is a third matrix C \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1 \times D_3} where:

C_{ij} = \sum_{d=1}^{D_2} A_{id} B_{dj}.
(B.10)
motivation_md: Matrix multiplication combines two matrices into a new matrix, enabling transformations and linear mappings in higher dimensions.
recap_md:
- Matrix product C = AB combines A ∈ ℝ^{D1×D2} and B ∈ ℝ^{D2×D3}.
- Resulting matrix C ∈ ℝ^{D1×D3}.
- Each element C_{ij} = ∑_{d=1}^{D2} A_{id} B_{dj}.

title: Dot product of vectors
one_liner: The dot product a^T b of two vectors a and b is a scalar defined as a^T b = ∑_{d=1}^D a_d b_d and equals ||a|| ||b|| cos(θ), where θ is the angle between them.
content:
Dot product of vectors
The dot product a^T b of two vectors a \in \mathbb{R}^D and b \in \mathbb{R}^D is a scalar and is defined as:

\[ a^T b = b^T a = \sum_{d=1}^D a_d b_d. \]
(B.11)

It can be shown that the dot product is proportional to the Euclidean norm of the first vector times the Euclidean norm of the second vector times the angle \( \theta \) between them:

\[ a^T b = ||a|| \, ||b|| \cos[\theta]. \]
motivation_md: The dot product quantifies the similarity and angle relationship between two vectors, linking algebraic and geometric interpretations.
recap_md:
- Dot product a^T b = ∑_{d=1}^D a_d b_d is a scalar.
- It is symmetric: a^T b = b^T a.
- Also equals ||a|| ||b|| cos(θ), relating to vector norms and angle θ.

title: **Dot product of vectors**
one_liner: The dot product a^T b of two vectors a and b is a scalar defined as a^T b = ∑_{d=1}^D a_d b_d and equals ||a|| ||b|| cos(θ), where θ is the angle between them.
content:
Dot product of vectors
The dot product a^T b of two vectors a \in \mathbb{R}^D and b \in \mathbb{R}^D is a scalar and is defined as:

\[ a^T b = b^T a = \sum_{d=1}^D a_d b_d. \]
(B.11)

It can be shown that the dot product is proportional to the Euclidean norm of the first vector times the Euclidean norm of the second vector times the angle \( \theta \) between them:

\[ a^T b = ||a|| \, ||b|| \cos[\theta]. \]
(B.12)
motivation_md: The dot product links algebraic operations on vectors to geometric concepts like length and angle, which is fundamental in many applications.
recap_md:
- Dot product a^T b = ∑_{d=1}^D a_d b_d is a scalar.
- It is symmetric: a^T b = b^T a.
- Also equals ||a|| ||b|| cos(θ), relating to vector norms and angle θ.

title: **Inverse**
one_liner: A square matrix A may or may not have an inverse A^{-1} such that A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I; if not, it is called singular.
content:
Inverse
A square matrix A may or may not have an inverse A^{-1} such that A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I.
If a matrix does not have an inverse, it is called singular.
If we take the inverse of a matrix product AB where A and B are square and invertible, then we can equivalently take the inverse of each matrix individually and reverse the order of multiplication:

(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}.
(B.13)

In general, it takes O[D^3] operations to invert a D×D matrix. However, inversion is more efficient for special types of matrices, including diagonal, orthogonal, and triangular matrices (see section B.4).
motivation_md: Understanding matrix inverses is crucial for solving linear systems and reversing linear transformations, with computational considerations for efficiency.
recap_md:
- Inverse A^{-1} satisfies A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I.
- Matrices without inverses are singular.
- (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1} for invertible square matrices A and B.

title: Inverse
one_liner: A square matrix A may or may not have an inverse A^{-1} such that A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I; if not, it is called singular.
content:
Inverse
A square matrix A may or may not have an inverse A^{-1} such that A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I.
If a matrix does not have an inverse, it is called singular.
If we take the inverse of a matrix product AB where A and B are square and invertible, then we can equivalently take the inverse of each matrix individually and reverse the order of multiplication:

(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}.
(B.13)

In general, it takes O[D^3] operations to invert a D×D matrix. However, inversion is more efficient for special types of matrices, including diagonal, orthogonal, and triangular matrices (see section B.4).
motivation_md: Understanding matrix inverses is crucial for solving linear systems and reversing linear transformations, with computational considerations for efficiency.
recap_md:

title: **Eigenspectrum**
one_liner: The eigenspectrum is the set of eigenvalues of a matrix, describing the magnitude of scaling applied by the matrix across all directions.
content:
Eigenspectrum
If we multiply the set of 2D points on a unit circle by a 2 × 2 matrix A, they map to an ellipse (figure B.3). The radii of the major and minor axes of this ellipse (i.e., the longest and shortest directions) correspond to the magnitude of the singular values \( \lambda_1 \) and \( \lambda_2 \) of the matrix. The same idea applies in higher dimensions. A D-dimensional spheroid is mapped by a D × D matrix A to a D-dimensional ellipsoid. The radii of the D principal axes of this ellipsoid determine the magnitude of the singular values. For symmetric square matrices, the same information is captured by the eigenvalues which are here the same as the singular values.

The spectral norm of a square matrix is the largest absolute eigenvalue. It captures the largest possible change in magnitude when the matrix is applied to a vector of unit length. As such, it tells us about the Lipschitz constant of the transformation. The set of eigenvalues is sometimes called the eigenspectrum and tells us about the magnitude of the scaling applied by the matrix across all directions. This information can be summarized using the determinant and trace of the matrix.
motivation_md: The eigenspectrum summarizes how a matrix scales space in different directions, which is essential for understanding matrix transformations and stability.
recap_md:
- Eigenspectrum is the set of eigenvalues of a matrix.
- Singular values correspond to principal axis lengths of the transformed ellipsoid.
- Spectral norm is the largest absolute eigenvalue, indicating maximum scaling.

title: **Change of variable**
one_liner: When the mean of a multivariate normal in x is a linear function Ay + b of a second variable y, this is proportional to another normal distribution in y, where the mean is a linear function of x.
content:
When the mean of a multivariate normal in x is a linear function Ay + b of a second variable y, this is proportional to another normal distribution in y, where the mean is a linear function of x:
Norm_x [Ay + b, \Sigma] \propto Norm_y[(A^T \Sigma^{-1} A)^{-1} A^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - b), (A^T \Sigma^{-1} A)^{-1}].
(C.30)
At first sight, this relation is rather opaque, but figure C.5 shows the case for scalar x and y, which is easy to understand. As for the previous relation, this can be proved by expanding the quadratic product in the exponential term and completing the square to make this a distribution in y (see problem 18.4).
motivation_md: This concept explains how a multivariate normal distribution transforms under a linear change of variables, enabling us to understand and compute distributions in transformed variables.
recap_md:
- A multivariate normal with mean Ay + b in x corresponds to a proportional normal distribution in y.
- The transformed mean and covariance involve expressions with A, \Sigma, and their inverses.
- The relation can be derived by completing the square in the exponential term.

title: Sampling
one_liner: To sample from a univariate distribution Pr(x), we first compute the cumulative distribution F[x] (the integral of Pr(x)).
content:
To sample from a univariate distribution Pr(x), we first compute the cumulative distribution F[x] (the integral of Pr(x)). Then we draw a sample z^* from a uniform distribution over the range [0, 1] and evaluate this against the inverse of the cumulative distribution, so the sample x^* is created as:
x^* = F^{-1}[z^*].
(C.31)
motivation_md: Sampling allows us to generate random values from a given probability distribution, which is essential for simulations and probabilistic modeling.
recap_md:
- Compute the cumulative distribution function F[x] from Pr(x).
- Draw z^* uniformly from [0,1].
- Obtain sample x^* by evaluating the inverse CDF at z^*: x^* = F^{-1}[z^*].

title: Sampling from normal distributions
one_liner: A sample from a normal distribution with mean µ and variance σ² can be created using equation C.22 after sampling from a standard normal distribution.
content: The method above can be used to generate a sample x^* from a univariate standard normal distribution. A sample from a normal distribution with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 can then be created using equation C.22. Similarly, a sample x^* from a D-dimensional multivariate standard distribution can be created by independently sampling D univariate standard normal variables. A sample from a multivariate normal distribution with mean \mu and covariance \Sigma can then be created using equation C.24.
motivation_md: Sampling from normal distributions is fundamental for probabilistic modeling and simulations involving Gaussian variables.
recap_md:
- Sample from a univariate standard normal distribution first.
- Use equation C.22 to transform to a normal with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2.
- For multivariate normals, sample each dimension independently and then transform using equation C.24.

title: Ancestral sampling
one_liner: When the joint distribution factors into conditional probabilities, samples can be generated by sequentially sampling from the root and subsequent conditionals, known as ancestral sampling.
content:
When the joint distribution can be factored into a series of conditional probabilities, we can generate samples using ancestral sampling. The basic idea is to generate a sample from the root variable(s) and then sample from the subsequent conditional distributions based on this instantiation. This process is known as ancestral sampling and is easiest to understand with an example.
Consider a joint distribution Pr(x, y, z) over three variables, x, y, and z, which (in this particular case) factors as:
Pr(x, y, z) = Pr(x) Pr(y|x) Pr(z|y).
(C.32)
To sample from this joint distribution, we first draw a sample x^* from Pr(x). Then we draw a sample y^* from Pr(y|x^*). Finally, we draw a sample z^* from Pr(z|y^*).
motivation_md: Ancestral sampling provides a systematic way to generate samples from complex joint distributions by leveraging their conditional structure.
recap_md:
- Factor joint distribution into conditionals: Pr(x,y,z) = Pr(x)Pr(y|x)Pr(z|y).
- Sample root variable x^* from Pr(x).
- Sample y^* from Pr(y|x^*), then z^* from Pr(z|y^*).

title: Distances between probability distributions
one_liner: We need a measure of distance between two probability distributions to frame supervised and unsupervised learning as minimizing distributional differences.
content: Supervised learning can be framed in terms of minimizing the distance between the probability distribution implied by the model and the discrete probability distribution implied by the samples (section 5.7). Unsupervised learning can often be framed in terms of minimizing the distance between the probability distribution of real examples and the distribution of data from the model. In both cases, we need a measure of distance between two probability distributions. This section considers the properties of several different measures of distance between distributions (see also figure 15.8 for a discussion of the Wasserstein or earth mover’s distance).
motivation_md: Measuring distances between probability distributions is essential to quantify how well a model fits data or approximates a target distribution.
recap_md:
- Supervised learning minimizes distance between model and sample distributions.
- Unsupervised learning minimizes distance between real data and model distributions.
- Various distance measures exist, including Wasserstein distance.

title: Kullback-Leibler divergence
one_liner: The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measures the distance between probability distributions p(x) and q(x) as \( D_{KL}[p(x)||q(x)] = \int p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} dx \).
content:
The most common measure of distance between probability distributions p(x) and q(x) is the Kullback-Leibler or KL divergence and is defined as:
D_{KL}[p(x)||q(x)] = \int p(x) \log \left( \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \right) dx.
(C.33)
This distance is always greater than or equal to zero, which is easily demonstrated by noting that \(-\log[y] \geq 1 - y\) (figure C.6) so:
D_{KL}\left[ p(x) \middle\| q(x) \right] = \int p(x) \log \left( \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \right) dx = - \int p(x) \log \left( \frac{q(x)}{p(x)} \right) dx \geq \int p(x) \left( 1 - \frac{q(x)}{p(x)} \right) dx = \int p(x) - q(x) dx = 1 - 1 = 0.
(C.34)
motivation_md: KL divergence quantifies how one probability distribution diverges from a reference distribution, fundamental for statistical inference and machine learning.
recap_md:
- KL divergence: \( D_{KL}[p||q] = \int p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} dx \).
- It is always non-negative.
- Proof uses inequality \(-\log[y] \geq 1 - y\).

title: Jensen-Shannon divergence
one_liner: The Jensen-Shannon divergence is a symmetric measure of distance between probability distributions constructed from KL divergences.
content:
The KL divergence is not symmetric (i.e., D_{KL}[p(x)||q(x)] \neq D_{KL}[q(x)||p(x)]). The Jensen-Shannon divergence is a measure of distance that is symmetric by construction:
D_{JS}[p(x)||q(x)] = \frac{1}{2} D_{KL}\left(p(x) \middle\| \frac{p(x) + q(x)}{2} \right) + \frac{1}{2} D_{KL}\left(q(x) \middle\| \frac{p(x) + q(x)}{2} \right).
(C.35)
motivation_md: Jensen-Shannon divergence provides a symmetric and finite measure of difference between distributions, useful when KL divergence's asymmetry is problematic.
recap_md:
- KL divergence is asymmetric.
- Jensen-Shannon divergence symmetrizes KL divergence.
- Defined as average KL divergence to the midpoint distribution.

title: Fréchet distance
one_liner: The Fréchet distance between two distributions p(x) and q(x) is defined via an optimal coupling minimizing the expected squared distance.
content:
The Fréchet distance D_{Fr} between two distributions p(x) and q(x) is given by:
D_{Fr}[p(x)||q(y)] = \sqrt{ \min_{\pi(x,y)} \iint \pi(x, y) |x - y|^2 dx dy },
(C.36)
motivation_md: Fréchet distance measures the minimal average squared distance between points drawn from two distributions, useful for comparing distributions in metric spaces.
recap_md:
- Fréchet distance involves finding an optimal coupling \( \pi(x,y) \).
- It minimizes the expected squared distance between paired points.
- Provides a metric for comparing probability distributions.

title: **Random variables and probability distributions**
one_liner: A random variable x denotes a quantity that is uncertain and is described by a probability distribution Pr(x).
content:
A random variable x denotes a quantity that is uncertain. It may be discrete (taking only certain values, for example integers) or continuous (taking any value on a continuum, for example real numbers). If we observe several instances of a random variable x, it will take different values, and the relative propensity to take different values is described by a probability distribution Pr(x).

For a discrete variable, this distribution associates a probability Pr(x=k) ∈ [0, 1] with each potential outcome k, and the sum of these probabilities is one. For a continuous variable, there is a non-negative probability density Pr(x = a) ≥ 0 associated with each value a in the domain of x, and the integral of this probability density function (PDF) over this domain must be one. This density can be greater than one for any point a.

From here on, we assume that the random variables are continuous. The ideas are exactly the same for discrete distributions but with sums replacing integrals.
motivation_md: Random variables model uncertain quantities, and probability distributions describe how likely different values are, enabling us to analyze randomness mathematically. This concept is foundational for understanding uncertainty and variability in data. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- A random variable x can be discrete or continuous, representing uncertain quantities.
- Probability distributions Pr(x) describe the likelihood of different values.
- For continuous variables, the PDF integrates to one over the domain.

title: **Joint probability**
one_liner: The joint distribution Pr(x, y) describes the propensity that x and y take particular combinations of values.
content:
Consider the case where we have two random variables x and y. The joint distribution Pr(x, y) tells us about the propensity that x and y take particular combinations of values (figure C.1a). Now there is a non-negative probability density Pr(x = a, y = b) associated with each pair of values x = a and y = b and this must satisfy:

\[
\iint Pr(x, y) \cdot dx dy = 1.
\]

(C.1)
motivation_md: Joint probability distributions describe how two variables vary together, capturing their combined behavior and dependencies. This is essential for understanding relationships between variables. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- Joint distribution Pr(x, y) gives probabilities for pairs of values (x, y).
- It is a non-negative probability density function.
- The integral over all x and y equals one: \(\iint Pr(x, y) dx dy = 1\).

title: **Marginalization**
one_liner: Marginal distributions Pr(x) and Pr(y) can be recovered by integrating the joint distribution Pr(x, y) over the other variable.
content:
If we know the joint distribution Pr(x, y) over two variables, we can recover the marginal distributions Pr(x) and Pr(y) by integrating over the other variable (figure C.1b-c):

\[
\int Pr(x, y) \cdot dx = Pr(y)
\]

\[
\int Pr(x, y) \cdot dy = Pr(x).
\]

(C.2)
motivation_md: Marginalization allows us to find the distribution of one variable by summing or integrating out the other, simplifying analysis when interested in individual variables. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- Marginal distribution Pr(x) is found by integrating Pr(x, y) over y.
- Marginal distribution Pr(y) is found by integrating Pr(x, y) over x.
- Marginalization reduces joint distributions to single-variable distributions.

title: **Conditional probability and likelihood**
one_liner: The conditional probability Pr(x|y) is the probability of x given y, found by slicing the joint distribution and normalizing.
content:
The conditional probability Pr(x|y) is the probability of variable x taking a certain value, assuming we know the value of y. The vertical line is read as the English word “given,” so Pr(x|y) is the probability of x given y. The conditional probability Pr(x|y) can be found by taking a slice through the joint distribution Pr(x, y) for a fixed y. This slice is then divided by the probability of that value y occurring (the total area under the slice) so that the conditional distribution sums to one (figure C.2):

\[
Pr(x|y) = \frac{Pr(x, y)}{Pr(y)}.
\]

(C.3)

Similarly,

\[
Pr(y|x) = \frac{Pr(x, y)}{Pr(x)}.
\]

(C.4)

When we consider the conditional probability Pr(x|y) as a function of x, it must sum to one. When we consider the same quantity Pr(x|y) as a function of y, it is termed the likelihood of x given y and does not have to sum to one.
motivation_md: Conditional probability quantifies the probability of one event given knowledge of another, enabling updated beliefs and inference. Likelihood is related but treats the function differently. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- Conditional probability Pr(x|y) is the probability of x given y.
- It is computed by slicing the joint distribution at fixed y and normalizing.
- Likelihood treats Pr(x|y) as a function of y and need not sum to one.

title: **Bayes’ rule**
one_liner: Bayes’ rule relates conditional probabilities: Pr(x|y) = Pr(y|x)Pr(x) / Pr(y).
content:
From equations C.3 and C.4, we get two expressions for the joint probability Pr(x, y):

\[
Pr(x, y) = Pr(x|y)Pr(y) = Pr(y|x)Pr(x),
\]

(C.5)

which we can rearrange to get:

\[
Pr(x|y) = \frac{Pr(y|x)Pr(x)}{Pr(y)}.
\]

(C.6)
motivation_md: Bayes’ rule provides a way to update the probability of a hypothesis given new evidence, fundamental for inference and learning. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- Joint probability can be expressed as Pr(x|y)Pr(y) or Pr(y|x)Pr(x).
- Bayes’ rule rearranges this to relate conditional probabilities.
- Bayes’ rule: \(Pr(x|y) = \frac{Pr(y|x)Pr(x)}{Pr(y)}\).

title: **Independence**
one_liner: Two variables x and y are independent if knowing one tells us nothing about the other, so Pr(x, y) = Pr(x)Pr(y).
content:
If the value of the random variable y tells us nothing about x and vice-versa, we say that x and y are independent, and we can write Pr(x|y) = Pr(x) and Pr(y|x) = Pr(y). It follows that all of the conditional distributions Pr(y|x = •) are identical, as are the conditional distributions Pr(x|y=•).

Starting from the first expression for the joint probability in equation C.5, we see that the joint distribution becomes the product of the marginal distributions:

\[
Pr(x, y) = Pr(x|y)Pr(y) = Pr(x)Pr(y)
\]

when the variables are independent (figure C.3).
motivation_md: Independence means variables do not influence each other, simplifying probability calculations and modeling. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- Independence means Pr(x|y) = Pr(x) and Pr(y|x) = Pr(y).
- Conditional distributions are identical to marginals when independent.
- Joint distribution factors as Pr(x, y) = Pr(x)Pr(y).

title: **Expectation**
one_liner: The expectation of a function f[x] with respect to Pr(x) is the average value weighted by the probability distribution.
content:
Consider a function f[x] and a probability distribution Pr(x) defined over x. The expected value of a function f[•] of a random variable x with respect to the probability distribution Pr(x) is defined as:

\[
E_x \bigl[f[x]\bigr] = \int f[x] Pr(x) dx.
\]

(C.8)

As the name suggests, this is the expected or average value of f[x] after taking into account the probability of seeing different values of x. This idea generalizes to functions f[•, •] of more than one random variable:

\[
E_{x,y} \bigl[f[x, y]\bigr] = \iint f[x, y] Pr(x, y) dx dy.
\]

(C.9)

An expectation is always taken with respect to a distribution over one or more variables. However, we don’t usually make this explicit when the choice of distribution is obvious and write E[f[x]] instead of E_x[f[x]].

If we drew a large number I of samples \(\{x_i\}_{i=1}^I\) from Pr(x), calculated f[x_i] for each sample and took the average of these values, the result would approximate the expectation E[f[x]] of the function:

\[
E_x \bigl[f[x]\bigr] \approx \frac{1}{I} \sum_{i=1}^I f[x_i].
\]

(C.10)
motivation_md: Expectation gives the average or mean value of a function under uncertainty, summarizing distributions into single representative values. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- Expectation \(E[f[x]] = \int f[x] Pr(x) dx\) averages f[x] weighted by Pr(x).
- Generalizes to multiple variables with joint distributions.
- Sample averages approximate expectations.

title: **Rules for manipulating expectations**
one_liner: There are four rules for manipulating expectations involving constants, sums, and independence.
content:
There are four rules for manipulating expectations:

\[
E[k] = k
\]

\[
E[k \cdot f[x]] = k \cdot E[f[x]]
\]

\[
E[f[x] + g[x]] = E[f[x]] + E[g[x]]
\]

\[
E_{x,y}[f[x] \cdot g[y]] = E_x[f[x]] \cdot E_y[g[y]] \quad \text{if } x, y \text{ independent},
\]

where k is an arbitrary constant. These are proven below for the continuous case.

Rule 1:
The expectation E[k] of a constant value k is just k.

\[
E[k] = \int k \cdot Pr(x) dx = k \int Pr(x) dx = k.
\]

(C.12)

Rule 2:
The expectation E[k \cdot f[x]] of a constant k times a function of the variable x is k times the expectation E[f[x]] of the function:

\[
E[k \cdot f[x]] = \int k \cdot f[x] Pr(x) dx = k \int f[x] Pr(x) dx = k \cdot E[f[x]].
\]

(C.13)

Rule 3:
The expectation of a sum E[f[x] + g[x]] of terms is the sum E[f[x]] + E[g[x]] of the expectations:

\[
E[f[x] + g[x]] = \int (f[x] + g[x]) Pr(x) dx = \int f[x] Pr(x) dx + \int g[x] Pr(x) dx = E[f[x]] + E[g[x]].
\]

(C.14)

Rule 4:
The expectation of a product E[f[x] \cdot g[y]] of terms is the product E[f[x]] \cdot E[g[y]] if x and y are independent.

\[
E[f[x] \cdot g[y]] = \iint f[x] \cdot g[y] Pr(x, y) dx dy = \iint f[x] \cdot g[y] Pr(x) Pr(y) dx dy = E[f[x]] E[g[y]].
\]

(C.15)

where we used the definition of independence (equation C.7) between the first two lines.

The four rules generalize to the multivariate case:

\[
E[A] = A
\]

\[
E[A \cdot f[x]] = A E[f[x]]
\]

\[
E[f[x] + g[x]] = E[f[x]] + E[g[x]]
\]

\[
E_{x,y}[f[x]^T g[y]] = E_x[f[x]]^T E_y[g[y]] \quad \text{if } x, y \text{ independent}.
\]

(C.16)
motivation_md: Rules for manipulating expectations simplify calculations and allow breaking down complex expressions into manageable parts, especially when dealing with constants and independent variables. [LLM-inferred]
recap_md:
- Expectation of a constant k is k.
- Expectation is linear: constants factor out and sums split.
- Expectation of product factors if variables are independent.

title: **Mean, variance, and covariance**
one_liner: Mean, variance, and covariance summarize properties of distributions: mean is the center, variance measures spread, and covariance measures how two variables co-vary.
content:
For some choices of function f[•], the expectation is given a special name. These quantities are often used to summarize the properties of complex distributions. For example, when f[x] = x, the resulting expectation E[x] is termed the mean, µ. It is a measure of the center of a distribution. Similarly, the expected squared deviation from the mean E[(x −µ)2] is termed the variance, σ2. This is a measure of the spread of the distribution. The standard deviation σ is the positive square root of the variance. It also measures the spread of the distribution but has the merit that it is expressed in the same units as the variable x.

As the name suggests, the covariance E[(x −µx)(y −µy)] of two variables x and y measures the degree to which they co-vary. Here µx and µy represent the mean of the variables x and y, respectively. The covariance will be large when the variance of both variables is large and when the value of x tends to increase when the value of y increases. If two variables are independent, then their covariance is zero. However, a covariance of zero does not imply independence. For example, consider a distribution Pr(x, y) where the probability is uniformly distributed on a circle of radius one centered on the origin of the x, y plane. There is no tendency on average for x to increase when y increases or vice-versa. However, knowing the value of x = 0 tells us that y has an equal chance of taking the values ±1, so the variables cannot be independent.

The covariances of multiple random variables stored in a column vector x ∈RD can be represented by the D×D covariance matrix E[(x −µx)(x −µx)T ], where the vector µx contains the means E[x]. The element at position (i, j) of this matrix represents the covariance between variables xi and xj.
motivation_md: Mean, variance, and covariance provide essential summaries of distributions, helping us understand central tendency, spread, and relationships between variables, which are fundamental for statistical analysis and machine learning.
recap_md:
- Mean (µ) is the expectation E[x], representing the center of a distribution.
- Variance (σ²) is the expected squared deviation from the mean, measuring spread.
- Covariance measures how two variables co-vary; zero covariance implies no linear relationship but not necessarily independence.

title: **Variance identity**
one_liner: The variance can be expressed as $E[(x - \mu)^2] = E[x^2] - (E[x])^2$.
content:
The rules of expectation (appendix C.2.1) can be used to prove the following identity that allows us to write the variance in a different form:

\[
E\big((x - \mu)^2\big) = E(x^2) - E(x)^2.
\]

Proof:

\[
\begin{aligned}
E\big((x - \mu)^2\big) &= E\big(x^2 - 2\mu x + \mu^2\big) \\
&= E(x^2) - E(2\mu x) + E(\mu^2) \\
&= E(x^2) - 2\mu \cdot E(x) + \mu^2 \\
&= E(x^2) - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2 \\
&= E(x^2) - \mu^2 \\
&= E(x^2) - E(x)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
motivation_md: This identity provides a convenient way to compute variance using expectations of x and x squared, simplifying variance calculations in practice.
recap_md:
- Variance can be rewritten as $E[(x - \mu)^2] = E[x^2] - (E[x])^2$.
- The proof uses linearity of expectation and properties of constants.
- This form is often easier to compute in practice.

title: **Standardization**
one_liner: Standardization sets a variable's mean to zero and variance to one via $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$.
content:
Setting the mean of a random variable to zero and the variance to one is known as standardization. This is achieved using the transformation:

\[
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma},
\]

where \(\mu\) is the mean of \(x\) and \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation.

Proof:

The mean of the new distribution over \(z\) is given by:

\[
E[z] = E\left[\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right] = \frac{1}{\sigma} E(x - \mu) = \frac{1}{\sigma} (\mu - \mu) = 0,
\]

where the four rules for manipulating expectations are used. The variance of the new distribution is given by:

\[
E\big((z - \mu_z)^2\big) = E\big((z - E[z])^2\big) = E(z^2) = E\left[\left(\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\right] = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} E[(x - \mu)^2] = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \sigma^2 = 1.
\]

By a similar argument, we can take a standardized variable \(z\) with mean zero and unit variance and convert it to a variable \(x\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) using:

\[
x = \mu + \sigma z.
\]

In the multivariate case, we can standardize a variable \(x\) with mean \(\mu\) and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) using:

\[
z = \Sigma^{-1/2}(x - \mu).
\]

The result will have a mean \(E[z] = 0\) and an identity covariance matrix \(E[(z - E[z])(z - E[z])^T] = I\). To reverse this process, we use:

\[
x = \mu + \Sigma^{1/2} z.
\]
motivation_md: Standardization transforms variables to have mean zero and variance one, simplifying analysis and comparison across variables with different scales or units.
recap_md:
- Standardization transforms $x$ to $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ with mean zero and variance one.
- The inverse transform is $x = \mu + \sigma z$.
- Multivariate standardization uses $z = \Sigma^{-1/2}(x - \mu)$ to get zero mean and identity covariance.

title: **Normal probability distribution**
one_liner: The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the most common distribution in machine learning.
content: Probability distributions used in this book include the Bernoulli distribution (figure 5.6), categorical distribution (figure 5.9), Poisson distribution (figure 5.15), von Mises distribution (figure 5.13), and mixture of Gaussians (figures 5.14 and 17.1). However, the most common distribution in machine learning is the normal or Gaussian distribution.
motivation_md: The normal distribution is fundamental in machine learning due to its mathematical properties and prevalence in modeling real-world data.
recap_md:
- The normal distribution is the most common distribution in machine learning.
- Other distributions include Bernoulli, categorical, Poisson, von Mises, and mixtures of Gaussians.
- The normal distribution is also called the Gaussian distribution.

title: **Univariate normal distribution**
one_liner: A univariate normal distribution over scalar $x$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ and is defined by $\Pr(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$.
content:
A univariate normal distribution (figure 5.3) over scalar variable \(x\) has two parameters, the mean \(\mu\) and the variance \(\sigma^2\), and is defined as:

\[
\Pr(x) = \text{Norm}_x[\mu, \sigma^2] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2}\right).
\]

Unsurprisingly, the mean \(E[x]\) of a normally distributed variable is given by the mean parameter \(\mu\) and the variance \(E[(x - E[x])^2]\) by the variance parameter \(\sigma^2\). When the mean is zero and the variance is one, we refer to this as a standard normal distribution.

The shape of the normal distribution can be inferred from the following argument. The term \(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\) is a quadratic function that falls away from zero when \(x = \mu\) at a rate that increases when \(\sigma\) becomes smaller. When we pass this through the exponential function (figure B.1), we get a bell-shaped curve, which has a value of one at \(x = \mu\) and falls away to either side. Dividing by the constant \(\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}\) ensures that the function integrates to one and is a valid distribution.

It follows from this argument that the mean \(\mu\) controls the position of the center of the bell curve, and the square root \(\sigma\) of the variance (the standard deviation) controls the width of the bell curve.
motivation_md: The univariate normal distribution models continuous data with parameters for center and spread, forming the basis for many statistical methods and machine learning models.
recap_md:
- The univariate normal distribution is defined by mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$.
- Its PDF is $\Pr(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$.
- Mean controls center; standard deviation controls width of the bell curve.

title: **Multivariate normal distribution**
one_liner: The multivariate normal distribution generalizes the normal distribution to vector variables with mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$.
content:
The multivariate normal distribution generalizes the normal distribution to describe the probability over a vector quantity \(x\) of length \(D\). It is defined by a \(D \times 1\) mean vector \(\mu\) and a symmetric positive definite \(D \times D\) covariance matrix \(\Sigma\):

\[
\text{Norm}_x[\mu, \Sigma] = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2} |\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)}{2}\right).
\]

The interpretation is similar to the univariate case. The quadratic term \(-\frac{(x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)}{2}\) returns a scalar that decreases as \(x\) grows further from the mean \(\mu\), at a rate that depends on the matrix \(\Sigma\). This is turned into a bell-curve shape by the exponential, and dividing by \((2\pi)^{D/2} |\Sigma|^{1/2}\) ensures that the distribution integrates to one.

The covariance matrix can take spherical, diagonal, and full forms:

\[
\Sigma_{\text{spher}} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma^2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\Sigma_{\text{diag}} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_2^2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\Sigma_{\text{full}} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{11}^2 & \sigma_{12}^2 \\ \sigma_{21}^2 & \sigma_{22}^2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
motivation_md: The multivariate normal distribution models vector-valued data with correlations, extending the univariate normal to multiple dimensions for complex data analysis.
recap_md:
- The multivariate normal distribution is parameterized by mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$.
- Its PDF involves a quadratic form $(x - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)$ inside an exponential.
- Covariance matrix forms include spherical, diagonal, and full.

title: Covariance matrix
one_liner: The covariance matrix can take spherical, diagonal, and full forms.
content:
The covariance matrix can take spherical, diagonal, and full forms:

\[
\Sigma_{\text{spher}} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma^2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\Sigma_{\text{diag}} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_2^2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\Sigma_{\text{full}} = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{11}^2 & \sigma_{12}^2 \\ \sigma_{21}^2 & \sigma_{22}^2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
motivation_md: Different covariance matrix forms allow modeling different correlation structures and complexity levels in multivariate distributions.
recap_md:
- Spherical covariance matrix has equal variances on the diagonal and zeros off-diagonal.
- Diagonal covariance matrix has different variances on the diagonal and zeros off-diagonal.
- Full covariance matrix includes variances and covariances with nonzero off-diagonal elements.
